Manure pits, manholes, vegetable cellars, and similar places accumulate toxic gases and lack oxygen; a person can collapse in seconds. Before entering, you must ventilate, ensure gas measurements meet requirements, use proper protection, and have a supervisor outside at all times; do not enter if even one requirement is missing. Simply opening the cover and waiting a while does not confirm it is safe inside. If you see someone collapse, do not follow them down; call 119 and 120.

Ventilation, gas measurement, protection, and supervision all require spending money on equipment and hiring people, and they also take time. For cleaning household manure pits, prioritize hiring trained teams with equipment; ask local service providers for costs. Do not go down yourself if conditions are not met. The difficulty is restraining yourself from jumping in when someone collapses inside.

"Confined spaces" are enclosed or partially enclosed areas not intended for continuous occupancy, such as manure pits, manholes, sewage tanks, underground vaults, and storage tanks. The Ministry of Emergency Management (China) analyzed relatively large accidents in confined spaces in industrial and commercial enterprises since 2013. Poisoning and suffocation accounted for 96.8% of accidents and 96.9% of deaths. The main culprits were hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide. Accidents involving poor protection and blind rescue attempts accounted for 87.4% of cases and 86.8% of deaths. The 2020 safety manual from the Ministry of Emergency Management (China) states that nearly 80% of accidents had increased casualties due to blind rescue attempts. Among those who died in confined spaces, over 50% were rescuers. In 2018, the Office of the State Council Safety Committee (China) reported 8 accidents. In all 8 cases, only 1 person was initially in danger; due to blind rescue, each accident eventually resulted in 3 to 4 deaths. In 2019, a paper mill in Dongguan was cleaning a sewage tank when 3 people inhaled hydrogen sulfide and fainted. 6 people went down one after another to rescue them, and ultimately 7 people died. In 2020, at a flour product factory in Jiaozuo, a worker fell into a raw material tank in a fermentation workshop. Others attempted a blind rescue, and a total of 6 people died. The US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health investigated 70 confined space fatalities between 1983 and 1993, totaling 109 deaths. Among them, 39 people (36%) entered to rescue others. Of these 39, only 4 were professional rescuers like police or firefighters. A 1986 warning from the institute stated that about 60% of victims are would-be rescuers. The manual says hydrogen sulfide smells like rotten eggs, but at high concentrations, the nose can no longer detect it. Concentrations exceeding 1,000 mg per cubic meter can kill a person in seconds. High concentrations of carbon dioxide can cause a person to lose consciousness and collapse in seconds. The manual requires: if the scene does not allow for self-rescue, call 119 and 120 immediately, "absolutely no rescue at all costs is allowed." Pulling someone out from the outside requires the victim to be wearing a full-body harness with a lifeline connected to the outside. Order No. 13 of the Ministry of Emergency Management (China) requires industrial and commercial enterprises to "ventilate first, measure gas second, then work." Enterprises must be equipped with gas measurement, ventilation, protection, and rescue equipment according to risk levels, with a supervisor present throughout. Continuous ventilation and gas measurement must also be performed during work; entry is prohibited if safety conditions are not met. Supervisors must prevent blind rescue attempts before safety measures are in place. The Anshun City Health Bureau notes: vegetable cellars closed for a long time will have vegetables consuming oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide. Before entering, the ventilation hole must be opened to allow thorough airing. Note that this ventilation does not replace gas measurement, protection, and supervision (China / USA).
If you are over 45, live in an area with high rates of stomach or esophageal cancer, have a family history, or test positive for H. pylori, get a screening gastroscopy
A

For people over 45 in high-risk groups for stomach or esophageal cancer, having a gastroscopy reduces the chance of dying from these two cancers by about half. However, people who proactively seek check-ups are already more health-conscious, so this figure may be exaggerated. Using the strictest comparison, esophageal cancer mortality was only about two-tenths lower, which is within the margin of error. Guidelines do not recommend screening for those not in high-risk groups.

A gastroscopy usually costs a few hundred yuan; a painless gastroscopy (with anesthesia) costs an additional few hundred yuan, with prices varying by location. You must fast before going, and the process takes half a day. If choosing painless gastroscopy, someone must accompany you. The uncomfortable part is the few minutes the tube passes through the throat.

The 2024 plan from the National Health Commission (China) defines high-risk groups as follows. First, one must be at least 45 years old and meet one of the following criteria. One: living in a county with high rates of stomach or esophageal cancer. Stomach cancer is defined as an age-standardized incidence rate exceeding 20 cases per 100,000 people; esophageal cancer is over 15 cases. Two: parents, children, or siblings have had these types of cancer. Three: testing positive for H. pylori (Helicobacter pylori); this only applies to stomach cancer. Four: heavy smoking, heavy drinking, high salt intake, or a preference for pickled foods; for esophageal cancer, a preference for hot food is added. Five: having had diseases such as atrophic gastritis, gastric ulcers, gastric polyps, Barrett's esophagus, or reflux esophagitis. Screening age is usually 45 to 74, with gastroscopy prioritized, generally performed once every 5 years. The 2022 national guidelines state clearly that stomach cancer screening is not recommended for those outside high-risk groups. A study in 6 high-prevalence areas in China followed about 637,500 people aged 40 to 69. Comparing those who had one gastroscopy with those not invited, the risk of dying from upper gastrointestinal cancer was about 57% lower (Original RR = 0.43, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.47). The incidence of upper gastrointestinal cancer was about 23% lower (RR = 0.77). Among those invited, only 33.53% actually went. Including everyone invited, mortality was about 31% lower (RR = 0.69, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.72). Another study in villages with high esophageal cancer rates, without random assignment, followed participants for 10 years. Cumulative mortality from esophageal squamous cell carcinoma was 3.35% in the screening group and 5.05% in the control group. In South Korea's national screening program, those who had a gastroscopy were about 47% less likely to die from stomach cancer (Original OR = 0.53, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.56). No difference was found for those who had an upper GI series X-ray (OR = 0.98). More frequent endoscopies led to lower risk. Pooling 10 studies in Asia, those who had a gastroscopy had about 40% lower stomach cancer mortality (Original RR = 0.60, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.73). The number of stomach cancer cases did not change. In northern China, a cluster-randomized trial by village enrolled 33,800 people aged 45 to 69 and followed them for 9 years. Those assigned to the screening group had about 18% lower esophageal cancer mortality (HR = 0.82, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.26), which was within the margin of error. The incidence rate was about 19% lower (HR = 0.81, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.09), also not statistically significant. In 2023, a meta-analysis adjusted for the "healthy volunteer bias." Those who actually underwent gastroscopy had about 48% lower stomach cancer mortality (RR = 0.52, CI 0.39 to 0.79). When calculated for the entire screening program, it was only RR = 0.94 (CI 0.71 to 1.28), showing no effect (China / South Korea / Asia)

Eat soaked wood ear mushrooms and silver ear mushrooms within the same meal and do not leave them overnight; eat fresh rice noodles, rice rolls, and other fresh rice products on the day of purchase; do not make fermented corn flour at home
B

Wood ear mushrooms and silver ear mushrooms soaked for too long, fresh rice products kept for too long, and home-fermented corn flour can all produce a toxin called bongkrekic acid. Boiling does not destroy it, and there is no antidote. Over eleven years, among reported poisoning cases of this type nationwide (China), about three-tenths of those who fell ill died.

Costs no money. Soak only as much wood ear or silver ear mushrooms as you will eat and discard the rest. Buy only enough fresh rice products to finish in one day. The difficulty is being reluctant to throw away excess soaked mushrooms, and some families are accustomed to making home-fermented corn flour sour soup.

In the national foodborne disease outbreak surveillance system (China), a total of 19 bongkrekic acid poisoning outbreaks were reported between 2010 and 2020. 146 people fell ill and 43 died, a fatality rate of 29.5% (meaning 29.5% of those who fell ill died). Broken down by food: home-fermented corn flour products caused 9 outbreaks and 33 deaths. Fresh rice products caused 5 outbreaks and 7 deaths. Wood ear mushrooms caused 3 outbreaks, with 5 illnesses and 3 deaths. In 2020, 143 people nationwide died from food poisoning, with bongkrekic acid accounting for 12 deaths. It was preceded by poisonous mushrooms (80 deaths) and methanol (14 deaths). A notice from the Beijing Municipal Administration for Market Regulation states clearly: bongkrekic acid cannot be destroyed by boiling at 100 °C or pressure cooking, and there is currently no specific antidote. Since 2018, Guangdong has required fresh rice products to be in small, sealed packages with clear expiration dates. Comparing before and after, the number of cases per year across the province dropped from an average of 6.25 to 0.5
Quit smoking as soon as possible
A

In US studies, smokers live on average more than ten years shorter than non-smokers. Quitting before age 40 eliminates about nine-tenths of the mortality risk caused by continued smoking. The earlier you quit, the more you regain. If you smoke after a bone fracture, the chance of the bone not healing is about 2.3 times higher than for non-smokers, so do not smoke while the bone has not healed.

Costs no money; in fact, it saves money. A pack of cigarettes a day costs about ⟦20~30⟧; quitting keeps this money. The difficulty is enduring the withdrawal phase, which usually takes a few weeks to a few months.

A US study following a group of people (observational, not randomized) found: current smokers have an expected lifespan more than 10 years shorter than never-smokers. Quitting before age 40 can eliminate about 90% of the mortality risk from continued smoking. Quitting at age 25–34 adds about 10 years of life, at 35–44 about 9 years, and at 45–54 about 6 years (original report based on years of life). A similar study in China: in the 2010s, urban male smokers had a mortality risk 1.65 times that of non-smokers (RR = 1.65), and in rural areas, it was 1.22 times. Actively quitting for 10 years almost eliminates the risk from smoking. The same applies after fractures. Pooling 19 observational studies, smokers are about 2.3 times more likely to have non-union (bone not healing) than non-smokers (OR = 2.32, 95% CI 1.76 to 3.06, adjusted for other factors). Similar increases were seen for tibial fractures and open fractures. In a randomized trial in Sweden, 50 people participating in a 6-week smoking cessation program after emergency fracture surgery had a 20% rate of at least one postoperative complication. For 55 people who did not participate, it was 38%. For scheduled surgeries, starting cessation 4 to 8 weeks before surgery with weekly counseling and nicotine replacement products reduced postoperative complications by about 58% (RR = 0.42, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.65, 2 trials, 210 people).
Do not smoke indoors or in cars, and do not let guests smoke in your home
A

In 2004, about 600,000 people worldwide died from inhaling other people's smoke, nearly three-tenths of whom were children. People exposed to secondhand smoke have a risk of hypertension, heart disease, and stroke that is about three-tenths higher. Inhaling it indoors is more harmful than inhaling it outdoors.
Costs no money and takes no time. The difficulty is speaking up and telling family members and guests not to smoke indoors.

In 2004, 603,000 people worldwide died from secondhand smoke, about 1.0% of global deaths, of which 28% were children. Pooling 57 studies: people exposed to secondhand smoke are about 1.28 times more likely to have hypertension than those not exposed (odds ratio). For heart disease, it is 1.39 times; for myocardial infarction, 1.50 times; and for stroke, 1.36 times. Exposure to secondhand smoke indoors carries a higher risk than exposure outdoors
Don't just rely on willpower to quit smoking; get support medication first: using varenicline more than doubles the success rate
A

Varenicline users have a successful quit rate more than twice that of placebo users. Users of nicotine replacement products such as patches or gum have a success rate about five-tenths higher than those not using medication. Using patches and gum simultaneously increases the rate by more than another two-tenths.

Nicotine patches and gum are over-the-counter drugs (in China), available directly at pharmacy counters. A course of 8 to 12 weeks costs from a few hundred to over ⟦1000⟧. Varenicline and bupropion are prescription drugs; you must go to a smoking cessation clinic or respiratory department for a doctor's prescription. This amount is nearly equal to the money saved by not buying cigarettes during the same period.

Pooling 41 randomized trials involving 17,395 people, the varenicline group had a successful quit rate 2.32 times that of the placebo group (RR = 2.32, 95% CI 2.15 to 2.51; high-certainty evidence). Varenicline was also superior to bupropion (RR = 1.36, about 36% higher) and superior to using a single type of nicotine replacement product (RR = 1.25, about 25% higher). Comparing nicotine replacement products with no medication: 133 trials, 64,640 people, the success rate was about 55% higher (RR = 1.55, 95% CI 1.49 to 1.61). Patches plus a fast-acting form (gum, lozenge) were about 27% higher than using a single type (RR = 1.27, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.37, 16 trials, 12,169 people, high-certainty evidence). Side effects: compared to placebo, varenicline users experienced nausea about 2.6 times more often (RR = 2.61), insomnia about 37% more often (RR = 1.37), and vivid dreams were also common. The review stated the most common side effect is nausea, mostly mild to moderate, which usually subsides gradually. The instruction manual for one type of nicotine patch in the US specifies a three-step dose reduction: apply a 21 mg patch for 6 weeks, then a 14 mg patch for 2 weeks, and finally a 7 mg patch for 2 weeks, then stop.
Pick a quit date and quit cold turkey on that day; do not taper off beforehand
A

Many people plan to smoke a few fewer cigarettes each day, gradually reducing to zero. However, by the sixth month, among those who chose a date and quit cold turkey, 22% had not relapsed, while only 15.5% of those who tapered off remained smoke-free. Therefore, pick a day and quit completely on that day.
No cost. Just pick a day on the calendar and inform family members and colleagues in advance.

697 smokers in the UK were randomly assigned to two groups. One group quit cold turkey on the quit day, while the other group reduced their cigarette intake by 75% in the two weeks prior to the quit day. Both groups received behavioral support from nurses and used nicotine replacement products before and after the quit day. At week 4, the cold turkey group had a non-relapse rate of 49.0% (95% CI 43.8 to 54.2), while the tapering group was 39.2% (34.0 to 44.4), relative risk ratio 0.80 (0.66 to 0.93). By month 6, the cold turkey group was 22.0% (18.0 to 26.6) and the tapering group was 15.5% (12.0 to 19.7), relative risk ratio 0.71 (0.46 to 0.91). Even among those who originally preferred tapering, the success rate at week 4 was lower than those who preferred quitting cold turkey (38.3% vs 52.2%).
Go to a smoking cessation clinic, or call 12320 to ask if there are cessation services in your area
A

Medication and "having someone check in on you periodically" are two different things; combining them is more effective. People who use medication while being closely followed have a successful quit rate nearly double that of those who only receive brief advice. Phone calls also count: proactive callbacks from a smoking cessation hotline result in a success rate between two-and-a-half tenths and nearly four-tenths higher.

A single registration fee ranges from a few to several dozen yuan. Behavioral support usually consists of 4 to 8 sessions, each lasting half an hour to an hour, totaling mostly under 5 hours. Calling the hotline is free.

Pooling 52 trials involving 19,488 people, the group receiving medication plus behavioral support had a successful quit rate 1.83 times that of the usual care or brief advice group (RR = 1.83, 95% CI 1.68 to 1.98; high-quality evidence). In 43 trials recruiting participants at healthcare facilities, it was 1.97 times (1.79 to 2.18). Regarding telephone counseling specifically: among those who called a cessation hotline themselves, those who received proactive callbacks were about 38% more successful than those who only received materials or spoke once (RR = 1.38, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.61, 14 trials, 32,484 people); for those who did not call themselves but were proactively counseled by the research team via phone, the rate was about 25% higher (RR = 1.25, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.35, 65 trials, 41,233 people). Both are moderate-certainty evidence.
Only consider e-cigarettes if you have failed to quit; those who do not smoke should never touch them
A

Switching from combustible cigarettes to nicotine-containing e-cigarettes results in about six-tenths more people successfully quitting compared to using nicotine replacement therapy; this conclusion is very reliable. However, long-term safety data is insufficient, and they cannot be considered harmless. These trials were all conducted on people who wanted to quit smoking; those who do not smoke should not touch them.

The device plus e-liquid pods cost several dozen to several hundred yuan per month. In China, only tobacco-flavored types can be purchased, and only at stores with a tobacco monopoly retail license (China).

A continuously updated review included 80 randomized trials with 29,861 people. Nicotine e-cigarettes compared to nicotine replacement therapy showed a successful quit rate about 61% higher (RR = 1.61, 95% CI 1.23 to 2.12; high-certainty evidence, 11 trials, 4,114 people). In absolute numbers, about 4 more people out of 100 successfully quit (an additional 1 to 7 people). The rate of serious adverse events was nearly the same in both groups (risk difference 0.01, 95% CI −0.01 to 0.02, moderate-certainty evidence). Compared to behavioral support alone or no support, the rate was about 75% higher (RR = 1.75, 95% CI 1.39 to 2.20, low-certainty evidence).
Do not drink sugar-sweetened beverages; switching to sugar-free versions is not a solution yet
A

In a US study, people who drank two or more servings of soft drinks per day had a probability of death during the same period about two-tenths higher than those who almost never drank them. One to two servings per day was also more than one-tenth higher. Switching to sugar-free versions showed no benefit: people who drank two or more cups of artificially sweetened beverages per day were about one-quarter higher.
No money or time required. Switching to plain water or unsweetened tea even saves money. The difficulty lies in breaking the habit of drinking sweet beverages, including sugar-free ones.

Two large observational studies in the US followed a group of people. These two studies were observational, not randomized, involving approximately 118,000 people and 36,000 deaths. People who drank 2 or more servings per day had a risk of death about 21% higher than those who drank less than 1 serving per month (HR = 1.21). 1–2 servings per day was about 14% higher (HR = 1.14). The EPIC follow-up study in Europe was also observational, involving 450,000 people in 10 countries. Comparing people who drank 2 or more cups per day with those who drank less than 1 cup per month: sugar-sweetened beverages were about 8% higher (HR = 1.08, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.16). Artificially sweetened beverages (sugar-free types) were about 26% higher (HR = 1.26, 1.16 to 1.35). Pooling all types of soft drinks, the risk was about 17% higher (HR = 1.17, 1.11 to 1.22).
Do not chew betel nut
A

Betel nut chewers have a probability of death during the same period about two-tenths higher than non-chewers. The risk of diabetes and metabolic syndrome is about five-tenths higher. The risks of oral cancer and esophageal cancer must be calculated separately.
No money or time required, and it saves money on buying betel nuts. The difficulty lies in breaking the chewing habit.

Pooling 17 studies in Asia involving 388,000 people, betel nut chewers had a risk of death about 21% higher than non-chewers (relative risk 1.21, P = 0.02). The mortality portion specifically was calculated based on 179,600 of those individuals. The risk of developing diabetes was about 47% higher (1.47). The risk of metabolic syndrome was about 51% higher (1.51). Betel nut itself is a known risk factor for oral and esophageal cancer. Oral cancer: pooling 50 studies in the Indian subcontinent, chewing betel nut without tobacco carried a risk of oral and oropharyngeal cancer about 2.56 times that of non-chewers (95% CI 2.00 to 3.28). Types with added tobacco were about 7.74 times (5.38 to 11.13). In Taiwan, chewing betel nut without tobacco was about 10.98 times (4.86 to 24.84). In India and Taiwan, the risk increased with higher daily consumption and more years of chewing. Esophageal cancer: pooling 12 studies in Asia, betel nut chewers had a risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma about 3.05 times that of non-chewers (2.41 to 3.87). Chewing betel nut while smoking was about 6.79 times (4.71 to 9.79). After quitting: pooling 13 studies, those who quit betel nut with tobacco had a risk of head and neck cancer about 34% lower than current chewers (RR = 0.66, 0.54 to 0.81). Quitting tobacco-free types was about 27% lower (RR = 0.73, 0.56 to 0.95). Quitting for more than 20 years was about 63% lower (RR = 0.37, 0.22 to 0.61).
Switch household table salt to low-sodium salt (potassium salt)
A

In rural China, for individuals who have had a stroke or are over 60 with hypertension, switching household salt to low-sodium salt and following them for nearly five years resulted in a probability of death about 12% lower and stroke about 14% lower.
Each pack is a few yuan more expensive than regular salt. It takes no extra time to switch while shopping. The taste is almost identical.

A randomized trial conducted in rural China with 20,995 people, all of whom had a history of stroke or were over 60 with hypertension, followed for 4.74 years. Results: the low-sodium salt group compared to the regular salt group had a risk of death about 12% lower (RR = 0.88). Stroke was about 14% lower (RR = 0.86). Major cardiovascular events were about 13% lower (RR = 0.87). There was no statistically significant difference in hyperkalemia events between the two groups.
Brush your teeth thoroughly, clean between teeth once a day, and see a dentist if you lose teeth
B

In a Japanese study, people who used dental floss or interdental brushes had a probability of death during the same period about one-tenth lower. Elderly people who had lost all their teeth had a probability of death about nine-tenths higher. Those with fewer than 20 teeth were about twice as likely to die. Electric toothbrushes remove one to two-tenths more plaque than manual brushes, and gingivitis is also slightly milder, but the clinical significance of this difference is unclear.

Dental floss or interdental brushes cost several dozen yuan per year; professional cleaning costs one to two hundred yuan per visit. It takes an extra two to three minutes daily. The difficulty is making interdental cleaning a daily habit. If manual brushing is ineffective, you can switch to an electric toothbrush, costing several hundred yuan each, with brush heads needing periodic replacement.

A study in Japan of 9,676 people followed for 6 years found that those using interdental cleaning tools had a risk of death about 11% lower (hazard ratio 0.89). Those using tongue scrapers were about 23% lower (0.77). Additionally, pooling multiple studies of community-dwelling elderly: those with no remaining teeth were about 1.87 times more likely to die (odds ratio, 95% CI 1.35 to 2.59). Those with fewer than 20 teeth were about 2.04 times more likely (1.67 to 2.49). Comparing electric to manual toothbrushes: pooling 51 randomized trials, using an electric toothbrush for 1 to 3 months resulted in about 11% less plaque, and over 3 months, about 21% less. Gingivitis was milder by about 6% and 11% respectively. The review authors stated it is unclear how important these differences are for overall health.
Walk 7,000–8,000 steps daily, or accumulate 150–300 minutes of brisk walking per week
A

People who walk about 7,800 steps daily have a probability of death during the same period about four-and-a-half tenths lower than those who only walk 3,500 steps. Calculating by time yields similar results: 150–300 minutes of brisk walking per week is about three-tenths lower than being sedentary. Benefits plateau at a certain level; for those over 60, 6,000–8,000 steps is sufficient. Either counting method works; achieving one is enough.

No cost. Based on step count, it takes 60–90 minutes daily, which can be divided between commuting and shopping. Based on exercise time, it takes 20–45 minutes daily. The difficulty is long-term consistency.

Pooling 15 observational cohort studies involving 47,471 people and 3,013 deaths. Participants were divided into four levels based on daily steps; the lowest level had a median of 3,553 steps/day. The other three levels had medians of 5,801, 7,842, and 10,901 steps/day. The risk of death for these three levels was lower than the lowest level by about 40%, 45%, and 53% respectively (HR = 0.60; 0.55; 0.47). For those over 60, benefits plateaued after 6,000–8,000 steps. For those under 60, benefits plateaued after 8,000–10,000 steps. Another meta-analysis showed effects starting at about 3,867 steps/day. Thereafter, every additional 1,000 steps per day reduced the risk of death by about 15%. Based on exercise time: a synthesis of observational studies found that people with an activity volume 1–2 times the minimum guideline level had a risk of death about 31% lower than sedentary individuals (HR = 0.69). This volume is 7.5–15 MET-hours/week, approximately 150–300 minutes of brisk walking/week. Those who did not reach the minimum were still about 20% lower (HR = 0.80). Those reaching 3–5 times the minimum were about 39% lower (HR = 0.61), which is the peak reduction. Further increases did not lower risk more, but were not harmful (over 10 times was HR = 0.69). Another meta-analysis using accelerometers found that the quarter of people with the most moderate-to-vigorous activity had a risk of death about 48% lower than the quarter with the least (HR = 0.52). Accelerometers are wearable devices that measure actual activity. This synthesis included 8 studies, 36,383 people, mean age 62.6, median follow-up 5.8 years. The authors recalculated after excluding those who died in the first two years; results were nearly unchanged, though they noted that reverse causality bias ("moving less because of illness") might still exist.

Get regular blood lipid tests as an adult: every 2 to 5 years before age 40, and annually from age 40; if you have hypertension or high lipids, take medication regularly as prescribed and do not stop on your own
A

For every 10 mmHg reduction in systolic blood pressure (the top number), the probability of death decreases by about 13% and stroke by about 27%. For every 1 unit reduction in LDL cholesterol by statins, the probability of death decreases by about one-tenth. People who take medication on time have a probability of death between three-tenths and four-and-a-half tenths lower than those who often forget. Test blood lipids every 2 to 5 years before age 40, and annually from age 40.

Blood pressure medications and statins are part of centralized procurement (in China), costing a few to several dozen yuan per month. Taking them once a day takes very little time. The difficulty is that they must be taken indefinitely; you cannot stop just because you feel fine. Blood lipid tests require a blood draw. People aged 65 and over are entitled to one free health check-up per year (in China), which includes blood lipid testing; see Chapter 6, Section 18 (Common Health Check-up Package).

Pooling multiple randomized trials: every 10 mmHg reduction in systolic blood pressure was associated with a risk of death about 13% lower (RR = 0.87). Systolic blood pressure is the top number. Major cardiovascular events were about 20% lower (RR = 0.80). Stroke was about 27% lower (RR = 0.73). Heart failure was about 28% lower (RR = 0.72). Using statins to lower low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol: every 1.0 mmol/L reduction in LDL was associated with a risk of death about 10% lower (RR = 0.90). At the same reduction level, major vascular events were about 22% lower (RR = 0.78). Additionally, pooling multiple observational studies: people with medication adherence of 80% or higher had a lower risk of death than those who often forgot. For statins, it was about 45% lower (RR = 0.55). For blood pressure medication, it was about 29% lower (RR = 0.71). Regarding the frequency of blood lipid testing, according to the Healthy China Action recommendations: individuals under 40 with normal lipids should be tested every 2 to 5 years. Individuals aged 40 and over should be tested at least once a year. Those at high risk for cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases should be tested every 6 months. The 2023 edition of the Chinese Lipid Management Guidelines states the same for the age 40 threshold, while for high-risk individuals, it changes to testing based on individual needs.
Sleep about 7 hours every night at a fixed time
A

People who regularly sleep less than 7 hours have a probability of death during the same period about one-tenth higher. The more irregular the schedule, the higher the risk. Compared to the group with the most irregular schedules, others are between two-tenths to nearly five-tenths lower. Whether the schedule is regular or not predicts mortality risk more clearly than how long one sleeps.
Free. Time must be set aside for sleep; for most people, this means swapping phone-scrolling time for sleep. The difficulty lies in fixing the time for going to bed and waking up.

Meta-analysis of 16 follow-up studies, observational only, no grouping, 1.38 million people, 113,000 deaths. Short sleepers have a mortality risk about 12% higher (RR = 1.12). Long sleepers are about 30% higher (RR = 1.30). Another synthesis divided by sleep duration: the 7-hour level had the lowest risk. Below 7 hours, for every 1 hour less, the risk is about 6% higher (RR = 1.06). Above 7 hours, for every 1 hour more, it is about 13% higher (RR = 1.13). UK Biobank has wrist-worn accelerometer data from about 61,000 people, observational only, no grouping. People were divided into five levels based on sleep regularity. The four more regular levels had a mortality risk 20% to 48% lower than the most irregular level. Sleep regularity predicted mortality better than sleep duration. Another study on UK Biobank used wristwatches to measure sleep times of 51,562 people, during which 3,853 people developed cardiovascular disease. Social jetlag is the difference between the midpoint of sleep on workdays and weekends. People with social jetlag of 2 hours or more have a cardiovascular disease risk about 30% higher (HR = 1.30, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.54). This association persisted even in people who slept enough hours.
Regularly play racket sports such as tennis, badminton, or table tennis
A

People who frequently play tennis, badminton, or table tennis have a probability of death during the same period about half that of those who do not play, and cardiovascular mortality is about 56% lower. Swimmers are about 28% lower. Running and football showed no difference in this dataset.
Court fees are a few dozen yuan each time. About 2 hours per week. The difficulty is gathering enough people and securing a court, and going every week.

A follow-up study of 80,300 people in the UK compared people playing a specific sport with those who did not. Racket sport players had a mortality risk about 47% lower (Hazard Ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.69). Cardiovascular mortality was about 56% lower (0.44, 0.24 to 0.83). Racket sports here include tennis, badminton, and table tennis. For swimmers, these two figures were 0.72 and 0.59 respectively; for aerobics, 0.73 and 0.64; for cycling, 0.85. Running and football showed no statistically significant differences.
Accumulate small bursts of exertion such as climbing stairs or walking fast to catch up with work for four to five minutes a day
A

For an average person who does not exercise at all, just having three bursts of exertion for one or two minutes a day makes the probability of death during the same period about four-tenths lower than someone with none, and cardiovascular mortality nearly half as low. Exertion here refers to tasks like climbing stairs or walking briskly to stay on schedule.
Free, and no need to squeeze in extra exercise time. The difficulty is remembering to take the stairs and walk a bit faster instead of choosing convenience.

UK Biobank conducted a study on 25,200 average people who did not engage in dedicated exercise. Followed for an average of 6.9 years, during which 852 people passed away. Some people had 3 bouts of vigorous incidental physical activity per day, each lasting 1–2 minutes. Compared to those with none, their risk of mortality and cancer mortality decreased by 38%–40%. Cardiovascular mortality risk decreased by 48%–49%. People who accumulated 4.4 minutes of this activity per day had a mortality and cancer mortality risk reduction of 26%–30%. Cardiovascular mortality risk decreased by 32%–34%.
Do 30–60 minutes of strength training per week
A

People who do 30–60 minutes of strength training per week have a probability of death during the same period one to two-tenths lower than those who do not. Training more is not necessarily better. Doing strength training and aerobic exercise simultaneously is most effective.
Bodyweight squats and push-ups are free. Train 1–2 times per week, 20–30 minutes each time. The difficulty is fitting it into the weekly schedule.

Meta-analysis of multiple follow-up studies (observational only, no grouping): people who do strength training have a mortality risk 10%–17% lower than those who do not. It is not a case of the more the better; about 30–60 minutes per week yields the largest reduction, about 10%–20%, with more training providing no additional benefit. People who do both strength and aerobic training have a lower mortality risk than those who do neither.
Do not sit for too long at once; stand up and move around occasionally
A

People who sit the longest have a probability of death during the same period 2.6 times that of those who sit the least. Sitting for long uninterrupted bouts adds an independent risk factor. However, just 60–75 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per day almost entirely offsets the risk from prolonged sitting.
Free, and standing up a few times takes very little time. The difficulty is forgetting the time once seated; an alarm should be set.

A follow-up study in the US, observational only, no grouping, used actual accelerometer measurements. People were divided into quartiles based on total daily sitting time. The quartile that sat the most had a mortality risk 2.63 times that of the quartile that sat the least (HR = 2.63). Further divided into quartiles based on the duration of each sitting bout: the longest bouts were 1.96 times the shortest bouts (HR = 1.96). Therefore, total sitting time and the duration of each bout are independently associated. Another meta-analysis of studies on over one million people, observational only, no grouping: people who sit over 8 hours a day and are almost inactive have a mortality risk 1.59 times the rest (HR = 1.59). The "rest" group sat less than 4 hours a day and was most active. About 60–75 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per day can offset the risk of long sitting. The most active group, even if sitting over 8 hours a day, had an HR of only 1.04, which was not statistically significant.
Eat less processed meat (ham, bacon, sausages, canned meat)
A

People who eat the most ham, bacon, and sausages have a probability of death during the same period about two-tenths higher than those who eat the least. For every additional serving of processed meat per day, the probability also increases by two-tenths.
Free, even saves money, and takes no time. The difficulty is cutting back on foods you enjoy.

Meta-analysis of multiple follow-up studies (observational only, no grouping): the group eating the most processed meat had a mortality risk about 23% higher than the group eating the least (RR = 1.23). Red meat in general was about 29% higher (RR = 1.29). Unprocessed red meat was about 10% higher (RR = 1.10), but this item was not statistically significant. Another synthesis calculated by daily intake: every additional serving of processed meat per day increases mortality risk by about 23% (RR = 1.23). Every additional serving of red meat per day increases it by about 10% (RR = 1.10).
Drink little or no alcohol
A

Drinking more than 100 g of pure alcohol per week leads to earlier death as consumption increases. 100 g of pure alcohol is approximately 2.5 liters of beer. At age 40, people drinking 100–200 g per week live about half a year less; 200–350 g live one to two years less; over 350 g live four to five years less. In terms of overall health, the most worthwhile amount is zero.
Free, even saves money, and takes no time. The difficulty is the slight awkwardness when being offered a drink in social settings.

Meta-analysis of 83 prospective follow-up studies, observational only, no grouping, 600,000 current drinkers. The lowest point of mortality risk was at a level of no more than 100 g of pure alcohol per week. This amount is approximately 2.5 liters of 5% beer, or 300 mL of 40% spirits. At age 40, people drinking 100–200 g per week have an expected lifespan shortened by about 6 months. 200–350 g per week shortens it by 1–2 years. Over 350 g shortens it by 4–5 years. These three figures were reported in the original paper as years of life. The Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD 2016) aggregated all types of health loss; the consumption level with the lowest risk was 0 drinks/week. Another synthesis corrected for study design biases: people drinking 1.3–24 g per day compared to lifetime abstainers had a mortality risk about 7% lower (RR = 0.93), but this was not statistically significant. Drinking 45–64 g per day was about 19% higher (RR = 1.19). Drinking 65 g or more per day was about 35% higher (RR = 1.35).
If you drink alcohol every day and experience tremors or palpitations upon stopping, do not attempt to quit on your own
B

People who drink heavily every day and stop abruptly will experience withdrawal syndrome. Mild cases involve hand tremors, sweating, palpitations, and insomnia; severe cases involve seizures or delirium tremens, which are life-threatening emergencies. Norway followed over thirty thousand people; the group that had experienced delirium tremens had an 8% annual mortality rate thereafter. If you want to quit, go to a hospital first and state clearly how much you drink daily.
One registration fee for psychiatry or addiction medicine, from a few yuan to a few dozen yuan. Severe cases require several days of hospitalization.

A 2026 clinical review states: heavy long-term drinkers who abruptly stop or sharply reduce alcohol intake will develop withdrawal syndrome, manifesting as tremors, autonomic hyperactivity, anxiety, insomnia, sensory disturbances, seizures, and delirium tremens, which are "common and potentially life-threatening" in general medical practice. A Norwegian national registry cohort of 36,287 people diagnosed with alcohol use disorder, withdrawal state, or delirium tremens between 2009 and 2015: the annual mortality rate for the delirium tremens group was 8.0%, the withdrawal state group 5.0%, and the alcohol use disorder group 3.6%. The standardized mortality ratio for the delirium tremens group was 9.8 (95% CI 8.9 to 10.7), meaning the mortality risk was about 9.8 times that of the general population of the same age.
To reduce alcohol consumption, first count how much you drink in a week, then talk to a doctor for a few minutes
A

A doctor spending a few minutes reviewing your alcohol intake, explaining the risks, and helping you set goals results in an average reduction of 20 grams of pure alcohol per week one year later, approximately half a liter of beer. Longer conversations provide no additional benefit. For those who cannot stop, two types of medication have been proven effective abroad; for every 12 people treated, 1 additional person avoids returning to binge drinking.
Free. Counting drinks only requires writing one line a day. Asking a question during a regular check-up costs no extra money.

Meta-analysis of 34 randomized trials, 15,197 people: those receiving a brief intervention drank 20 grams less pure alcohol per week after one year than those receiving minimal or no intervention (95% CI 12 to 28 grams less; moderate-quality evidence). In these studies, participants' baseline intake averaged 244 grams per week. A brief intervention is advice or lifestyle counseling no more than 5 times, totaling under 60 minutes; longer talks add no benefit. Regarding medication: meta-analysis of 122 randomized trials, 22,803 people; for acamprosate, the Number Needed to Treat (NNT) is 12 (95% CI 8 to 26) for 1 additional person to remain abstinent; for oral naltrexone at 50 mg daily, the NNT is 12 (8 to 26) for 1 additional person to avoid heavy drinking.
Eat a small handful of nuts every day
A

People who frequently eat nuts have a probability of death during the same period about two-tenths lower than those who do not. Eating them once a week already shows a difference, about one-tenth lower. Eating a handful every day shows the most significant difference.
Eating 28 grams a day costs about two to three hundred yuan a year. It is a quick snack and takes no time.

Two follow-up studies in the US, 119,000 people, over 3 million person-years. Person-years is the number of people multiplied by the years each was followed. Compared to those who do not eat nuts: eating them less than once a week has a mortality risk about 7% lower (Hazard Ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.90 to 0.96). Once a week is about 11% lower (0.89, 0.86 to 0.93). 2–4 times a week is about 13% lower (0.87, 0.83 to 0.90). 5–6 times a week is about 15% lower (0.85, 0.79 to 0.91). 7 or more times a week is about 20% lower (0.80, 0.73 to 0.86)
Replace a portion of red meat with fish and poultry
A

Eating two additional servings of processed meat or red meat per week is associated with an approximately 3% higher probability of death during the same period. Switching to the same number of servings of fish or poultry showed no such increase. The effect of switching meat is relatively small in this chapter; it is something to do if convenient, no need to be stressed.
No money or time required. This is switching to a different type of meat, not buying more. The difficulty lies in slightly adjusting one's palate.

Pooled analysis of 6 prospective studies in the US, nearly 30,000 people. Each additional two servings of processed meat per week was associated with an approximately 3% higher risk of death (hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.05). Each additional two servings of unprocessed red meat per week was also approximately 3% higher (1.03, 1.01 to 1.05). Switching that same amount to poultry resulted in 0.99 (0.97 to 1.02); switching to fish was 0.99 (0.97 to 1.01). Neither of these two items showed a statistically significant difference.
Replace a portion of white rice and refined flour with whole grains
A

People who eat an additional 90 g of whole grains per day have an approximately 17% lower probability of death during the same period. 90 g is roughly three servings. Reductions continue up to about 200 g per day.
Brown rice, oats, and whole-wheat noodles are slightly more expensive than white rice and refined flour, but require no extra time. The difficulty is getting used to the coarse texture when eating.

Meta-analysis of multiple prospective studies (observational only, no group assignment): each additional 90 g of whole grains per day was associated with an approximately 17% lower risk of death (RR = 0.83). 90 g is approximately 3 servings. This benefit extends up to the level of 210–225 g per day. In another synthesis, each additional 1 serving per day was associated with an approximately 8% lower risk (RR = 0.92).
Drink tea three or more times per week
A

Habitual tea drinkers have an approximately 15% lower probability of death during the same period. Calculated from age 50, they live an average of 1.26 years longer and have 1.41 more years free of cardiovascular disease.
A few dozen to a few hundred yuan per year. Brewing a pot takes a few minutes, costing almost no time.

A study in China on 100,900 people (China-PAR), with half of the participants followed for at least 7.3 years. Habitual tea drinkers had an approximately 15% lower risk of death (hazard ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.90). Using age 50 as a benchmark: habitual tea drinkers had 1.41 more years free of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and a 1.26-year longer life expectancy.
Drink three to four cups of coffee daily, total caffeine not exceeding 400 mg, no added sugar, no added cream or cheese foam
A

People who drink three to four cups of coffee per day have an approximately 17% lower probability of death during the same period compared to non-drinkers. In another study, those who concentrated their coffee consumption in the morning had a 12% lower probability, while those who drank it throughout the day showed no difference. Caffeine content per cup varies greatly, so control total daily intake to no more than 400 mg.

If self-brewed, it costs one or two yuan per day. Brewing a cup takes a few minutes, costing almost no time. If buying large sizes, pay attention to how many mg of caffeine you have consumed in a day.

An umbrella review of 201 meta-analyses; the original studies underlying these meta-analyses were all observational, not randomized. For all-cause mortality, the review cited a meta-analysis on dose-response relationship. Compared to non-drinkers, those drinking 3–4 cups per day had a 17% lower risk of death (relative risk 0.83, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.88). At 7 cups per day, the reduction narrowed to 10% (relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.85 to 0.96), with no reverse increase in risk observed yet. A study using US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) data followed 40,725 adults, with half followed for at least 9.8 years, also observational. The study categorized coffee drinkers into two patterns. The morning pattern (36%) drank coffee concentrated between 4:00–11:59, with almost none in the afternoon or evening. Compared to non-drinkers, their all-cause mortality risk was 12% lower (hazard ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.96). Adjusting for sleep deprivation and difficulty sleeping, it was 16% lower (hazard ratio 0.84, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.95). Cardiovascular mortality risk was 19% lower (hazard ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.94). Adjusting for sleep, it was 31% lower (hazard ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.87). The all-day pattern (16%) drank coffee in the morning, afternoon, and evening. Their all-cause mortality risk showed no difference (hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.10). Cancer mortality risk for both patterns showed no difference. Daily caffeine limits have official bases. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) and Health Canada both set a limit for healthy adults at 400 mg per day. This is the total from all sources; tea, cola, and energy drinks must be included. EFSA also requires spacing intake throughout the day, with no more than 200 mg at a time. Caffeine content per cup varies greatly. According to EFSA tables, a 200 mL cup of filter coffee has about 90 mg. According to Health Canada tables, an 8-ounce (237 mL) cup of brewed coffee averages 135 mg. According to US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) tables, a 12-ounce (about 355 mL) brewed coffee has 113–247 mg. Therefore, the FDA equates 400 mg to about 2 to 3 cups of 12-ounce coffee, while the umbrella review equates it to about 4 cups.
Eat 5 portions (about 400 g) of vegetables and fruits daily
A

Eating an additional 200 g of vegetables and fruits daily is associated with an approximately one-tenth lower probability of death during the same period. People who eat 5 portions daily have a 13% lower probability compared to those who eat only 2 portions. In US studies, eating more than that did not result in further reductions.
A few yuan to over ten yuan per day. Washing and cutting takes a bit of time every day. The difficulty lies in having to buy and eat the full amount every single day.

Meta-analysis of multiple prospective studies (observational only, no group assignment): each additional 200 g of vegetables and fruits per day was associated with an approximately 10% lower risk of death (RR = 0.90). This benefit extends up to 800 g per day. Two large US prospective studies plus a meta-analysis of 26 studies: people eating 5 portions per day had an approximately 13% lower risk of death compared to those eating only 2 portions (HR = 0.87). The best combination is 2 portions of fruit plus 3 portions of vegetables; eating more did not further reduce risk.
Eat less ultra-processed food (packaged potato chips, instant noodles, pastries, ready-to-eat meals)
A

People who eat the most ultra-processed food have an approximately two-tenths higher probability of death during the same period compared to those who eat the least, and cardiovascular mortality is about five-tenths higher. However, evidence of this type is rated as not very certain, so the figures should be discounted.

No money required, just changing what you buy. You must cook for yourself or spend time selecting minimally processed foods, which takes a bit of time every day. The difficulty lies in resisting the long-term habit of "convenience first."

An umbrella review of multiple meta-analyses; the underlying original studies were all observational. Results: people with the highest intake of ultra-processed foods compared to those with the lowest had an approximately 21% higher risk of death (RR = 1.21) and an approximately 50% higher risk of cardiovascular mortality (RR = 1.50). The evidence levels for these two results were ranked as "highly suggestive" and "convincing," respectively. However, according to the common evidence grading system (GRADE), the certainty is low or very low.
Do not burn coal or wood for cooking and heating; switch to electricity or gas
A

People who cook with coal or wood have an approximately one-tenth higher probability of death during the same period; heating with coal or wood is about 14% higher. People who have switched to electricity or gas have a 13%–33% lower probability of death compared to those still burning coal or wood.

Rural households must replace stoves plus pay for fuel, costing a few hundred to over ⟦1000⟧ per year. It is a one-time change and does not take time in the long run. Urban residents have basically already switched to electricity or gas.

A long-term prospective study on chronic diseases in China, observational, involving 271,000 adults without cardiovascular disease. People cooking with solid fuels like coal or wood had an approximately 11% higher risk of death compared to those using electricity or gas (HR = 1.11). Those heating with solid fuels were 14% higher (HR = 1.14). People who switched from solid fuels to clean fuels, compared to those still burning: cooking-related risk was about 13% lower (HR = 0.87), and heating-related risk was about 33% lower (HR = 0.67). Outdoor PM2.5 fine particulate matter is a separate factor. Meta-analysis of 104 prospective studies: for every 10 µg/m³ increase in long-term inhalation concentration, the risk of death from natural causes is approximately 8% higher (RR = 1.08). Natural causes refer to death from disease, not accidents.
Let hot drinks cool down before drinking; do not drink scalding hot tea, soup, or coffee
A

In a study in a region of Iran with high esophageal cancer rates, people who drank very hot tea were 8 times more likely to develop esophageal cancer than those who drank warm tea. Even just "hot" tea doubled the risk. Drinking within two minutes of pouring resulted in a 5-fold higher risk compared to those waiting four minutes or more.
No money required, just waiting an extra two or three minutes each time. The difficulty lies in resisting the urge to drink when craving it.

In a region with high esophageal cancer rates in northern Iran, 300 patients were compared with 571 non-patients. All comparisons below are against warm tea drinkers. People drinking "hot" tea were approximately 2.07 times more likely to develop esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (odds ratio, 95% CI 1.28 to 3.35). People drinking "very hot" tea were approximately 8.16 times more likely (3.93 to 16.9). People who drank within 2 minutes of pouring were approximately 5.41 times more likely compared to those waiting 4 minutes or more (2.63 to 11.1).
Go outside for some sunlight during the day; do not go all day without seeing the sun
B

In a Swedish study, women who intentionally avoided the sun had a life expectancy 0.6 to 2.1 years shorter than those with the highest sun exposure. Non-smokers who avoided the sun had a life expectancy approximately equal to smokers in the highest sun exposure group.
No money required. Ten-plus minutes a day, such as during the commute or lunch break, is sufficient.

A study in Sweden of 29,500 women followed for 20 years. Compared to the group with the highest sun exposure, those who intentionally avoided sun exposure had a life expectancy 0.6 to 2.1 years shorter. The authors wrote: "non-smokers who avoided sun exposure had a life expectancy similar to smokers in the highest sun exposure group."
Maintain a BMI between 20–25; if overweight, lose weight
A

The probability of death is lowest in the BMI range of 20–25. A BMI of 27.5–30 is about two-tenths higher, 30–35 is about four and a half tenths higher, and 35–40 is nearly double. For East Asians with a BMI of 25 or higher, every 5-unit increase raises the risk by about four-tenths.

No money required. Dieting plus exercise takes time every day. This is the most willpower-intensive item in the chapter: it requires long-term dietary restraint and diligent exercise; maintaining weight loss is even harder than losing it.

Pooled individual data from 239 prospective studies (observational only). This analysis only included three types of people: never-smokers, those without chronic diseases at baseline, and those who survived more than 5 years after enrollment. Results: mortality risk was lowest at BMI 20–25. BMI 25–27.5 was about 7% higher (HR = 1.07). 27.5–30 was about 20% higher (HR = 1.20). 30–35 was about 45% higher (HR = 1.45). 35–40 was about 94% higher (HR = 1.94). 40–60 was 2.76 times higher (HR = 2.76). Among those with a BMI of 25 or higher, for every 5 kg/m² increase, the risk for East Asians was approximately 39% higher (HR = 1.39).
Eat chili peppers four or more times per week
B

In an Italian study, people who ate chili peppers four or more times per week had a mortality rate approximately 23% lower over the same period compared to those who rarely ate them, and cardiovascular mortality was about one-third lower.
No money and no time required.

An Italian study of 22,800 people, half of whom were followed for at least 8.2 years, with a total of 1,236 deaths. People who ate chili peppers 4 or more times per week had a mortality risk approximately 23% lower than those who rarely ate them (hazard ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.90). Cardiovascular mortality was about 34% lower (0.66, 0.50 to 0.86).
Drink one or two servings of milk or yogurt daily
B
People who drink two or more servings of milk or yogurt daily have a mortality rate approximately 17% lower over the same period compared to those who do not drink any.
A few yuan per day, no time required.

The PURE follow-up study in 21 countries, 136,000 people, average follow-up of 9.1 years, with a total of 6,796 deaths. People who consumed two or more servings of dairy products daily had a mortality risk approximately 17% lower than those who did not (hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.96), P-trend = 0.0052.
No need to abstain from eggs; up to one egg per day is fine
B

Eating an extra half a whole egg daily is associated with a mortality rate approximately 7% higher over the same period. Replacing that half egg with egg whites, fish, poultry, or nuts results in a lower mortality risk. However, another research group found that eating no more than one egg per day showed no association with cardiovascular disease, so there is no need to abstain from eggs.
No money and no time required.

A follow-up study in the US on 521,000 people, with a total of 129,000 deaths. Eating an extra half a whole egg daily was associated with a mortality risk approximately 7% higher (hazard ratio 1.07, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.08). Replacing that half egg with an equivalent amount of egg whites, poultry, fish, dairy products, or nuts/beans resulted in lower mortality risk, as well as lower risks of cardiovascular, cancer, and respiratory mortality. Conversely: three large US studies, totaling 216,000 people, with a maximum follow-up of 32 years. People who ate at least one egg per day compared to those who ate less than one egg per month showed no difference in cardiovascular disease risk (HR = 0.93, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.05). The same paper pooled 33 datasets totaling 1.72 million people and found that eating one extra egg per day did not change cardiovascular disease risk (RR = 0.98, 0.93 to 1.03). The authors concluded that consuming up to one egg per day is not associated with cardiovascular disease.
Take baths if possible, don't just shower
B

In a Japanese study, people who took a bath almost every day had a cardiovascular event risk approximately 28% lower than those who bathed less than twice a week, and cerebral hemorrhage risk was about 46% lower.
A bit extra for water and electricity. Half an hour each time.

A Japanese study of 30,000 people, aged 40 to 59, followed for 19 years, with a total of 2,097 cardiovascular events. People who took a bath almost every day had a cardiovascular event risk approximately 28% lower than those who bathed no more than twice a week (hazard ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.84). Coronary heart disease was about 35% lower (0.65, 0.45 to 0.94). Stroke was about 26% lower (0.74, 0.62 to 0.87). Cerebral hemorrhage was about 46% lower (0.54, 0.40 to 0.73).
Nap for within half an hour, not more than an hour; if you must sleep one or two hours to function, see a doctor to find the cause
B

People who nap for no more than an hour do not have an increased risk of mortality or chronic disease and are more mentally alert. Those who nap for more than an hour have a coronary heart disease risk about three-tenths higher, and diabetes and obesity risks about two-tenths higher. Therefore, set an alarm and wake up after half an hour. If you must sleep one or two hours every day to function, it is a sign to see a doctor.
No money required. Just set an alarm before sleeping; requires almost no willpower.

An umbrella review pooling 16 meta-analyses and 244 health outcomes. An umbrella review is a meta-analysis of existing meta-analyses. Conclusion: people who nap for less than 60 minutes do not have an increased overall mortality rate or chronic disease risk, and show the clearest cognitive improvement (SMD = 0.69, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.00). Short naps of 20 to 30 minutes improve athletic performance the most (SMD = 0.99, 0.67 to 1.31). People who nap for more than 60 minutes have a coronary heart disease risk about 30% higher, and diabetes and obesity risks about 20% higher. Another study had 1,338 people over age 56 wear wristwatches to measure actual nap duration, rather than relying on self-reported questionnaires. Maximum follow-up was 19 years, during which 926 people died. For every 1 hour increase in daily nap duration, mortality risk was about 13% higher (HR = 1.13, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.23). For each additional nap per day, it was about 7% higher (HR = 1.07, 1.02 to 1.13). People who napped in the morning had a risk about 30% higher than those who napped in the early afternoon (HR = 1.30, 1.03 to 1.64).
After staying up late, catch up on sleep the next night immediately; don't wait until the weekend
B

People with sleep debt who do not catch up the next night have a mortality risk approximately 15% higher than those with regular schedules; those with significant debt and no catch-up have a risk about 42% higher. Those who caught up on sleep showed no increased risk. Therefore, if you stay up late, go to bed early the next night.
No money required. You would naturally want those one or two hours of catch-up sleep anyway.

UK Biobank, 85,618 people, average age 61.8, wearing wristwatches to record daily sleep, median follow-up of 8 years. The study first calculated "sleep debt nights" based on each individual's sleep needs, defined as sleeping 2.5 hours or more less than needed. The first night after a sleep debt period is the "catch-up night"; if sleep that night exceeded needs, it was counted as caught up. This divided subjects into five types. Compared to those with regular schedules, people with sleep debt who did not catch up had an all-cause mortality risk approximately 15% higher (HR = 1.15, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.31). Those with a cumulative debt of more than 3.5 hours without catch-up were about 42% higher (HR = 1.42, 1.24 to 1.63). Both groups that caught up showed no statistically significant association; the group that had sleep debt then caught up had an HR = 1.12 (0.98 to 1.28). Among those who were already short sleepers, sleep debt without catch-up was about 19% higher (1.19, 1.01 to 1.40), and severe debt without catch-up was about 38% higher (1.38, 1.17 to 1.63). These results were also replicated in a separate group of 4,586 people from a US health survey.
The longer you work night shifts, the higher the cardiovascular risk; if you can transfer positions, do it early
A

Night shift workers develop cardiovascular disease about 13% more than non-night shift workers and have about 27% more cardiovascular deaths. This increases with duration: for every 5 additional years of night shift work, cardiovascular disease increases by about 7%. Since this is calculated by years, transfer as early as possible.

Transferring positions or changing jobs might mean less money, and night shift allowances will be lost. Job hunting takes time, and the decision is difficult. If this is considered when choosing a job, the cost is zero.

Pooled 23 follow-up studies for calculation, observational only, no group assignment. Night shift workers had a cardiovascular event risk approximately 13% higher (RR = 1.13, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.16). Cardiovascular mortality was about 27% higher (RR = 1.27, 1.18 to 1.36). By years: for every 5 additional years of night shift work, the incidence of cardiovascular disease was about 7% higher (RR = 1.07, 1.04 to 1.09), and cardiovascular mortality was about 5% higher (RR = 1.05, 1.03 to 1.06). Broken down by disease: coronary heart disease incidence was about 22% higher (1.22, 1.16 to 1.28), coronary heart disease mortality was about 22% higher (1.22, 1.10 to 1.36), ischemic heart disease mortality was about 39% higher (1.39, 1.06 to 1.84), and stroke mortality was about 49% higher (1.49, 1.04 to 2.12). Stroke incidence alone was not statistically significant (1.06, 0.95 to 1.18).
Buy pre-packaged cooking oil with an SC code (China); do not buy bulk self-pressed peanut oil from small workshops
B

Moldy peanuts produce aflatoxin, a definite carcinogen that primarily damages the liver. After Guangzhou tightened regulations on small workshops, the rate of abnormal liver function among residents who frequently ate self-pressed oil decreased by about three and a half tenths. In Guangxi, pregnant women eating self-pressed peanut oil had a risk of low birth weight about nine-tenths higher and preterm birth about eight-tenths higher.

Change where you buy; the price is almost the same. Just check the packaging for a food production license code starting with SC (China). The difficulty lies in convincing elderly people accustomed to buying self-pressed oil.

Aflatoxin is classified as Group 1 (carcinogenic to humans) by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, primarily causing liver cancer. A study in Guangzhou measured aflatoxin B1 in self-pressed peanut oil from small workshops from 2010 to 2022. The median was 1.29 μg/kg, with the middle half of samples ranging from 0.12 to 6.58. After local regulations for small workshops were issued, toxins in the oil immediately dropped by 2.865 μg/kg, then decreased by an additional 2.593 each year. The rate of abnormal liver function in residents of areas where self-pressed oil was common decreased accordingly (PR = 0.650, 95% CI 0.469 to 0.902), i.e., about 35% lower. A study in Guangxi followed 1,611 pregnant women, 81.7% of whom ate self-pressed peanut oil. Children of those who ate it had a risk of low birth weight about nine-tenths higher (aOR = 1.9, 1.1 to 3.2) and preterm birth about eight-tenths higher (aOR = 1.8, 1.1 to 3.0).
Cook with vegetable oil instead of lard and butter; no need to switch between oils for health, and don't rely on flaxseed oil to protect the heart
A

Eating less saturated fat like lard and butter and replacing it with vegetable oil reduces events like heart disease and stroke by about one-sixth, but total mortality risk shows no change. Eating more of the main components of soybean oil or corn oil shows no benefit and no harm. Eating more flaxseed oil also shows no reduction in heart disease risk.
No extra money. Vegetable oil is already the main oil for most families. The difficulty lies in breaking the taste habit of stir-frying vegetables or mixing rice with lard.

Cochrane pooled 15 randomized trials, 56,675 people, each trial lasting at least two years. Eating less saturated fat resulted in total cardiovascular events about 17% lower (RR = 0.83, 0.70 to 0.98). Overall mortality was almost unchanged (RR = 0.96, 0.90 to 1.03), and cardiovascular mortality was also unchanged (RR = 0.95, 0.80 to 1.12). Replacing it with polyunsaturated fats (the main component of soybean and corn oil) or carbohydrates showed no difference in effectiveness. Replacing it with monounsaturated fats (the main component of rapeseed and olive oil) had too little data to draw conclusions. Another Cochrane paper pooled 19 randomized trials, 6,461 people: eating more omega-6 (linoleic acid) resulted in overall mortality RR = 1.00 (0.88 to 1.12) and cardiovascular events RR = 0.97 (0.81 to 1.15), showing neither benefit nor harm. A third paper pooled 86 randomized trials, 162,796 people: eating more plant-based omega-3 (the main component of flaxseed and perilla oil) resulted in overall mortality RR = 1.01 (0.84 to 1.20) and coronary heart disease events RR = 1.00 (0.82 to 1.22), essentially having no effect.
Turn on the range hood when stir-frying or frying; keep it on from the moment you start the stove until you finish cooking
B

Non-smoking Chinese women who do not or rarely use a range hood when stir-frying have about double the risk of lung cancer compared to those who use it frequently. Having lived in a kitchen with poor ventilation also increases the risk by about five-tenths, most notably in homes burning coal.

If a range hood is already installed, it only costs a bit of electricity. If not, buying one including installation costs from a few hundred to over ⟦1000⟧. The difficulty lies in remembering to turn it on every time you start the stove and not turning it off because of the noise.

Pooled 10 case-control studies, all subjects were non-smoking Chinese women. Case-control studies compare people with lung cancer to those without and ask retrospectively about past habits. People exposed to cooking oil fumes had about 1.74 times the likelihood of lung cancer (odds ratio, 95% CI 1.57 to 1.94). Among these, 4 studies comparing those exposed to oil fumes without using a range hood showed about 2.11 times the likelihood (1.54 to 2.89). A study in Taiwan compared 1,302 non-smoking women with lung cancer to 1,302 without. Only those who had cooked for ten years or more were considered. Those who used a range hood for more than two-thirds of those years, compared to those who used it for less than one-third, had about half the risk (odds ratio 0.49, 0.32 to 0.76). In Shanghai, a prospective follow-up study of 71,000 non-smoking women followed from 1996 to 2009 identified 429 lung cancer cases. Those who self-reported having lived in a kitchen with poor ventilation had a lung cancer risk about 49% higher (HR = 1.49, 1.15 to 1.95). Burning coal with poor ventilation for 20 years or more resulted in about 2.03 times the risk (HR = 2.03, 1.35 to 3.05). Simply considering whether they had ever burned coal showed no difference (HR = 1.03, 0.84 to 1.26). No difference was found regardless of the type of cooking oil used.

Around menopause, if hot flashes and night sweats affect your life, see a gynecologist for a hormone therapy assessment; do not just endure it, do not self-medicate, and especially do not use it to prevent heart disease
A

For hot flashes and night sweats around menopause, hormone therapy reduces the number of hot flashes by about 75% compared to a placebo. The trade-off is a slight increase in breast cancer, blood clots, and stroke, with about 8 additional cases of each per 10,000 women per year. Those starting between ages 50 and 59 do not show an increase in overall mortality. It cannot be used to prevent heart disease or dementia.

One visit to a gynecologist or menopause clinic. The doctor will take a medical history to see if you have any contraindications for hormones before prescribing. Once started, follow up as requested by the doctor. The difficulty lies in overcoming the fear that "hormones mean cancer," and not self-purchasing them because of anti-aging claims.

Cochrane pooled 24 randomized trials involving 3,329 people, comparing oral hormone therapy with placebo. Hormone users had about 75% fewer hot flashes per week than the placebo group (95% CI 64.3 to 82.3). The severity of hot flashes also significantly decreased (OR = 0.13, 0.07 to 0.23). Placebo users also saw a reduction in hot flashes of about 57.7%, so anything claiming to treat hot flashes must be compared to a placebo to count. Regarding risks, see the US WHI randomized trial. 16,608 women with an intact uterus, aged 50 to 79, used estrogen plus progestin, with a mean follow-up of 5.2 years. Coronary heart disease was about 29% higher (HR = 1.29, 1.02 to 1.63). Invasive breast cancer was about 26% higher (HR = 1.26, 1.00 to 1.59). Stroke was about 41% higher (HR = 1.41, 1.07 to 1.85). Pulmonary embolism was about 2.13 times higher (HR = 2.13, 1.39 to 3.25). In absolute numbers, for every 10,000 women per year, there were 7 additional cases of coronary heart disease, 8 cases of stroke, 8 cases of pulmonary embolism, and 8 cases of invasive breast cancer. Simultaneously, there were 6 fewer cases of colorectal cancer and 5 fewer hip fractures. For women who had a hysterectomy and used estrogen alone, with a cumulative follow-up of 13 years, breast cancer was actually about 21% lower (HR = 0.79, 0.65 to 0.97). The two trials combined with 18 years of follow-up showed no change in overall mortality (HR = 0.99, 0.94 to 1.03). When stratified by age at initiation, the 50 to 59 age group had an overall mortality rate about 31% lower during the years of medication use (HR = 0.69, 0.51 to 0.94). The 60 to 69 group was 1.04 (0.87 to 1.25), and the 70 to 79 group was 1.13 (0.94 to 1.36), neither being statistically significant. At 18 years of follow-up, the 50 to 59 group was 0.89 (0.79 to 1.01), also no longer statistically significant. A 2017 Cochrane review focusing only on women aged 50 to 59 found the only significant increase was blood clots when using combined estrogen and progestin, with an absolute risk of less than 1/500. For women over 65 using combined estrogen and progestin, dementia increased from 9 cases per 1,000 people to 11–30 cases over 4 years. The US Preventive Services Task Force in 2022 opposed using hormones to prevent chronic diseases (Grade D recommendation), concluding there is no net benefit.
If you already want to own a dog, count daily dog walking toward your step count, but do not get a dog specifically to live longer
B

Dog owners have an average mortality rate about one-quarter lower over the same period, and those with prior coronary heart disease have even lower rates. However, after adjusting for other differences, large studies in the UK and Norway found no difference, and cat ownership showed no association. Therefore, do not get a dog just to live longer; if you already want one, consider daily dog walking as your exercise.

Owning a dog is an ongoing expense: food, vaccines, deworming, medical check-ups, and paperwork must be paid for and managed until the dog passes away. You must dedicate time daily for walks, and arrange for care during business trips or vacations. The difficulty lies in the daily commitment; once you have a pet, you cannot just stop. There are no official statistics in China on the cost of raising a dog, so no figure is recorded here.

A meta-analysis of 10 follow-up studies involving approximately 3.84 million people with a mean follow-up of 10.1 years. Dog owners had about a 24% lower risk of mortality (RR = 0.76, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.86). Cardiovascular mortality was about 31% lower (RR = 0.69, 0.67 to 0.71). Among those with prior coronary heart disease, dog owners had a risk about 65% lower (RR = 0.35, 0.17 to 0.69). The authors noted this meta-analysis did not adjust for other factors. A Swedish national registry study of about 3.43 million people adjusted for factors like income and marriage. For the general population, dog owners had about a 20% lower mortality risk (HR = 0.80, 0.79 to 0.82). People living alone with a dog had about a 33% lower mortality risk (HR = 0.67, 0.65 to 0.69). Those living with others had an 11% lower risk (HR = 0.89, 0.87 to 0.91). Among Swedish patients after a myocardial infarction, those living alone with a dog had about a 33% lower mortality risk (HR = 0.67, 0.61 to 0.75), while those living with a spouse or children had a 15% lower risk (HR = 0.85, 0.80 to 0.90). After an ischemic stroke, the two groups were about 27% lower (HR = 0.73, 0.66 to 0.80) and 12% lower (HR = 0.88, 0.83 to 0.93) respectively. Conversely: 6 health surveys in the UK, totaling 59,352 people with a mean follow-up of 11.5 years. After full adjustment, dog ownership was not associated with mortality (HR = 1.03, 0.98 to 1.09), nor with cardiovascular mortality (HR = 1.07, 0.96 to 1.18). A Norwegian study with a median follow-up of 18.5 years found dog owners had nearly identical mortality risks (HR = 1.00, 0.91 to 1.09). There, dog owners did not exercise more than others. In the Swedish Twin Registry, 34,202 people were surveyed about lifestyle habits; in this group, the association between dog ownership and lower cardiovascular or mortality risk could not be replicated. An Australian study of 15,735 people followed for 4 years found dog owners had about a 23% lower mortality risk (OR = 0.77, 0.59 to 0.99), partly explained by increased physical activity. Owning cats, birds, or fish showed no association with mortality. A 2013 American Heart Association statement said pet ownership, particularly dog ownership, to reduce cardiovascular risk is "possibly reasonable," which is the weakest recommendation level. The same statement clearly opposed adopting, rescuing, or purchasing a pet primarily to reduce cardiovascular risk.
If pre-diabetes is detected (slightly high blood sugar, not yet diabetes), eat less, lose weight, and exercise more to reverse diabetes; check blood sugar every six months
A

People with slightly high blood sugar who eat less, exercise more, and lose a little weight have a three to six-tenths lower risk of developing diabetes. The Da Qing trial in China followed participants for 30 years; those who did this had about a one-quarter lower mortality rate and lived an average of about one and a half years longer. However, similar trials in the US and Finland did not find differences in mortality rates.

Costs nothing; eating less even saves a bit of money. Engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise like brisk walking per week, about twenty minutes a day. Eat 400 to 500 kcal less per day than before. The difficulty lies in long-term maintenance; once weight is lost, it must be kept off. Get a blood test every six months; fasting blood sugar costs about a dozen yuan.

The Da Qing study was a cluster-randomized trial conducted in Da Qing, Heilongjiang. 577 adults with impaired glucose tolerance (a form of pre-diabetes) were assigned to a control group or one of three intervention groups: diet only, exercise only, or both. The intervention lasted 6 years. Over 6 years, the cumulative incidence of diabetes in the control group was 67.7%. The diet group was 43.8%, the exercise group 41.1%, and the diet-plus-exercise group 46.0%. After adjusting for differences in BMI and fasting blood sugar, the diabetes risk for the three groups was about 31%, 46%, and 42% lower, respectively. Both lean and overweight individuals (using a BMI cutoff of 25) saw similar reductions. At 23 years of follow-up, the intervention group had about 41% lower cardiovascular mortality (HR = 0.59, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.96). Overall mortality was about 29% lower (HR = 0.71, 0.51 to 0.99). Diabetes incidence was about 45% lower (HR = 0.55, 0.40 to 0.76). At 30 years of follow-up, the onset of diabetes in the intervention group was delayed by 3.96 years (median).
