In high-salary areas, both payments and collections increase by the same ratio, so the break-even years remain unchanged. Payments in early years have a smaller face value, but at retirement, they are paid out according to the average salary at that time. Thus, if only looking at the face value of payments and collections, the break-even occurs earlier than 9.9 years. The law stipulates: at retirement, a total of 15 years of contributions must be met to receive monthly payments. If insufficient, one can continue paying until the requirement is met. From January 1, 2030, this minimum number of years will increase by 6 months each year, gradually rising to 20 years. If a person passes away, the remaining balance in the personal account is inherited. The state adjusts pensions timely based on the average salary growth of employees and price increases. If the pension fund is insufficient, the government subsidizes it (Nationwide China).

When buying a new car, inspect it on-site upon delivery and keep the invoice and 'Three Guarantees' certificate; if major failures occur within the first 7 or 60 days, you can demand a replacement or refund
A

If major components like the engine or transmission fail and need replacement within the first 7 days of a new car, you can directly demand a replacement or refund. Within the first 60 days or 3,000 km, if there is a loss of braking, loss of steering, body cracking, fuel leakage, or battery fire, you can also get a replacement or refund. During the 'Three Guarantees' period, if the same fault remains unresolved after multiple repairs, you can also get a replacement or refund, though a usage compensation fee based on mileage must be paid.

Zero cost. Spend half an hour with the salesperson inspecting the exterior and interior and verifying the vehicle documents upon delivery. The invoice and 'Three Guarantees' (repair, replacement, refund) certificate must be kept carefully. Obtain a repair slip for every visit to the workshop. If you truly want a replacement or refund, you will need to make several trips to the dealership; if no agreement is reached, you must file a complaint or lawsuit.

This set of rules is called the 'Three Guarantees' for family automobiles (China), applying to passenger vehicles like sedans, SUVs, and pickups purchased for personal consumption; commercial transport vehicles are excluded. The 'Three Guarantees' period is no less than 2 years or 50,000 km, and the repair warranty period is no less than 3 years or 60,000 km, whichever comes first. The period starts from the invoice date; if the delivery date differs from the invoice date, it starts from the delivery date. Quality defects during the warranty period are repaired for free, with no charges for labor or materials. Within the first 7 days, if the engine, transmission, power battery, drive motor, or their main components must be replaced due to quality defects, you can choose a replacement or refund based on the invoice and 'Three Guarantees' certificate. Within the first 60 days or 3,000 km, if quality defects cause loss of steering, loss of braking, body cracking, fuel leakage, or power battery fire, you can also choose a replacement or refund. During the 'Three Guarantees' period, replacement or refund is also granted in four cases: 1. A serious safety defect remains unresolved after 2 repairs, or a new serious safety defect appears. 2. Four major components like the engine have been replaced twice due to quality defects but still cannot function normally. 3. The same main component has been replaced twice but still cannot function normally. 4. Total repair time exceeds 30 days, or the same quality defect has been repaired 4 or more times. For these four cases, a usage compensation fee must be paid, calculated as: car price × mileage ÷ 1000 × n. 'n' is specified by the manufacturer on the certificate and cannot exceed 0.5%. If a single repair exceeds 5 days, the dealer must provide a replacement car or transportation compensation starting from the 6th day. Upon replacement or refund, the dealer must also refund your vehicle registration fees, additional decoration fees after depreciation, and any agency service fees collected. The dealer must respond to a replacement or refund request within 10 working days; if they refuse, they must provide a reason. Dealers cannot refuse 'Three Guarantees' responsibility because you did not perform maintenance at their shop. Intentionally delaying or refusing 'Three Guarantees' without a valid reason is punishable under Article 56 of the Consumer Rights Protection Law (China) (Nationwide China, effective from January 1, 2022).

When buying a used car from a dealer, check the insurance and repair history first, and include 'not an accident or flood-damaged car' in the contract; if hidden, you can demand a refund and triple compensation
A

If you buy a used car from a dealer and they intentionally hide its true condition, such as past accidents or flood damage, you can return the car and demand triple the car's price in compensation. However, triple compensation is only obtainable if you prove the dealer intentionally hid the information. If the dealer claims they didn't know and the court accepts this, only the car price plus interest is returned. Triple compensation does not apply to purchases from individuals.

You must pay for a third-party inspection, with prices varying by provider. Spend one or two hours checking the car's insurance and repair history before buying. When signing the contract, insist on including a written guarantee of the car's condition. If truly cheated, you must sue, which can take two to three years.

Sellers of used cars must provide buyers with the true condition regarding usage, repairs, accidents, inspections, whether it is mortgaged, whether taxes and fees are paid, and the scrappage deadline. If the seller hides or deceives, making it impossible to transfer ownership, the seller must take back the car and refund the purchase price unconditionally. Article 55 of the Consumer Rights Protection Law (China) stipulates that if a business operator commits fraud in providing goods, they shall increase compensation at the consumer's request. The amount is triple the purchase price, or ⟦500⟧ if the amount is less than 500. This only applies to business operators; it cannot be used when buying from an individual owner. There was a case in Rizhao, Shandong. In May 2023, Mr. Sun bought a car from a used car shop for a total price of ⟦53000⟧; the shop guaranteed it had never had a major accident. In October of the same year, an appraisal company found it was a major accident car, and records showed it had an accident in January that year and was declared a total loss. The first instance court rescinded the contract, the shop returned ⟦53000⟧ and paid triple compensation of ⟦159000⟧. In April 2025, the Rizhao Intermediate People's Court (China) upheld the verdict on appeal. Even though the two parties did not sign a written contract, Mr. Sun won based on a receipt stamped by the shop. There was also an opposite case. Mr. Wang in Henan spent ⟦240000⟧ on a car in January 2018, with a contract guaranteeing no accidents or flood damage. Later, it was discovered the car had an accident before delivery with repairs costing ⟦5100⟧. Both the first instance and retrial ruled for triple compensation, but the Zhengzhou Intermediate People's Court (China) amended the judgment on appeal, and the high court upheld the appeal verdict. The reason was that when the dealer acquired the car, the accident and repairs had already occurred, and there was no evidence the dealer knew and intentionally hid it. Thus, it was only a breach of contract: the contract was rescinded, ⟦240000⟧ plus interest was returned, but no triple compensation. The court reminded that buyers can check the insurance claim history of used cars through various channels or commission a professional third-party appraisal (Nationwide China).
When buying a car at a 4S dealership, do not pay 'financial service fees'; insurance, loans, and registration are not mandatory through the dealer
B

If a dealer says you must pay an additional 'financial service fee' to take out a loan, regulations (China) state that dealers are not allowed to collect such fees. You can find other providers or handle insurance, loans, and registration yourself; the dealer cannot force you to use their services or charge more than the listed price. Before borrowing, make the other party clearly state the annual interest rate and all costs for comparison.

Zero cost. Before signing the contract, spend a few minutes asking what each fee is for and insist the dealer includes them in the contract or issues an invoice. Handling insurance and registration yourself will require an extra trip.

The 汽车销售管理办法 (Measures for the Administration of Automobile Sales in China) stipulate that dealers must clearly display the prices and fees for vehicles, parts, and services in the shop. They are not allowed to sell at inflated prices or collect additional fees beyond the listed price. Dealers cannot restrict your place of household registration, nor can they restrict your use of parts, supplies, financing, insurance, rescue, or after-sales services. Parts and services paid for by the manufacturer under 'Three Guarantees' or recalls are exceptions. When selling a car, the dealer cannot force you to buy insurance or handle registration through them. Violations are subject to correction by commercial authorities at or above the county level, with possible warnings or fines up to ⟦30000⟧. In 2022, the former China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission required financial institutions providing auto loans to strictly manage partner dealers. Dealers are not allowed to collect fees in the name of the financial institution, nor use the provision of financial services as a reason to charge you. They must also inform you of the loan interest rate and fees on an annualized basis. They cannot use false claims like 'no prepayment penalty' or 'no mortgage needed' to lure you, nor bundle products or services against your will. Financial institutions themselves cannot collect fees through the loan. The 消费者权益保护法实施条例 (Regulations for the Implementation of the Consumer Rights Protection Law of the People's Republic of China) stipulate that business operators shall not coerce or disguisedly coerce you into purchasing goods, nor exclude or restrict your choice of other business operators (Nationwide China).
If a tour guide takes you to a shop not in the agreement and you buy items, contact the travel agency within 30 days to demand a return; the agency must advance the refund
A

It is illegal (China) for a travel agency to take you to a shop without prior agreement or to use unreasonably low tour prices to lure you into shopping. Within 30 days of returning, you have the right to demand the agency handle the return for you and advance the refund. If you have signed a supplementary agreement for 'voluntary shopping,' it is considered your consent, making it difficult to return items this way.

Zero cost. Keep the contract and itinerary during the trip; for purchases, get invoices and card receipts, and do not unwrap the items. After returning, you must contact the travel agency and send the items back. If no agreement is reached, you must file a complaint, which can take one or two months.

Article 35 of the 旅游法 (Tourism Law of the People's Republic of China) has three clauses. Clause 1 states that travel agencies must not organize tours at unreasonably low prices to lure tourists and then rely on shopping arrangements to earn commissions. Clause 2 states that travel agencies must not designate specific shopping locations. They can only do so if both parties agree through negotiation or if the tourist requests it without affecting others' itineraries. Signing a supplementary agreement for 'voluntary shopping' is usually considered a negotiated agreement. Clause 3 states that if the above two clauses are violated, tourists have the right to request the travel agency to handle return procedures and advance the refund within 30 days after the trip ends. Fees for additional self-paid items can also be reclaimed. This clause does not require you to prove the goods have quality defects first. Article 9 of the 旅游法 (Tourism Law of the People's Republic of China) also stipulates that tourists have the right to refuse coerced transactions. In 2025, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism (China) announced a case. A travel agency in Chengdu took 15 tourists to Jiuzhaigou, charging only ⟦6015⟧ in total. Instead, they paid ⟦8220⟧ in 'group purchase fees' to the agency that recruited the guests, then took ⟦13706⟧ in commissions from shops. This company was fined and had ⟦80000⟧ confiscated, with business suspended for 30 days for rectification. In 2024, the Department of Culture and Tourism of Guangdong Province (China) published a complaint case. Two tourists on a tour of Hong Kong, Macau, and Zhuhai priced at ⟦800⟧ each bought over twenty thousand RMB worth of jewelry and pillows at a duty-free shop. The tourists complained to the district-level culture and tourism authority; the two parties mediated, and the travel agency helped return the goods and fully refunded the money (Nationwide China).

Before purchasing investment products recommended by bank staff, verify them in the bank's official app or website; if they cannot be found, the staff may be selling unauthorized products outside the bank's approved portfolio
B

Bank employees selling products not issued by the bank or authorized for sale is called "unauthorized selling." Products sold by the bank as an agent can only be sold at transaction points, official websites, and the bank's own apps, where they can also be looked up; if you can't find them, don't buy in a hurry. When customers are defrauded by staff selling unauthorized products, some courts have ruled that the bank bears half the damages. There was also a case at a securities trading office where the first instance court awarded no compensation, but the appellate court amended it to partial compensation.

Costs no money. Before buying, search for the product name in the bank's app or official website, which takes a few minutes. The difficulty lies in telling a familiar relationship manager, "Let me look it up myself first."

The Beijing No. 3 Intermediate People's Court (China) stated that the unauthorized sale of wealth management products occurs when financial institution employees exploit their professional convenience to sell third-party products not issued by their unit nor authorized for sale. A 2025 regulation from the National Financial Regulatory Administration (China) states that banks acting as agents for other organizations' products must only set up designated areas for sale within their own operated channels such as transaction points, official websites, and apps. Banks must allow for the lookup of agent-sold products on their channels, clearly stating they are agent-sold, the type, and the issuer. Banks must not mix agent-sold products with deposits or the bank's own products for sale. The front page of promotional materials for agent-sold products must clearly state: "This product is issued and managed by organization ×× (cooperating organization), bank ×× is the agent seller and is not responsible for the investment and payment of the product." Banks must authorize which sales staff can sell which products and disclose this at transaction points. Sales at transaction points must be recorded via audio and video. Banks and employees must not "use the name of their organization to arbitrarily recommend or sell unapproved products" (China-wide, from 01/10/2025). In 2022, the Beijing No. 3 Intermediate People's Court (China) reported a case. In 2013, a bank wealth manager told a customer a product was a hot item from the bank and that the bank was the custodian. The customer signed a "partnership investment agreement" with a fund company and transferred ⟦1200000⟧ into the fund company's account. Later, the principal was not returned, and the actual controller of the fund company went to prison. The court held that because the employee recommended it during working hours, at the workplace, and exploited their position, it counted as official conduct. The customer, chasing high interest one-sidedly, was also at fault. The first instance ruled the bank and customer each bear half the loss, and the appeal upheld this. In October 2026, the Supreme People's Court along with the People's Bank, the National Financial Regulatory Administration, and the Securities Regulatory Commission (China) jointly announced a typical case. The head of a securities trading office sold private funds not authorized by the office; the customer invested ⟦1000000⟧. The customer sued in August 2023, and the first instance was dismissed. The appeal determined the trading office was at fault and the customer was also at fault, amending the ruling to the trading office paying compensation of approximately ⟦577000⟧ (exactly ⟦576716.97⟧); the case number is from 2024 (China-wide, years 2022, 2026).
Do not take multivitamins to live longer or prevent cardiovascular disease
A

14,000 male physicians took multivitamins for eleven years. The number of major cardiovascular events and deaths remained exactly the same as the group that did not take them. A meta-analysis of 9 trials involving over 50,000 people also found no effect on mortality. Not buying them saves ⟦200~700⟧ per year. This does not apply to people tested and found to be truly deficient in a specific nutrient or pregnant women taking folic acid supplements.
About ⟦0.5~2⟧ per day, ⟦200~700⟧ per year. Taking them takes no time, just one pill. Long-term use easily becomes a dependent habit, where forgetting a day feels like a missing task.

The PHS II trial involved 14,641 male physicians followed for 11.2 years (this is the median: half were followed longer, half shorter). The rate of major cardiovascular events was the same for those who took them and those who did not. Major cardiovascular events HR 1.01 (HR is the hazard ratio; 1 means both sides are the same). The 95% confidence interval from 0.91 to 1.10 is the reliable range for this figure. Mortality was the same: all-cause mortality HR 0.94 (0.88–1.02). The USPSTF, the US body that grades preventive measures, in 2022 pooled 9 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 51,550 people, concluding that multivitamins were not associated with total mortality. The rating is I, meaning insufficient evidence to make a recommendation. It seems worth the money because the phrase "one pill replaces all nutrients" sounds plausible, and it only costs a few cents a day.
Do not take regular fish oil to prevent cardiovascular disease
A

Two large trials, one with 26,000 people and one with 15,000 diabetic patients. People taking 1 gram of fish oil daily had the same number of major cardiovascular events and deaths as those who did not. "Eating fish is beneficial" does not mean "taking fish oil pills is beneficial." Not buying them saves ⟦400~1000⟧ per year.
About ⟦1~3⟧ per day, ⟦400~1000⟧ per year. Taking them takes no time.

The VITAL trial involved 25,871 people taking 1 gram of fish oil daily, followed for 5.3 years (median). Major cardiovascular events and mortality did not differ between the two sides. Major cardiovascular events HR 0.92 (HR is the hazard ratio; 1 means both sides are the same). The 95% confidence interval from 0.80 to 1.06 is the reliable range for this figure. This interval crosses 1, meaning no difference was found. All-cause mortality HR 1.02 (0.90–1.15). The ASCEND trial involved 15,480 diabetic patients, also taking 1 gram daily, followed for an average of 7.4 years, and also found no difference. Serious vascular events RR 0.97 (0.87–1.08). All-cause mortality RR 0.95 (0.86–1.05). It seems worth the money because many people equate "eating fish is beneficial" with "taking fish oil pills is beneficial."
Do not supplement vitamin D for people who are not deficient just to live longer
A

People who were not vitamin D deficient supplemented for 5 years; the number of people who developed cancer, cardiovascular disease, and the number of deaths were all the same as those who did not supplement. Adults who rarely go outside and do not get sun exposure can supplement 400 IU per day, but do not exceed 2,000 IU per day. Taking high doses can cause bone density to decrease even more and lead to more falls. Feeling tired alone cannot be considered a vitamin D deficiency; if tired for several weeks for no clear reason, see a doctor.
About ⟦0.2~0.5⟧ per day, ⟦100~200⟧ per year. The money is not much; the real price is the illusion of having prevented disease.

The VITAL trial involved 25,871 people taking 2,000 IU daily, followed for 5.3 years (median). No differences were found for cancer, cardiovascular disease, or mortality. Invasive cancer HR 0.96 (HR is the hazard ratio; 1 means both sides are the same; the 95% confidence interval from 0.88 to 1.06 is the reliable range). Major cardiovascular events HR 0.97 (0.85–1.12). All-cause mortality HR 0.99 (0.87–1.12). The D-Health trial involved 21,315 Australians over 60. They took 60,000 IU per month, followed for 5 years. This trial also found no difference, all-cause mortality HR 1.04 (0.93–1.18). The mortality rate was 5.3% compared to 5.1%. It seems worth the money because there are observational studies that only track records without intervention and find that people with low vitamin D levels die more, which is then misunderstood as "supplementing will have an effect." There are specific recommendations for people who rarely go outside. The UK Department of Health advises adults who rarely go outside, live in nursing homes, or wear clothes that cover most of their skin when outside to supplement 10 micrograms of vitamin D daily year-round. The NHS specifies that 1 microgram equals 40 IU, so 10 micrograms is 400 IU. Chinese health industry standards recommend 10 micrograms per day for adults aged 18 to 64, and 15 micrograms for those over 65. The same standard sets the tolerable upper intake level at 50 micrograms (2,000 IU) per day, as excessive use can cause blood calcium to become too high. The NHS gives adults a wider limit of 100 micrograms (4,000 IU). Fatigue has many causes; the NHS lists lack of sleep, stress and depression, iron deficiency anemia, diabetes, hyperthyroidism, and sleep apnea. The NHS advises seeing a doctor if tired for several weeks for no clear reason, or if fatigue is severe enough to affect daily life. Supplementing more is not better. VITAL specifically calculated fractures: those taking 2,000 IU daily and those not supplementing were the same (HR 0.98; 0.89–1.08). VITAL also looked at depression in 18,353 people over 50 who were not depressed at the time. Those supplementing had 12.9 cases of depression or recurrence per 1,000 people per year, while those not supplementing had 13.3 cases, which is not different (HR 0.97; 0.87–1.09). Mood scores also did not differ. The authors explicitly stated: results do not support vitamin D supplementation in adults to prevent depression. A trial in Canada took 311 healthy people aged 55 to 70 without osteoporosis. They were divided into three groups taking 400, 4,000, and 10,000 IU daily for 3 years. The higher the dose, the more the radial bone density at the wrist decreased; the three groups decreased by 1.2%, 2.4%, and 3.5% respectively. Bone strength showed no difference. The authors concluded: results do not support high-dose vitamin D supplementation as beneficial for bones. A trial in Switzerland took 200 people over 70 who had previously fallen. They took 24,000 IU or 60,000 IU per month for one year. The 60,000 IU group did not show improved leg function, and the number of people who fell during the year was actually higher (66.9% compared to 47.9%). A trial in Australia took 2,256 women over 70, taking a single dose of 500,000 IU once a year in autumn/winter. Their number of falls was about 15% higher (RR 1.15; 1.02–1.30), and fractures were about 26% higher (RR 1.26; 1.00–1.59).
Do not take antioxidant supplements (beta-carotene, vitamin E, vitamin A) to prevent cancer
A

Antioxidant supplements are not just useless. A meta-analysis of 78 trials involving nearly 300,000 people found that in the more rigorously designed trial groups, those taking them actually had a slightly higher mortality rate. In two large trials conducted specifically on smokers, beta-carotene increased the incidence of lung cancer by 18% to 28%. Mortality also increased by 8% to 17%. Smokers and those previously exposed to asbestos must especially not take them.
About ⟦0.5~2⟧ per day. For smokers, the real price is the increased risk of lung cancer.

Cochrane pooled 78 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 296,707 people. People taking antioxidant supplements had a total mortality RR of 1.02 (RR is relative risk; 1 means both sides are the same; the 95% confidence interval from 0.98 to 1.05 is the reliable range). Considering only the more rigorously designed, low-bias trial groups, the RR was 1.04 (1.01–1.07), slightly higher. Specifically for beta-carotene RR 1.05 (1.01–1.09), and for vitamin E RR 1.03 (1.00–1.05). The ATBC trial took 29,133 male smokers taking 20 mg daily; the lung cancer incidence was 18% higher (3%–36%), and total mortality was 8% higher (1%–16%). The CARET trial took 18,314 people who were smokers or had been exposed to asbestos. Their risk of lung cancer was about 28% higher (RR 1.28; 1.04–1.57). The risk of death was about 17% higher (all-cause mortality RR 1.17; 1.03–1.33). It seems worth the money because the logical chain "antioxidant is anti-aging, anti-aging prevents cancer" sounds like common sense at every step.
Do not rely on glucosamine or chondroitin to treat knee osteoarthritis
A

People with knee osteoarthritis who took a placebo for 24 weeks—six out of ten said their pain decreased. People taking glucosamine or chondroitin were only four or five percentage points higher, which is so small it could be random. Spending ⟦700~1800⟧ per year buys an effect nearly identical to taking a placebo.
About ⟦2~5⟧ per day, ⟦700~1800⟧ per year.

The GAIT trial took 1,583 people with knee osteoarthritis, taking supplements for 24 weeks. In the placebo group (fake medicine), 60.1% also reported pain reduction. Glucosamine was only 3.9 percentage points higher (P = 0.30). Chondroitin was 5.3 percentage points higher (P = 0.17). Taking both was 6.5 percentage points higher (P = 0.09). These differences are all too small to rule out the possibility of being random. The real drug used as a control in the same trial was celecoxib, which was 10.0 percentage points higher (P = 0.008). It seems worth the money because "cartilage supplement ingredients" sounds right for the disease, yet even taking a placebo results in six out of ten people saying it works.
Do not rely on vitamin C to prevent colds
A

Taking vitamin C every day almost never reduces your chances of catching a cold; taking it only after catching a cold has inconsistent effects. Daily intake shortens a cold episode by about 8%; whether that is worth three to five hundred yuan a year is for you to calculate. Marathon runners and soldiers marching in cold regions are exceptions: for them, taking it reduces the number of people catching colds by half.
Effervescent tablets are about ⟦1~2⟧ each, ⟦300~700⟧ per year.

Cochrane pooled 29 controlled trials with 11,306 people. Ordinary people taking vitamin C daily almost never reduced the number of colds. The cold incidence RR was 0.97 (RR is relative risk; 1 means both sides are the same). The 95% confidence interval from 0.94 to 1.00 is the reliable range. For trials where intake started only after catching a cold, the original paper stated "no consistent effect was found": some trials showed an effect, some did not. Also in this review, long-term daily intake shortened the duration of cold discomfort by about 8% (adults, 95% confidence interval from 3% to 12%) and children by 14% (7%–21%). Marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers marching in cold regions were exceptions. In 5 trials with 598 people, the number of people catching colds was reduced by about half. The incidence rate RR was 0.48 (95% confidence interval from 0.35 to 0.64). It seems worth the money because it is cheap, sweet and sour, and the phrase "vitamin C prevents colds" has been passed around for half a century.
Do not voluntarily undergo "whole-body PET-CT" or "cancer marker test packages" when asymptomatic
A

When asymptomatic people get screened, the most common result is a false alarm. More than eight out of ten people who get a whole-body CT scan find at least one "abnormality," and nearly four out of ten are called back for follow-up, but most are benign. For women testing for ovarian cancer markers, the number of deaths from ovarian cancer did not decrease, yet some underwent unnecessary surgery due to false alarms.

A whole-body PET-CT scan costs about ⟦7000~10000⟧ once, plus exposure to ionizing radiation. Cancer marker test packages cost a few hundred yuan. The real price lies afterward: finding an "abnormality" that is actually just a false alarm (called a false positive), followed by re-examination, biopsy, and surgery—the money and suffering are all in this part.

The USPSTF, the US body that grades preventive measures, ranks the use of CA-125 and ultrasound screening for ovarian cancer in asymptomatic women at level D, meaning they recommend against it. The basis is the PLCO trial. Ovarian cancer mortality rate: screening group 0.34%, routine group 0.29%. RR 1.18 (95% confidence interval from 0.82 to 1.71). Screening provided no benefit. The rate of unnecessary surgery due to misdiagnosis (false positives) in trials was 0.2%–3.25%, and among these, up to 15% suffered serious surgical complications. Another study performed whole-body CT screening on 1,192 asymptomatic people. 86% found at least one "abnormality," and 37% were advised to have further checks. The original paper stated "most findings were described as benign." It seems worth the money because "scanning the whole body at once, early detection for early cure" fits intuition perfectly.
Do not rely on fitness trackers or activity-counting watches to help you lose weight
B

Overweight people following the same diet and exercise regimen: those wearing activity trackers lost 3.5 kg over two years, while those not wearing them lost 5.9 kg. If you want to lose weight, the device is not a mandatory expense.
Devices cost ⟦200~2000⟧. Additionally, you have to be distracted by those numbers every day.

The IDEA trial took 471 overweight or obese adults and followed them for 24 months. Everyone followed the same diet and exercise regimen, differing only in whether they wore a device. The group wearing devices lost 3.5 kg (95% confidence interval from 2.6 to 4.5, which is the reliable range). The group not wearing devices lost 5.9 kg (5.0–6.8), which was more. The difference between the two groups was 2.4 kg (1.0–3.7; P = 0.002). It seems worth the money because the phrase "what gets measured gets managed" sounds logical, and the device is a one-time purchase.
Do not pay high prices for organic food just to be "healthier"
B

There is no strong evidence that organic food is more nutritious. Only 3 studies actually looked at the health outcomes of people after eating it, and none found a difference. Organic produce does have a 30 percentage point lower detection rate for pesticide residues, but detecting them does not mean they exceed allowable limits.
Usually 1 to 3 times more expensive than regular food of the same type.

A systematic review pooled 17 studies done on humans and 223 studies measuring food composition. The conclusion was a "lack of strong evidence that organic foods are significantly more nutritious than conventional foods." Among these, only 3 studies looked at health outcomes (examining allergies and symptomatic infections), and no difference was found between the two sides. Organic produce had a 30 percentage point lower detection rate for pesticide residues, but detection does not mean it exceeds limits. It seems worth the money because "no pesticides means safer, and safer means healthier" sounds like common sense at every step.
Don't spend a lot of money buying dietary supplements, herbal extracts, or tonics to "nourish the body"
C

Common ingredients like multivitamins, fish oil, and vitamin D—the first six sections of this chapter have reviewed each one, and none were found to be effective. The sentence on the packaging "Dietary supplements are not medicine and cannot replace medicine for treatment" is a statement that supplement regulators mandate must be printed. If this money is for buying gifts for parents or bringing to someone's house, the intention is not wrong, it's just the choice of item that is incorrect.
From a few hundred to over ten thousand yuan. When packaged as gift boxes, the price is often several times higher.

What you get back is the money saved. The reason lies in the first 6 sections of this chapter. The most common ingredients in dietary supplements—multivitamins, fish oil, vitamin D, antioxidants, glucosamine, vitamin C—showed no expected benefits in randomized controlled trials. The figures for each are in the Benefit field of those 6 sections. Regulatory rules only specify what a product is allowed to advertise; they cannot be taken as evidence that it is useless. The State Administration for Market Regulation (China) stipulates that the front of dietary supplement packaging must dedicate at least 20% of the area to printing the sentence: "Dietary supplements are not medicine and cannot replace medicine for treatment." The same regulation limits the function of dietary supplements to "supplementing nutrients in the diet, maintaining or improving health status, or reducing risk factors for disease." It seems worth the money because the phrase "not for curing, only for nourishing" is hard to prove wrong no matter how it's said. When bought as gifts, people pay for sentiment, not for evidence.
Don't take probiotics long-term when there are no intestinal problems
B

Pooling 45 trials conducted on healthy adults, taking probiotics did not cause long-term changes to the gut microbiota; once intake stops, it returns to the original state. Blood lipids also did not improve. Specific cases such as diarrhea caused by taking antibiotics have different evidence and are not included in this section.
About ⟦2~5⟧ per day, ⟦700~1800⟧ per year.

A review pooling 45 trials conducted on healthy adults concluded that it "does not support probiotics causing long-term changes in the gut microbiota, nor does it improve blood lipids in healthy adults." Bacteria in the gut do change, but only temporarily; they return to normal once stopped. It seems worth the money because the concept of "gut health" is broad enough to be applied to anything without being wrong, and the price of one bottle per day is cheap.
Don't force yourself to take cold showers to "increase resistance"
B

In a trial of 3,018 people, those who took cold showers took 29% fewer sick leave instances. However, the total number of sick days remained the same as others, so it cannot be said they were sick less often. In 2025, a pool of 11 trials showed that after dousing with cold water, the body's inflammatory markers even increased temporarily, while immune markers remained unchanged. If you like showering, go ahead, just don't consider it a health investment.

Costs no money. Every day you must endure 30 to 90 seconds of discomfort; maintaining this in winter requires willpower. People with cardiovascular disease must be careful, as cold stimulation poses risks for them.

The Netherlands conducted a randomized controlled trial with 3,018 people who, after a hot shower, doused themselves with cold water for 30, 60, or 90 seconds. Their sick leave instances decreased by 29% (IRR 0.71, which is the rate ratio). However, the original paper clearly states "the number of sick days did not differ significantly between groups": the total number of days sick was the same for both sides. Quality of life, work productivity, and anxiety also showed no significant differences. In 2025, a systematic review pooled 11 randomized trials with 3,177 people. Immediately after cold water immersion and after 1 hour, the body's inflammatory markers even increased. Immune markers remained unchanged. Stress only decreased at the 12-hour mark. The authors themselves stated the evidence was "limited by few RCTs and small sample sizes," meaning there are too few of these randomized trials and each has few participants. It seems worth the money because it costs nothing, and the intuition that "suffering brings results" is very persuasive.
Don't buy detox products, colon cleanses, fermented enzyme products, or alkaline water
C

The detox industry is very large, but clinical evidence supporting it is very scarce, and no one has conducted serious trials on commercial detox diets. Someone looked for whether the acid-alkaline levels of food or alkaline water were related to cancer and found only 1 study meeting the criteria, which also found no correlation.
A few hundred to several thousand yuan. "Detox" types involving fasting can also cause hypoglycemia and nutrient deficiencies.

That review concluded that "although the detox industry is booming, clinical evidence supporting these diets is very thin," and "there are no randomized controlled trials on commercial detox diets." Another systematic review specifically looked at whether the acid-alkaline levels of food or alkaline water were related to cancer: after reviewing 8,278 papers, only 1 met the criteria for inclusion, and the results showed no correlation. The authors wrote "promoting an alkaline diet and alkaline water to the public for the prevention or treatment of cancer is not justified." It seems worth the money because the two premises "there are toxins in the body that must be expelled" and "an acidic body causes cancer" sound very much like physiology.
Don't force yourself to drink water just to reach "8 glasses a day"
C

Someone specifically traced the source of the "8 glasses of water a day" claim and could not find a single study supporting it. Food and other beverages already contain a lot of water, so there is no need to drink that much. This conclusion only applies to healthy adults living in temperate climates who are normally sedentary. Those working in the heat, exercising heavily, or people who must drink more to treat or prevent illness should proactively drink more.
Costs no money. Takes a bit of time and effort to remember to drink, and you may have to wake up more at night to urinate.

A literature review specifically investigating the "8x8" claim—8 glasses of 8 ounces of water each day—concluded that "no scientific studies were found to support 8x8." The paper also stated that "surveys of food and fluid intake of thousands of adults strongly suggest that such large amounts are not needed," because food and other drinks already provide plenty of water. The author specified that this conclusion only applies to "healthy adults in temperate climates who are sedentary most of the time." He also noted that there are diseases where treatment or prevention requires 8x8 or more, and "heavy labor or exercise, especially in hot climates" naturally requires drinking more. This claim seems worth the money because water is free, the number 8 is round, and the advice to "drink plenty of water" seems harmless everywhere.
Don't spend money on fortune-telling, tarot cards, or zodiac signs to make decisions
B

There is a classic classroom experiment: the "personal personality analysis" that students receive is actually identical for everyone, yet everyone finds it very accurate. Fortune-telling seems correct for this reason. An astrologer choosing correctly is no better than guessing. The price isn't just a few dozen yuan: a fortune-telling gang in Xi County, Henan Province, collected "incense money" and "offering packages" up to ⟦3888⟧; the leader was sentenced to eleven years in prison.
Costs no money. The difficulty is giving up a shortcut for decision-making; from now on, you must think for yourself.

A classic classroom experiment: after students complete a personality test, they receive a "personal analysis" that is actually the same for everyone, yet the majority consider it very accurate. The author concluded that "the fact that the person being analyzed or the analyzer accepts it does not prove the explanation is correct." 39 students rated the accuracy of the analysis on a scale of 0 to 5; 34 people gave it a 4 or 5. Based on the distribution in the table, the average was about 4.26 points. This explains why fortune-telling always seems correct; this phenomenon is called the Barnum effect. Astrology was also tested in a double-blind study published in Nature. Astrologers had to choose one of three personality test results that matched a birth chart. Out of 116 charts, they chose correctly 40 times. Pure guessing would have yielded 38.5 correct choices, while the astrologers themselves predicted they would get 58.5 right. Official case: The People's Procuratorate of Xi County, Henan Province (China) announced an online fortune-telling fraud gang that used free palm reading to lure people in, then collected "incense money" and "offering packages" up to ⟦3888⟧. More than 50 victims were involved, over ⟦2000000⟧ in illegal funds were recovered, and the leader was sentenced to eleven years in prison with a fine of ⟦100000⟧.
Don't buy blue light blocking glasses to "protect your eyes," and don't believe that "looking at a screen for a few months will ruin your eyes," but treat eye strain, pain, or redness as an emergency
A

Blue light blocking lenses show no benefit; not buying them saves a price difference of a few hundred to over a thousand. Compared to regular lenses, whether the wearer feels eye fatigue or how clearly they see is the same, and no evidence was found that they protect the retina. Looking at a screen until eyes are tired or dry recovers with rest and does not cause permanent damage. What actually ruins eyes are welding arcs, lasers, and acute glaucoma attacks.
Costs no money, and saves a price difference of a few hundred to over a thousand yuan on lenses.

A 2023 Cochrane systematic review included 17 randomized controlled trials, each with 5 to 156 people, followed for less than 1 day to 5 weeks. Because the data was so sparse, the participants in the trials were very different, and the follow-up times were inconsistent, the authors did not pool them into a single overall figure. The results below are all compared to non-blue-light-filtering lenses. Following up for less than a week, self-reported eye fatigue "may not differ," with low certainty of evidence. In one trial of 120 people, the two groups differed by 9.76 units. The 95% confidence interval for this difference was −33.95 to 53.47. This interval crosses both negative and positive, meaning no difference was found. Critical flicker fusion frequency is an objective indicator of eye fatigue; the two groups "may have almost no difference," with low certainty. Best-corrected visual acuity after wearing glasses "is probably not affected." The two groups differed by 0.00 logMAR (95% confidence interval from −0.02 to 0.02). This result came from only 1 study of 156 people, with moderate certainty. Whether it affects daytime alertness could not be determined (2 trials, 42 people, very low certainty). This review also found no evidence that it protects the macula at the back of the eye. The American Academy of Ophthalmology's public education page clearly states that the claim "looking at screens for a long time will permanently harm your eyes" is "not true," it just makes eyes uncomfortable. China's "Catalogue and Classification of Occupational Diseases" (2024 version) lists eye inflammation from welding arcs and eye damage from lasers as occupational diseases.

Don't consider blood donation as a way to stay healthy: "detoxing, lowering blood lipids, and preventing myocardial infarction" are not supported by any randomized trials; donating too frequently actually causes iron deficiency
A

Claims that blood donation can detoxify, lower blood lipids, or prevent myocardial infarction are unreliable. Regular blood donors are inherently healthier; after accounting for this, the reduction in mortality for each additional donation per year shrinks from nearly two-tenths to 7.5%. In trials where people were actually divided for comparison, the number of deaths did not differ. Conversely, donating too frequently does make people tired and sensitive to cold, caused by iron deficiency.

Costs no money. One blood donation session—filling out forms, drawing blood, then staying for observation and rest—takes about an hour. For several weeks afterward, the body is still replenishing the lost iron.

The Kuopio study in Finland followed 2,862 men aged 42 to 60 for an average of nearly 9 years. In the 24 months before the start, 153 people had donated blood, of whom 1 (0.7%) had an acute myocardial infarction. Among the 2,529 who had not donated, 316 (12.5%) had one (difference in proportions P < 0.0001). Adjusting for age and other coronary risk factors, blood donors had about an 88% lower risk of myocardial infarction. Relative risk 0.12 (95% CI 0.02 to 0.86; P = 0.035). However, this was only observational, not a controlled group. The SCANDAT database in Northern Europe has 1,182,495 blood donors, totaling 9,526,627 person-years of follow-up, with 15,401 deaths. When only adjusting for characteristics like age and sex, each additional donation per year was associated with an 18.6% lower mortality rate (95% CI 16.8% to 20.4%). After further adjusting for the "healthy donor effect" (only healthy people are allowed to donate), the reduction was only 7.5% (5.7%–9.4%). The authors concluded this "cannot be interpreted as firm evidence of health benefits." The FeAST randomized controlled trial took 1,277 patients with symptomatic peripheral artery disease, randomly dividing them into two groups: one had periodic phlebotomy every 6 months to reduce iron, and one served as a control. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality, 125/636 (20%) compared to 148/641 (23%). HR 0.85 (HR is the hazard ratio; 1 means both sides are the same). 95% CI 0.67 to 1.08; P = 0.17. Combining mortality with non-fatal myocardial infarction and stroke, it was 180 (28%) vs 205 (32%), HR 0.88 (0.72–1.07; P = 0.20). Neither showed a difference. The INTERVAL randomized trial took 45,263 whole blood donors. They were divided into three donation intervals. For men: 12 weeks, 10 weeks, 8 weeks; for women: 16 weeks, 14 weeks, 12 weeks. Shortening the interval significantly increased the amount of blood collected over two years (men in the 8-week group donated 1.69 units more than the 12-week group, 95% CI 1.59 to 1.80). Quality of life, physical activity, and cognitive function did not differ between groups. However, donation-related symptoms were more frequent, including fatigue, breathlessness, faintness, dizziness, and restless leg syndrome (legs so uncomfortable at night they cannot stay still). Simultaneously, mean hemoglobin and ferritin values were lower, and deferrals for low hemoglobin were more frequent (each index P < 0.0001). Iron deficiency affects the body's thermogenesis: 10 women with iron-deficiency anemia, 8 women with depleted iron stores but no anemia, and 12 control women were immersed for 100 minutes in 28 °C water. The anemic group had a rectal temperature of 36.0 ± 0.2 °C, while the control group was 36.2 ± 0.1 °C (P = 0.001). Oxygen consumption was 5.28 ± 0.26 vs 5.99 ± 0.29 mL·min⁻¹·kg⁻¹ (P = 0.04). Two thyroid hormones, thyroxine and triiodothyronine, were also lower (P < 0.002). This rumor seems true because blood donors are already healthy people who have been screened repeatedly, while the hypothesis that "releasing iron protects the heart" has not been proven by randomized trials.
Don't rely on generic health check-up packages for disease prevention; instead, perform evidence-based screening items according to age and gender
A

People who have regular general health check-ups and those who do not have the same mortality rates; deaths from cardiovascular disease and cancer are also equally frequent. Performing evidence-based screening items according to age and gender is sufficient. From age 35, blood pressure is measured for free once a year, and from age 65, a free health check-up is provided once a year (China).
Costs no money, and saves several hundred to several thousand yuan per year on check-up packages. In return, you must remember which items need checking and how often each item should be checked.

A 2019 update of a Cochrane systematic review included 17 randomized controlled trials. When calculating total mortality, pooling 11 trials with 233,298 participants and 21,535 deaths, the general health check-up group and the control group were the same, RR 1.00. RR is the relative risk; 1 means both sides are the same. The 95% confidence interval from 0.97 to 1.03 is the reliable range of fluctuation. For mortality from cardiovascular disease, pooling 9 trials with 170,227 people and 6,237 deaths, RR 1.05 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.16). For mortality from cancer, pooling 8 trials with 139,290 people and 3,663 deaths, RR 1.01 (95% CI 0.92 to 1.12). These two indicators also showed no difference. The authors concluded "general health checks are unlikely to be beneficial." The National Basic Public Health Service Program (China) provides permanent residents aged 35 and older with one free blood pressure measurement per year. This program also provides seniors aged 65 and older with one free health check-up per year. This free check-up includes a physical exam, complete blood count, urinalysis, fasting blood glucose, and ECG. Liver function tests include AST, ALT, and total bilirubin. Kidney function tests include serum creatinine and blood urea. Blood lipid tests include total cholesterol, triglycerides, LDL-cholesterol, and HDL-cholesterol. Finally, abdominal ultrasound of the liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and spleen (nationwide).
Don't start taking uric acid-lowering medication just because a health check-up shows high uric acid if you have never had pain
A

For people with uric acid levels above the limit who have never had a gout attack or tophi, the American College of Rheumatology recommends not taking uric acid-lowering medication for now. 24 people must take it for a full 3 years to prevent just one gout attack. Trying to use it to protect the kidneys also fails: in people with kidney disease taking the drug, kidney function still declined as fast as those taking a placebo. Wait until an actual attack occurs before treating.
Costs no money, and saves on long-term medication costs and regular follow-up visits, while avoiding the risk of unnecessary medication use.

The 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout discusses asymptomatic hyperuricemia. This refers to people with serum uric acid > 6.8 mg/dL who have never had a gout attack and have no subcutaneous tophi. The guideline conditionally recommends that these individuals should not start any uric acid-lowering therapy. Medications include allopurinol, febuxostat, and probenecid. The certainty of evidence was rated as "high." A note below the table specifies "based on attributable risk, 24 patients need to be treated for 3 years to prevent one gout attack." The CKD-FIX randomized controlled trial took 363 people. They had stage 3 or 4 chronic kidney disease, had never had gout, but were at risk of progression. One group took 100–300 mg of allopurinol daily, while the other took a placebo. The trial lasted 104 weeks. eGFR is an indicator of kidney function, in mL/min/1.73 m². One group changed by −3.33 per year (95% CI −4.11 to −2.55). The other group changed by −3.23 per year (−3.98 to −2.47). The difference between the two groups was −0.10 (−1.18 to 0.97), P = 0.85; kidney function declined equally fast. Serious adverse events were 46% vs 44%. The PERL randomized controlled trial took 530 people with type 1 diabetes and early-to-mid-stage diabetic kidney disease, who took allopurinol for 3 years, then stopped for 2 months to wash out the drug's effects. Allopurinol did lower serum uric acid from 6.1 to 3.9 mg/dL. However, after stopping the drug, the GFR kidney function index difference between the two groups was only 0.001 mL/min/1.73 m². The 95% CI for this difference was −1.9 to 1.9, P = 0.99. The amount of albumin leaking into the urine in the allopurinol group was even 40% higher (0 to 80). It seems worth the money because the intuition that "if the index is over the limit, you must take medicine to force it down" is very persuasive.
Do not undergo preventive gallbladder removal just because gallstones were found during a check-up if you have never experienced pain
A

Among people with gallstones who have never experienced pain, about eight out of ten remain asymptomatic for nearly nine years. Without intervention, only about 1 to 3 per 1,000 people per year encounter emergencies such as cholecystitis or pancreatitis. Gallbladder removal is not without risks: about 1.5% of patients suffer bile duct injury. Therefore, both European and British guidelines state: if there are no symptoms, do not perform surgery yet.
Costs nothing and avoids a surgery under general anesthesia and a hospital stay. In return, you must remember which signs require immediate hospital visits.

The MICOL community survey in Italy performed ultrasounds on 11,229 people aged 29 to 69. They detected 856 people with gallstones, of whom 580 were asymptomatic, with an average follow-up of 8.7 years. Among these 580 people, 453 (78.1%) remained asymptomatic, 61 (10.5%) developed mild symptoms, and 66 (11.4%) developed severe symptoms. During the follow-up period, there were a total of 189 cholecystectomies, 41.3% of which were performed on asymptomatic individuals. The authors concluded "expectant management remains an effective approach for the majority of patients"; expectant management means monitoring first without surgery. An HMO organization in the US tracked statistics for 691 people diagnosed with gallstones, with an average follow-up of 78 ± 61.6 months. Among them, 135 asymptomatic individuals were followed for 58 ± 50.2 months (median 46.3 months); only 10% developed biliary symptoms, and 7% required surgery. Among 50 deaths in the entire group, only 2 were related to the biliary tract, and both were in the symptomatic group. The authors concluded "patients with silent stones do not need surgery before symptoms appear"; silent stones are stones that remain still and do not cause pain. NICE (UK) guideline CG188, section 1.2.1, states: "for people with a normal gallbladder and biliary tree, incidentally identified asymptomatic gallstones, they should be informed that treatment is not necessary before symptoms occur." The 2016 gallstone guidelines from the European Association for the Study of the Liver weigh the risks on both sides. Asymptomatic individuals have a 0.7% to 2.5% annual risk of developing symptoms. Each year, 0.1% to 0.3% suffer from acute cholecystitis, acute pancreatitis, obstructive jaundice (blocked bile duct, turning yellow), or cholangitis. After the first biliary colic, the risk of complications increases to 1% to 3% per year, so most people will experience pain once before a major event occurs. Regarding surgery, in 51,041 cholecystectomies in the Swedish national registry, 1.5% suffered bile duct injury. About one-fifth of those (0.3%) involved partial or complete bile duct transection. People with bile duct injury have a one-year mortality rate of 3.9%, compared to 1.1% for those without. The guidelines also note: after removal, 10% to 40% of patients still experience discomfort, or improve for a while then relapse. The guideline's conclusion: operating on asymptomatic people, whether through open or laparoscopic surgery, does not extend life expectancy. This is because the risk of death and complications from the surgery itself exceeds the risk of not removing it. Waiting for symptoms to appear before treating also results in lower total costs. A 1983 calculation provided specific figures: a 30-year-old male undergoing preventive removal lives an average of 4 days less than if monitored first; a 50-year-old male lives 18 days less. To date, no randomized trials have compared removal versus non-removal. Preventive removal seems worthwhile due to the intuition that "it will hurt sooner or later, so it's better to remove it once and for all while young."
Do not avoid calcium to prevent kidney stones
A

People who have had calcium oxalate stones are often advised to eat less calcium, but trial results show the exact opposite. Men with recurrent stones who consumed normal amounts of calcium, while also reducing animal protein and salt, had a recurrence rate only half that of the low-calcium group over five years. British guidelines also clearly state not to restrict calcium.
Costs nothing. On the contrary, it saves effort as you don't have to be wary of everything containing calcium every day.

A 5-year randomized controlled trial involved 120 men with recurrent calcium oxalate stones and high urinary calcium (called idiopathic hypercalciuria). They were randomly divided into two groups. One group consumed a normal calcium diet of 30 mmol per day. This group also ate less animal protein (52 g per day) and less salt (50 mmol of sodium chloride per day). The other group followed a traditional low-calcium diet of 10 mmol per day. Over 5 years, the number of recurrences was 12/60 compared to 23/60. The unadjusted relative risk was 0.49 (95% confidence interval from 0.24 to 0.98, a reliable range), P = 0.04; the normal calcium group had only half the risk of recurrence. During follow-up, urinary calcium in both groups decreased by about 170 mg per day. However, urinary oxalate excretion differed. The low-calcium group increased by an average of 5.4 mg per day, while the normal calcium group decreased by an average of 7.2 mg per day. NICE (UK) guideline NG118, section 1.8.1, clearly states: do not restrict daily calcium intake. Adults should maintain 700 to 1,200 mg per day. Children and adolescents should maintain 350 to 1,000 mg per day depending on age. Avoiding calcium seems worthwhile due to the intuition that "if stones are made of calcium, then eat less calcium."
Do not buy quartz, bracelets, Pixiu, and similar items to "change your luck," "attract wealth," or "nourish the body"
B

Claims that wearing these items can change luck, attract wealth, or nourish the body have no verifiable evidence. It seems to follow the same logic as fortune-telling: if the words are general enough, you will apply them to yourself. Sellers claiming medicinal benefits are using false advertising; in 2026, a livestream room was penalized for this. Buying them as jewelry is fine.

Costs nothing. All you need to do is not include "changing luck" or "nourishing the body" as reasons for purchase. The difficulty lies in not following the trend when everyone else is wearing them and claiming they work.

A classic classroom experiment showed that everyone received the same generic "personal analysis," yet the majority found it very accurate; this phenomenon is called the Barnum effect. It explains where the feeling that "wearing it truly makes things smoother" comes from. The author concluded that "personal acceptance does not prove the explanation is correct." Official case: on June 4, 2026, the State Administration for Market Regulation (China) announced a series of typical cases regarding "combating counterfeits and cleaning the source" in the traditional handicraft market. Among them was a jewelry store in Sihui, Guangdong, that fabricated product materials in a livestream room. The store also falsely claimed the products had functions such as "preventing and treating rheumatism, increasing resistance, improving sleep quality, and clearing blood vessels." This store staged scripted performances to mislead and deceive consumers. This violated Article 9, Paragraph 1 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law (China) (national).
Do not rely on shopping to improve your mood or feel more status
B

The more people value money and material possessions, the less happy they feel, but the correlation is very weak, and it is impossible to separate which causes which. Some studies also find that spending money on an experience makes people happier than buying things. Therefore, for the same expenditure, spending on an experience like a trip is more likely to make you happy than filling a shopping cart.
Costs nothing. The difficulty lies in refraining from clicking 'order' when your mood is bad.

A meta-analysis (combining many studies) included 259 independent samples and 753 effect sizes. Result: the more people value materialism, the lower their self-reported happiness. On the most commonly used multidimensional scale, the correlation coefficient r = −0.19 (after adjustment ρ = −0.24). On scales measuring only the "valuing money" aspect, the correlation was weaker, r = −0.08 to −0.11. When separated by outcome type, the strength varied. It was strongest for health behaviors and risky consumption, and negative self-evaluation, r = −0.28 to −0.44. It was weakest for life satisfaction and negative emotions, r = −0.13 to −0.15. The authors also performed a mediation analysis (to see which factors transmit the relationship), suggesting this inverse relationship might be due to unmet psychological needs. Another study: two surveys with two different groups of people found that respondents said money spent on a life experience made them happier than money spent on buying things. In a subsequent laboratory experiment, the positive mood when recalling spending money on an experience was also higher than when recalling a purchase (no national data for China; both studies used foreign samples).
Do not spend extra money to upgrade your house, car, or social circle just to "be one step above those around you"
B

Comparing people with equal incomes, the more their neighbors earn, the lower their self-reported happiness. This mainly occurs with neighbors of similar education levels and is more pronounced for those who interact frequently with neighbors. Thus, the extra money spent to move to a place where everyone is wealthier than you is essentially buying a one-step demotion for yourself. However, when everyone's income increases together, people still find life easier.

Costs nothing. All you need to do before increasing your budget is ask one more question: does this difference buy a gift for yourself, or buy your position among these people? The difficulty lies in not following the trend when everyone around you has upgraded.

The US National Survey of Families and Households (NSFH) interviewed the same group of people in two waves. The authors cross-referenced this data with local average incomes. Local average income (PUMA) was estimated from a 5% sample of the 1990 census. After subtracting personal income and a range of individual characteristics, the result was: the higher the neighbors' income, the lower the self-reported happiness. This effect is large, robust to different calculation methods, and highly statistically significant. The authors stated that "an increase in neighbors' income" and "a decrease in one's own income by the same amount" reduce happiness by the same order of magnitude. Switching to a before-and-after comparison of the same person (adding individual fixed effects), the coefficient remained in the same direction and nearly the same magnitude, though the significance level dropped to 10%. Limiting the analysis further within the same state and survey wave (adding state and wave fixed effects), the results remained basically unchanged. This indicates it is not because "people who like moving to poor areas are inherently happier," nor is it due to some unmeasured state-level factor. The impact was stronger for those who interact frequently with neighbors and was not statistically significant for those who only socialize with friends outside the neighborhood. There was no difference between renters and homeowners; this does not support the explanation that "expensive areas have high housing costs, so there is less money actually available to spend." Happiness only decreased relative to the income of neighbors with similar education levels, with almost no reaction to the income of neighbors with different education levels. And it is transmitted mainly through "satisfaction with one's own material circumstances," not through satisfaction with other aspects like family life. Finally, if both personal and neighbors' incomes increase by the same proportion, happiness still increases.
Do not believe that "willpower is like a muscle, it runs out after use"
A

A popular saying is: doing a task that requires self-control effort first makes it easier to let go afterward, so willpower must be rationed. 23 laboratories and 2,141 people replicated this experiment using the same protocol, and the results were nearly zero. Stop using "I'm out of willpower today" as an explanation for yourself, and do not spend money on courses that teach how to accumulate willpower.
Costs nothing. Just requires a change in phrasing.

A multi-lab pre-registered replication study involving 23 laboratories and a total of 2,141 participants. They replicated the sequential-task paradigm following the standardized protocol of Sripada et al.: first performing a task that depletes self-control, followed by a second task requiring self-control. The pooled results showed a very small ego depletion effect, and the 95% confidence interval included 0 (d = 0.04; 95% CI from −0.07 to 0.15). Based on this, the authors discussed whether the "self-control as a limited resource" model still holds. Another pre-registered replication with 36 laboratories and 3,531 people found an effect size of d = 0.06, also too small to be considered significant.
Do not rely on breakfast or 16:8 intermittent fasting for weight control; choose an eating schedule you can maintain long-term
A

A common claim is that skipping breakfast causes people to overeat aggressively at lunch and dinner, making the daily total even higher. In trials, this is not the case: people who skip breakfast eat over two hundred kcal less per day and weigh slightly less. Comparing 16:8 to simply eating less, there is no difference in weight after one year. Long-term breakfast skippers have about 17% more cardiovascular disease, but this is only a correlation; no difference was found in total mortality.
Costs nothing. Saves some daily mental effort spent struggling with meal times.

First, consider the claim "skipping breakfast leads to eating more later." A meta-analysis of 13 randomized trials found that the group assigned to eat breakfast consumed 259.79 kcal more per day than the breakfast-skipping group (95% CI 78.87 to 440.71, a reliable range). Their weight was 0.44 kg higher (0.07–0.82). Breakfast skippers did not compensate by eating more at lunch or dinner. These trials had very short follow-ups: average weight measured at 7 weeks, average intake at 2 weeks. Next, consider time-restricted eating like 16:8. A trial of 116 overweight adults for 12 weeks found that the group eating only from 12 PM to 8 PM, compared to a group eating three regular meals a day, had a weight difference of −0.26 kg (−1.30 to 0.78), which was not statistically significant. Another trial in Guangzhou with 139 obese individuals followed for 12 months found that time-restricted eating with calorie control reduced weight by 1.8 kg more than calorie control alone (−4.0 to 0.4), also not statistically significant. Finally, consider if long-term breakfast skipping is harmful. A synthesis of 2.38 million people found that breakfast skippers had about a 17% higher risk of cardiovascular disease (OR 1.17; 1.09–1.26) and about a 49% higher risk of cardiovascular death (OR 1.49; 1.20–1.84). However, these were observational studies, not randomized groups. In the original study following participants for 17 to 23 years, the hazard ratio for all-cause mortality was 1.19, with a confidence interval from 0.99 to 1.42, which includes 1, so no statistically significant difference was found.
Do not believe that "masturbation harms the body" or that "abstinence is the only way to improve"; what truly needs monitoring is whether it interferes with sleep, work, and relationships
B

No evidence shows masturbation harms health. Men who ejaculate frequently have about two-tenths less prostate cancer, though some studies found a slightly higher risk for those who were very active when young. A small number of people feel exhausted after every ejaculation, as if they have a cold, taking several days to recover; this is a rare disease, and one should see a urologist or andrologist. Feeling "addicted to pornography" is usually because the behavior conflicts more with one's own moral values.
Costs nothing. Saves money on "kidney-tonifying" remedies and "abstinence" courses, along with prolonged self-blame.

First, look at the body. A US study followed 31,925 men until 2010. Each reported monthly ejaculation frequency and was grouped accordingly. Compared to those with 4 to 7 times per month, those with 21 or more times per month had a prostate cancer HR of 0.81 (95% CI 0.72 to 0.92, about 19% lower). This was calculated based on frequency at ages 20 to 29. Based on frequency at ages 40 to 49, the HR was 0.78 (0.69–0.89, about 22% lower). The reduction was mainly in low-risk prostate cancer. Conversely, a case-control study in the UK comparing 431 men diagnosed before age 60 with 409 controls found that frequent masturbation in one's twenties and thirties carried a slightly higher risk, while frequent masturbation in one's fifties carried a slightly lower risk. Next, look at pornography. A systematic review and meta-analysis suggested many people feel "addicted" primarily because the behavior does not align with their beliefs, not just because of high usage. A small number of people truly feel ill after ejaculation, but this is not "harming the body"; it is a rare disease called Post-Orgasmic Illness Syndrome (POIS). If affected, one should seek medical consultation, not abstinence. Among 45 patients in the Netherlands, 87% had onset within 30 minutes of ejaculation, 80% had debilitating fatigue, and 78% felt like they had a cold. 37 patients at a hospital in France took an average of 4.7 days to recover. The cause is unknown. In the Dutch study, 29 out of 33 patients (88%) tested positive for a skin allergy to their own semen. A study of 24 patients in China found no allergic antibodies targeting semen, but patients had higher anxiety and depression scores. A 2025 review found only 14 treatment studies, 12 of which were single case reports. Among 211 sexual medicine experts worldwide, only 18% said more than three-tenths of patients could improve (USA / UK / Netherlands / France / China).
Do not spend money on "curing sexual orientation" or "curing homosexuality," and do not take family members to such places
B

An expert group from the American Psychological Association reviewed studies and stated that this type of "cure" does not change sexual orientation and can cause harm. In a US survey, those who underwent "cures" had nearly nine-tenths more suicidal thoughts. In China, a psychiatric hospital once used the label "sexual preference disorder" to forcibly hospitalize a man; the court ruled it a rights violation and awarded ⟦5000⟧ in compensation.
Costs nothing. Saves money paid to "cure" facilities, psychological clinics, and "gay conversion" camps. The difficulty lies in family members insisting on going.

A 2009 report by an American Psychological Association task force stated that efforts to change sexual orientation are "unlikely to be successful and involve some risk of harm." Regarding placing minors in forced or residential "cure" programs, the report advised that neither parents nor children should consider them. A nationally representative survey in the US interviewed 1,518 sexual minority adults; about 7% had undergone "cures," eight-tenths of which were performed by religious figures. Adjusting for factors like age and adverse childhood experiences, those who underwent "cures" had a lifetime suicidal ideation OR of 1.92 (95% CI 1.01 to 3.64, about nine-tenths higher). Suicidal planning OR was 1.75 (1.01–3.06). Suicide attempts with no or minor injury OR was 1.88 (1.01–3.50). Another study interviewed 245 young adults aged 21 to 25. Among those whose parents did not try to change their orientation during puberty, 22.0% had attempted suicide. For those whose parents tried to change it themselves, it was 48.1%. For those whose parents also took them to a therapist or religious figure, it was 62.8%. The World Health Organization's ICD-10 classification clearly states: "sexual orientation by itself is not to be considered a disorder." In 2017, the Yicheng District Court in Zhumadian, Henan (China) heard a case: a psychiatric hospital used the label "sexual preference disorder" to forcibly hospitalize a man. The court held that he was "in a normal condition and had no behavior or risk of suicide, injury, or property damage, and did not meet the criteria for mandatory treatment." The court ordered the hospital to publicly apologize and pay ⟦5000⟧ for mental distress (USA / China).
Do not rely on learning "proper lifting posture" or attending lifting workshops to prevent back pain; what needs to be reduced is the weight and frequency of lifting, and normally, exercise more
A

Workers who attended lifting posture training did not experience less back pain than those who did not. People who bend their backs frequently while lifting were not found to be more prone to back pain. Factors related to back pain are lifting heavy loads and lifting frequently: for every 10 kg increase in weight or 10 additional lifts per day, the risk increases by about one-tenth. People who exercise regularly have three-tenths to over four-tenths fewer episodes of back pain.

Costs nothing. No need to struggle with whether to bend your back while lifting, and no need to spend money on back protection classes or back belts. There are two things to do: split heavy loads, use a trolley, or ask for help, which only takes a few extra minutes. Spend a few times a week exercising; this requires long-term persistence.

First, look at training. A 2011 Cochrane systematic review synthesized 9 randomized trials involving 20,101 employees. Results from 7 trials with 19,317 people showed that those who received lifting training and those who did nothing reported nearly identical back pain (OR 1.17; 95% CI 0.68 to 2.02, including 1). Compared to those who only watched a video, the RR was 0.93 (0.69–1.25), also nearly the same. Evidence quality was moderate. The authors concluded: lifting advice and training, with or without assistive devices, do not prevent back pain or disability due to back pain. Next, look at back bending. A 2020 systematic review synthesized studies on the frequency of back bending during lifting; evidence quality was low. In the only follow-up study, the difference in the maximum bending angle between those who later developed back pain and those who did not was only 1.5 degrees (−0.7 to 3.7), which was not statistically significant. 9 out of 11 studies found no difference between the two groups. 7 other studies using different measurements found that those with back pain actually bent their backs 6.0 degrees less (−11.2 to −0.9). The authors concluded: there is no evidence that frequent back bending causes back pain. Finally, look at what to do. A meta-analysis synthesized 8 follow-up studies: for every 10 kg increase in weight lifted, the risk of back pain OR was 1.11 (1.05–1.18, about 11% higher). For every 10 additional lifts per day, the OR was 1.09 (1.03–1.15, about 9% higher). Another paper synthesized 21 randomized trials with 30,850 people. Exercise combined with education reduced the risk of back pain episodes RR 0.55 (0.41–0.74, about 45% lower), moderate quality evidence. Exercise alone RR 0.65 (0.50–0.86, about 35% lower), low to very low quality evidence. Education alone RR 1.03 (0.83–1.27) and back belts RR 1.01 (0.71–1.44) showed no effect. Official guidance from the UK Health and Safety Executive (HSE) also clearly states that relying solely on training does not guarantee safety during manual handling. Good lifting techniques cannot replace the provision of lifting equipment and improvements to tasks and loads.
Do not rely on taking massive calcium supplements or drinking bone broth for faster bone healing after a fracture
B

In trials of vitamin D supplementation after fractures, none showed better bone healing. Research on supplementing both calcium and vitamin D is very limited, making it unclear if it is beneficial. The calcium in a large bowl of bone broth is only a few dozen times less than the daily recommended intake. People with existing vitamin D deficiency or osteoporosis are separate cases.

Zero cost; it even saves money and effort spent on buying calcium pills, vitamin D, and simmering broth daily. The only necessary action is to supplement if a test shows a deficiency and avoid extra supplementation if not.

First, regarding vitamin D: A 2023 systematic review of 14 studies involving 2,734 fracture patients concluded that vitamin D supplementation alone has very little effect on bone healing, union rates, or post-recovery function. Studies showing benefits were mostly of low quality. The authors explicitly stated that when considering only randomized trials, none showed a benefit from supplementation. One trial took 100 patients with long bone fractures and low vitamin D; half took a single dose of 100,000 IU within two weeks of injury, and half took a placebo. Each group had 2 cases of non-union, totaling 4%. Another trial of 102 people aged 18 to 50 with femur or tibia fractures divided them into four groups receiving different doses or a placebo. At months 3 and 12, bone healing scores did not differ. Another trial involved 32 postmenopausal women with wrist fractures; compared to those not supplementing, the high-dose group (equivalent to 1,800 IU daily) actually had lower bone compressive stiffness. Next, regarding calcium: A 2014 systematic review stated there is very little clinical research on how vitamin D deficiency or supplementation affects bone healing, concluding the results are unclear. Two studies found that supplementing both calcium and vitamin D increased bone density or callus (new bone growth) at the fracture site but did not assess healing speed. Finally, regarding bone broth: A study in Kaohsiung, Taiwan, measured three types of bone broth noodles, with each portion of broth being 450 to 550 grams. The calcium in each portion averaged 14 to 39 mg, representing 1.4% to 3.9% of the recommended 1,000 mg daily intake. The authors concluded that calcium in one portion of broth is less than 5% of the daily recommendation.
