If the policyholder intentionally causes the death, disability, or illness of the insured, the insurer is not liable to pay the insurance money. If the policyholder has paid premiums for two or more years, the cash value is paid to other entitled persons. If a beneficiary intentionally causes the death, disability, or illness of the insured, or intentionally attempts to kill the insured but fails, they lose the right to the benefit. Article 27, paragraph 2: if the policyholder or insured intentionally creates an insured event, the insurer has the right to terminate the contract, bears no responsibility for compensation or payment, and except for cases in Article 43, does not refund the premiums. Article 1125 of the Civil Code (China): intentionally killing the decedent results in the loss of inheritance rights. Article 198, paragraph 1, point 5 of the Criminal Law (China) includes "the policyholder or beneficiary intentionally causing the death, disability, or illness of the insured to defraud insurance money" under the crime of insurance fraud. If the amount is relatively large, it is punishable by up to 5 years in prison, with a fine of ⟦10000~100000⟧. If the amount is large, it is 5 to 10 years in prison. If especially large, it is 10 years or more in prison. Paragraph 2: committing the act in that point while simultaneously constituting another crime shall be punished according to the provisions on the combined punishment for multiple crimes; combined punishment means adding the crimes together to determine the penalty. Article 232: murder is punishable by death, life imprisonment, or fixed-term imprisonment of ten years or more. An illustrative case is that of Zhang Mou Song in Xuancheng, Anhui (China). In the early morning of July 18, 2016, he drove his car into a pond, and his wife drowned. Less than half a month earlier, he had bought 4 insurance policies for his wife, each for ⟦1000000⟧. He was arrested on July 25. The court combined the crimes of murder and insurance fraud, sentencing him to death with a reprieve, plus a fine of ⟦50000⟧.

When reporting to the police, demand a case acceptance receipt immediately; if they don't file the case, demand a written notice: you have 7 days to request a reconsideration, another 7 days to request a review, and the procuratorate can require the police to file the case
A

After reporting to the police, you must get a case acceptance receipt immediately; it is proof that you reported the case. If the police decide not to file the case, they must give you a written notice of non-filing. If you disagree, you can apply for reconsideration within 7 days; if still disagreeing, you can apply for a review within the next 7 days. You can also approach the procuratorate to have them supervise the police's filing of the case.

Costs no money. Ask one more question on the spot to ensure you get the case acceptance receipt. Afterward, follow the time markers above to inquire about progress. The difficulty is repeatedly speaking up to ask.

Article 171 of the Provisions on the Procedures for Handling Criminal Cases by Public Security Organs (China) (after revision by Order No. 159 of the Ministry of Public Security) discusses receipts. Original text: "When accepting a case, the public security organ shall create an acceptance registration form and a case acceptance receipt, and deliver the receipt to the person who handed over the offender, the person who reported the case, the accuser, or the informant." Article 174: "For cases accepted or criminal clues discovered, the public security organ shall quickly review them." Article 178 discusses whether to file a case. After acceptance and review, if it is found that a crime has occurred and criminal responsibility needs to be pursued, and it falls under its jurisdiction, the case must be filed. Filing must be approved by the person in charge of the public security organ at or above the county level. If the case is not filed, they must also give you a paper: "For cases with an accuser, if a decision is made not to file the case, the public security organ shall create a notice of non-filing and send it to the accuser within three days." Article 179 discusses what to do when disagreeing. Original text: "If the accuser disagrees with the decision not to file the case, they may, within seven days after receiving the notice of non-filing, apply for reconsideration to the public security organ that made the decision; the public security organ shall make a decision within thirty days after receiving the application for reconsideration." Furthermore: "If the accuser disagrees with the reconsideration decision regarding non-filing, they may, within seven days after receiving the reconsideration decision, apply for a review to the higher public security organ; the higher public security organ shall make a decision within thirty days after receiving the application for review. If the higher public security organ vacates the decision not to file the case, the lower public security organ must execute it." For large, complex cases, the time limit for reconsideration and review can be extended, but "it shall not exceed thirty days, and the applicant must be notified in writing." Article 112 of the Criminal Procedure Law (China): if it is found that a crime has occurred and criminal responsibility needs to be pursued, the case must be filed; if not filed, "the reasons for non-filing shall be notified to the accuser. If the accuser disagrees, they may apply for reconsideration." Article 113: "If the victim believes that the public security organ should have filed a case for investigation but did not, and applies to the people's procuratorate, the people's procuratorate shall require the public security organ to explain the reasons for non-filing. If the people's procuratorate believes the reasons for non-filing are untenable, it shall notify the public security organ to file the case, and the public security organ shall file the case upon receiving the notice." Article 61 of the Provisions on the Procedures for Handling Administrative Cases by Public Security Organs (China) also requires this. For cases within their unit's jurisdiction, they "must investigate and handle them immediately, create an acceptance registration form and a case acceptance receipt, and deliver the receipt to the person who reported the case, the accuser, the informant, or the person who handed over the violator." The time limit for handling public security cases "shall not exceed 30 days from the date of acceptance; for large, complex cases, with approval from the higher public security organ, it may be extended by 30 days," and appraisal time is not included in the handling period. Article 9 of the Regulations on Supervision of Public Security Organs (China) discusses complaints against the police. Original text: "The supervision organ, regarding ongoing illegal or disciplinary acts of public security organs and people's police reported by the public, shall arrive promptly, handle them on the spot according to regulations, and promptly feedback the handling results to the complainant" (National China).

Do not give money or cards to people handling cases or enforcing the law: giving a bribe means you will also be punished, and bribing those in supervision, administrative law enforcement, or justice results in even harsher punishment
A

"Paying a little to settle things" is a separate crime in the Criminal Law (China), and the person giving the money is also punished. Giving a bribe is punishable by up to 3 years in prison; for serious circumstances, 3 to 10 years; for especially serious circumstances, 10 years or more or life imprisonment. Giving a bribe to personnel in supervision, administrative law enforcement, or justice is specifically listed as a case for heavier punishment. If money is given because it was demanded and no illegitimate benefit is received, it does not count as bribery.
Costs no money. Simply do not do it.

Article 389 of the Criminal Law (China) defines the crime of bribery: "Giving property to a state functionary for the purpose of seeking illegitimate benefits is the crime of bribery." The same article also states: "In economic activities, violating state regulations by giving property to a state functionary in a relatively large amount, or violating state regulations by giving a state functionary kickbacks or handling fees under any name, shall be punished as bribery." It also leaves an exception: "Giving property to a state functionary due to being demanded, without receiving illegitimate benefits, is not bribery." The penalties are stated in Article 390 of the Criminal Law (China) (amended by the Twelfth Amendment to the Criminal Law, effective March 1, 2024). Original text: "Whoever commits the crime of bribery shall be sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of not more than three years or criminal detention, and shall be fined; if the bribery is for seeking illegitimate benefits and the circumstances are serious, or causes heavy losses to national interests, the sentence shall be fixed-term imprisonment of three to ten years, and shall be fined; if the circumstances are especially serious, or cause especially heavy losses to national interests, the sentence shall be fixed-term imprisonment of not less than ten years or life imprisonment, and shall be fined or have property confiscated." There are seven cases for heavier punishment: "(1) bribing multiple times or bribing multiple people; (2) state functionaries giving bribes; (3) giving bribes in national key projects or major projects; (4) giving bribes to obtain appointment, promotion, or transfer of positions; (5) giving bribes to personnel engaged in supervision, administrative law enforcement, or judicial work; (6) giving bribes in the fields of ecological environment, finance, production safety, food and drugs, disaster prevention and mitigation, social security, education, healthcare, etc., to carry out illegal or criminal acts; (7) using illegal gains to give bribes." The final paragraph leaves a path for reduction or exemption when voluntarily confessing: "A briber who voluntarily confesses their act of bribery before being prosecuted may be given a lighter or mitigated punishment. Among them, if the crime is relatively minor and plays a key role in investigating and solving a major case, or if there is a major meritorious service, the punishment may be mitigated or exempted" (National China).
For calls or meetings that might lead to a fallout, just turn on the recording: if you are a participant in the conversation, you do not need to ask the other person's permission first
A

Loans, debts, compensation, refunds, labor disputes—if discussed clearly over the phone without leaving a record, both sides might tell different stories a few months later. Conversations you participate in can be recorded, and not notifying the other person beforehand does not strip the recording of its value as evidence. What you must not do is eavesdrop or spy on others' private matters, break into someone's home to record secretly, or use threats to make the other person speak.
Costs no money. Turning on the phone's call recording or recording software is enough. Record from beginning to end, and after recording, keep the original file intact without editing or overwriting.

Article 66 of the Civil Procedure Law (China) includes audio-visual materials and electronic data in the list of evidence. Article 106 of the Interpretation of the Civil Procedure Law by the Supreme People's Court (China) only excludes evidence obtained in three ways. Those three ways are: seriously infringing upon the legitimate rights and interests of others, violating prohibitive provisions of the law, or seriously violating public order and good morals. "Not notifying the other person beforehand" is not among these three ways. Article 15 of the Provisions on Evidence in Civil Procedures of the Supreme People's Court (China): when using audio or video recordings as evidence, the original storage medium, such as the actual phone used to record, must be submitted. Article 90: if audio-visual materials or electronic data have suspicious points, they cannot be used alone to determine facts. An article by a judge reposted on the official website of the Supreme People's Court (China) also says the same: the recording must be obtained legally, the content must be true, without editing, and it must be relevant to the case (National China).
If an incident occurs at the scene, take panoramic photos first, then relative positions, and finally damages and injuries; do not delete original photos or videos
C

If you only take a close-up of a scratch on a car or an item on the ground, a few days later no one will know where it was originally located. Record a panoramic segment first, capturing the entire intersection, house numbers, vehicles, people, and surroundings, then photograph their positions relative to each other, and finally take detailed shots. If objects or vehicles must be moved, take photos before doing so if possible. Keep original photos and videos on your phone; do not just keep a version transferred through a chat app.
Free. Hold your phone and record continuously for several dozen seconds to a few minutes. First, ensure your own safety; do not delay life-saving efforts or processing.

Article 66 of the Civil Procedure Law (China) includes physical evidence, audio-visual materials, and electronic data in the list of evidence. Article 14 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence (China) classifies images, audio, and video as electronic data. Article 15 requires the submission of original electronic data; if using recordings as evidence, the original media carrier must be submitted. Photos and videos preserve the state of a scene that is about to change, which can then be cross-referenced with police reports, repair records, medical records, and witness statements. The sequence of "panorama, position, detail" is an empirical practice; it is not prescribed by law (National China).

In cases of domestic violence: report to the police first to have a record of police intervention, then apply to the court for a personal safety protection order; no prior divorce is required, and there are no fees
A

According to data from many countries, more than one-third of women murdered are killed by an intimate partner, often the culmination of prolonged domestic violence. Among women who have been beaten, those who have been strangled have a risk of being killed more than 7 times higher than those who have never been strangled. Therefore, if beaten, report to the police, then apply to the court for a protection order. Courts usually must respond within 72 hours.

Free. Applying for a personal safety protection order does not require court fees or security deposits. The cost is the time spent reporting to the police, undergoing injury assessment, and writing the application. The hardest part is speaking out about someone in the household.

First, regarding risks. Aggregating data from 66 countries (systematic review): among female homicide cases, 38.6% are committed by an intimate partner, compared to 6.3% for males. The authors state these murders are often the final step in a long process of abuse. Another study compared 506 cases of homicide and attempted homicide with 427 women who had been beaten but did not experience those outcomes. Those strangled by a partner had a 6.70 times higher risk of attempted homicide than those never strangled (OR = 6.70, 95% CI 3.91 to 11.49). The risk of being killed was 7.48 times higher (OR = 7.48, 95% CI 4.53 to 12.35). Regarding the law: victims and close relatives can report to the police. Police agencies must promptly dispatch personnel, stop domestic violence, investigate and collect evidence, and assist with medical examinations and injury assessments. In minor cases, police may issue a warning letter to the other party. Those suffering from or facing a real risk of domestic violence can apply for a court-issued personal safety protection order. Once accepted, the court must decide within 72 hours, or 24 hours in emergencies. The order can prohibit the other party from committing violence, harassing, stalking, or contacting you and your close relatives, and can even force them to move out of your residence. The order is valid for up to 6 months and can be extended before expiration. Applying does not require a prior divorce. If the court finds domestic violence is "relatively likely," it can issue the order. If the other party violates the order, the court can fine them up to ⟦1000⟧ or detain them for up to 15 days. If it constitutes a crime, it is prosecuted as intentional failure to comply with a judgment or ruling. Frequent insults, threats, stalking, harassment, and even forced exposure to cold or hunger are considered domestic violence.
If a family member incurs gambling debts, do not rush to pay them off: gambling debts are not protected by law, and money borrowed for gambling is not considered joint marital debt
B

Debts incurred at the gambling table are not protected by the court. If a creditor knows a person is borrowing to gamble and still lends the money, the court will not protect this amount either. Money borrowed by one party for gambling is not counted as a debt for both spouses to repay. Without a trial, the court cannot force the non-borrowing party to take responsibility.
Free. The difficulty lies in resisting when creditors come to the house and family members cry and beg. If the creditor actually sues, you must appear in court.

A 2017 notice from the Supreme People's Court (China) notes four points. Debts incurred by one party in illegal or criminal activities such as gambling or drug use are not protected by law. If a creditor knows or should have known the person was borrowing to gamble or use drugs and still lends, it is not protected. If one party borrows in their own name for illegal or criminal activities and then requests it be treated as joint marital debt, the court will not accept it. Without trial procedures, the non-borrowing party cannot be held civilly liable (National China, since 2017).

If an acquaintance asks you to "help scan your face or act as a witness" to borrow money, or asks for a verification code, do not agree: this is an AB loan scheme where you are the borrower, not the guarantor
B

So-called "face scanning or witnessing" is actually using your name to borrow from a bank. You are the borrower, not the guarantor; even if the money is transferred to the acquaintance, the bank will still demand repayment from you. The broker deceived you, but as long as the bank was unaware, you cannot cancel this loan contract. The "I will pay" commitment letter written by your acquaintance is not binding on the bank.

Free. The difficulty is refusing relatives or friends to their face. Even if they say "just be a witness" or "you won't be responsible for anything," still refuse. Do not give your phone, ID card, or bank card to brokers, and do not scan your face or sign names as arranged by brokers. Verification codes are for your use only; do not disclose them even if asked by acquaintances.

A 2022 risk warning from the Fujian Bureau of the National Financial Regulatory Administration (China) describes this tactic. Customer A is ineligible for a loan. A broker says a guarantor is needed and tells A to find B, who has good credentials. In practice, the broker uses B's identity information to apply for the loan, and the money is given to A. The text states "the actual borrower is B," and B "only realizes they are the borrower and not the guarantor when the bank demands debt repayment." A 2024 warning from the Shandong Bureau (China) states brokers promise B they "will not bear any responsibility." Brokers also coach B on how to handle bank pre-loan assessments, where B effectively acts as the borrower. In 2024, the Putuo District Court in Shanghai (China) published a case. Staff used B's phone to download a bank app and applied for a loan directly in B's name. The money entered B's account, B transferred it to A, and A paid over ⟦80000⟧ in processing fees. A group of 8 brokers was sentenced to 10 months to 4 years for contract fraud. Even if the broker is convicted, the loan does not automatically transfer to someone else. Article 149 of the Civil Code (China) states that if a third party commits fraud, the other party must have "known or should have known" for the defrauded party to request cancellation. The "other party" here is the bank; if the bank didn't know, it cannot be cancelled. If cancellable, the request must be made to the court within 1 year of discovering the fraud (Article 152). Borrowers must repay according to the agreed term (Article 675). Contracts only bind the signatories (Article 465). Transferring debt to another requires bank consent (Article 551). Therefore, the commitment letter A wrote is not binding on the bank. Money can only be recovered by suing A personally. If you scan your face for someone without reading the contract, the court will recognize that contract. In 2025, the Shizhong District Court of Neijiang City (China) settled a case: Jiang borrowed from a microloan company but could not do so alone. Ms. Zhang's son hid the truth from his mother and gave her identity info to Jiang to make her a co-borrower. The process required Ms. Zhang to scan her face; she did so without reading the contract. The court stated she "should have anticipated the importance and legal consequences of facial recognition" and ordered her to join Jiang in repaying the remaining principal of over ⟦60000⟧. The Electronic Signature Law (China) clearly states, "reliable electronic signatures have the same legal effect as handwritten signatures or seals." The Anti-Telecom and Online Fraud Law (China) stipulates that no one "may assist in real-identity verification"; violations result in fines or detention for serious cases. First-instance trials under ordinary procedures must be completed within 6 months by regulation, though this can be extended. Attorney fees are not included in statutory court costs and must be paid personally (National China).

Install good locks on doors and windows, install a motion-sensor light outside the door, and actually lock up when leaving: preventing burglaries relies on these; installing only an alarm shows no effect
B

UK data shows that homes with both door and window locks are only one-twelfth as likely to be burglarized as homes with nothing. Adding an outdoor motion-sensor light reduces the risk to about one-thirty-something. Installing only an alarm without other measures shows no anti-theft effect. This section refers to burglary, not robbery when someone is home.

Changing door locks to deadbolts (requiring a key to engage the bolt), installing window locks, and an outdoor sensor light usually costs several dozen to several hundred yuan. Replacing an entire security door costs ⟦1000⟧ or more. The difficulty is actually locking doors and windows every time you leave, even remembering to close windows in summer.

The Crime Survey for England and Wales asked 37,416 households between 2008 and 2012 which security devices they had installed. These were compared to burglarized households. Households with no security made up only 4.9% of total households but 36.6% of burglarized ones. The authors calculated a "protection factor": the likelihood of being burglarized compared to households with no security. Door locks plus window locks were 12.54 times safer, reducing the likelihood to about one-twelfth. Door locks here refer to double locks or "deadlocks" (where the bolt requires a key to retract). Door locks, window locks, plus sensor lights or outdoor timers were 34.41 times safer. Adding indoor timers reached 49 times. For single items, outdoor lights were about 3 times safer, door locks about 2.8 times. Window locks alone showed no difference. Five devices were not significantly better than three correctly installed ones. Installing only an alarm without anything else resulted in a higher likelihood of burglary than having nothing. Households with fake alarm boxes had a higher chance of attempted but failed entries. Locks must actually be locked to count. Burglary cases involving picking locks, breaking windows, or removing doors dropped from 31 to 7 per thousand households from 1993 to 2006/07—a 77% decrease. Entry through unlocked doors remained constant at 7 per thousand households, showing no decrease (England and Wales).
In chat groups, do not share news about disasters, epidemics, or security incidents of unverified authenticity; do not edit photos or use AI to generate scene images
A

Sharing news about disasters, epidemics, or security incidents that you know to be false is punished as severely as inventing it yourself. Even if you didn't invent it: administrative detention for 5 to 10 days, plus a possible fine of up to ⟦1000⟧. Severely disrupting social order can lead to up to 3 years in prison, or 3 to 7 years for serious consequences. Edited photos or fake scene images made by AI are considered self-invented.

Free. Before sharing, check if it is an official announcement from a formal agency. If unsure, do not share, do not edit the photo, and do not add "I heard that." The difficulty is suppressing the urge to be the first to break the news.

Intentionally spreading rumors or reporting false information about hazards, epidemics, disasters, or security incidents that disrupts public order results in 5 to 10 days of administrative detention. A fine of up to ⟦1000⟧ may also be imposed. Minor cases result in up to 5 days detention or a fine of up to ⟦1000⟧. Fabricating false information about hazards, epidemics, disasters, or security incidents and spreading it online is punishable by up to 3 years in prison. Knowingly spreading such falsehoods carries the same penalty. The condition is a severe disruption of social order, termed "seriously disrupting social order" in the statute. Causing serious consequences is punishable by 3 to 7 years (National China).
Do not post or share photos, memes, or comments that insult heroes and martyrs; do not make jokes involving the national flag or national anthem
A

Joking about heroes, martyrs, the national flag, or the national anthem can lead to 5 to 10 days of administrative detention or a fine of ⟦1000~3000⟧. More serious cases lead to 10 to 15 days detention. If it constitutes a crime, it is punishable by up to 3 years in prison. Someone who posted two sentences defaming Yuan Longping in a village WeChat group of 499 people was sentenced to 6 months of public surveillance: no prison time, but restricted movement.

Free. Do not comment on, parody, or share content involving heroes, martyrs, the national flag, national emblem, or national anthem. The difficulty is refraining from joining in when others in a group make jokes.

Using insults or fabrication to infringe upon the name, image, reputation, or honor of heroes and martyrs, harming public interest, is punished as follows: 5 to 10 days of administrative detention or a fine of ⟦1000~3000⟧. Blaspheming or denying the deeds and spirit of heroes and martyrs, or creating and spreading speech, images, audio, or video that glorifies wars of aggression and disrupts public order, carries the same penalty. Relatively serious cases result in 10 to 15 days detention and a possible fine of up to ⟦5000⟧. "Serious circumstances" constitute a crime punishable by up to 3 years in prison. Insulting the national flag or emblem in public, or modifying the lyrics or music of the national anthem, or singing it in a distorted or derogatory manner with serious circumstances, is also punishable by up to 3 years. Official case: A person named Xiao posted 2 defamatory messages about Yuan Longping in a village WeChat group of 499 people and was sentenced to 6 months of public surveillance. Surveillance is a punishment without imprisonment but with restricted movement. A person named Qiu used a Weibo account with over 2.5 million followers to post 2 articles distorting the deeds of border guards and was sentenced to 8 months in prison and required to make a public apology in national media (National China).
Close foreign websites after viewing: do not take screenshots, do not share, do not bring content into groups, and do not join in the comments
A

These laws punish dissemination, not viewing. Sharing, bringing content into groups, or joining comments are all considered dissemination during case processing. Dissemination to the level of inciting subversion or inciting secession is punishable by up to 5 years in prison, or 5 years or more for ringleaders. Books, audio, and video regarding terrorism or extremism are exceptions: knowingly possessing them under serious circumstances is punishable by up to 3 years.

Free. Closing the page ends the matter. Do not save, share, or bring content to domestic platforms. Do not use accounts traceable to your identity to post long-term political content on foreign platforms. Do not accept remuneration or funding from foreign agencies, organizations, or individuals. The difficulty is resisting the urge to screenshot or share shocking content.

Using rumors, slander, or other means to incite the subversion of state power or the overthrow of the socialist system is punishable by up to 5 years in prison. Ringleaders (termed "chief elements" in the law) or those with major crimes face 5 years or more, up to a maximum of 15 years. Inciting secession or undermining national unity carries the same penalties. Colluding with foreign agencies, organizations, or individuals to commit these acts results in heavier punishment. Domestic or foreign agencies, organizations, or individuals providing funding for others to commit these acts results in the directly responsible person facing up to 5 years, or 5 years or more for serious circumstances. Stealing, spying, bribing, or illegally providing state secrets or intelligence to foreign agencies, organizations, or individuals is punishable by 5 to 10 years. For this crime, especially serious circumstances lead to 10 years to life imprisonment, while minor cases lead to up to 5 years. All crimes endangering national security carry a supplementary penalty of deprivation of political rights for 1 to 5 years, during which one loses voting rights and eligibility for civil service. Confiscation of property may also be applied. Administrative penalties also apply: no individual or organization may use the network to infringe upon national security, honor, or interests. Nor may they incite subversion of state power, overthrow of the socialist system, secession, or undermining of national unity. Posting or transmitting such information is punished according to relevant laws and administrative regulations (National China). One type constitutes a crime without dissemination: knowingly and illegally possessing materials promoting terrorism or extremism, provided circumstances are serious. Materials include books, audio-visual materials, or other items. The penalty is up to 3 years of fixed-term imprisonment, criminal detention (short-term), or public surveillance (restricted movement). A fine may also be imposed alongside or instead of imprisonment. The basis is Article 120-6 of the Criminal Law (China), added by Criminal Law Amendment (IX).
Watching adult films privately is your business; do not send them to groups, do not sell "resources," and do not start groups
A

Private viewing is not within the scope of punishment. Sending to a group constitutes online dissemination; the law does not specify a minimum number of times. It results in 10 to 15 days of administrative detention and a possible fine of up to ⟦5000⟧; serious circumstances lead to up to 2 years in prison. Selling "resources" for profit is punishable by up to 3 years, with a maximum of life imprisonment. If a group for dissemination has 30 or more members, the founder, administrators, and primary senders are all considered to have committed a crime.
Free. Do not share, do not save to group files, and do not act as a group owner or administrator for such groups.

Disseminating obscene information online results in 10 to 15 days of administrative detention and a possible fine of up to ⟦5000⟧. This does not specify a number of times. In the same law, the clause for sending harassing messages specifies it must be "multiple times." Minor cases result in up to 5 days detention or a fine of ⟦1000~3000⟧. Content involving minors is punished more severely. Disseminating obscene materials to the level of "serious circumstances" is punishable by up to 2 years in prison. Selling or disseminating for profit is punishable by up to 3 years plus a fine. For this crime, serious circumstances lead to 3 to 10 years, and especially serious circumstances lead to 10 years or more or life imprisonment. Establishing a group primarily to disseminate obscene electronic information with 30 or more members is prosecuted as a crime. Causing serious consequences is also prosecuted. The group founder, administrators, and primary senders are all convicted of disseminating obscene materials (National China).
"Part-time jobs" that require you to use your own card to receive money, withdraw cash, or transfer funds: do not do them, regardless of the commission
A

This type of work might earn a few hundred yuan, but the price is a criminal record. One person took their ID and one bank card to a designated location, cooperated with transfers and withdrawals, and earned over ⟦500⟧. The Procuratorate did not prosecute him, but the police still detained him for 10 days and fined him ⟦1000⟧. Another person provided their own and others' bank cards and SIM cards to a gang to receive and withdraw cash and was sentenced to 2 years and 3 months in prison and fined ⟦22000⟧.
Free. Ignore jobs like "daily pay of several hundred, take your card to the bank."

Knowingly helping to transfer, purchase, sell, or otherwise conceal money or property obtained through crime is punishable by up to 3 years in prison, plus or instead of a fine. Official case: A person named Wang followed instructions, took an ID and one bank card to a designated spot to cooperate with transfers and withdrawals, earning over ⟦500⟧. The Procuratorate (China) did not prosecute, but police handled it under the Anti-Telecom and Online Fraud Law (China), resulting in 10 days detention and a ⟦1000⟧ fine. A person named Man provided their own and others' bank cards and SIM cards to a gang for receiving, transferring, and withdrawing cash, resulting in 2 years and 3 months in prison and a ⟦22000⟧ fine (National China). Converting to cryptocurrency and then transferring is the same. A person named An and two others followed instructions from a telecom fraud gang to receive money using their bank cards. They used the money to buy cryptocurrency on an exchange and transferred it to designated accounts for a percentage commission. The investigation identified over ⟦500000⟧ of victims' money. The three were convicted of concealing or disguising criminal proceeds, receiving sentences from 2 years 8 months to 3 years 3 months, and each was fined ⟦30000~40000⟧ (Tongzhou, Beijing).
If someone asks you to "beautify a profile" to borrow money and split the commission based on the loan amount: do not do it even once
A

Helping others "beautify profiles" to borrow money and taking a percentage is treated as fraud. There was a gang of 126 people who turned unemployed individuals into "good customers," fraudulently borrowing more than ⟦30000000⟧ at over 80 bank transaction points. The person whose name was on the signature received 30% of the loan amount as a fee; among the 80 people already sentenced, 76 received from 1 year and 4 months to 6 years and 6 months in prison. Whoever's name is on the loan, the debt belongs to that person.
Costs no money. Refuse outright. Do not lend your ID or credit history to others, do not sign loan contracts without reading them, and do not go to the bank to sign on behalf of others.

Using deceptive tactics to obtain loans, accepted bills, letters of credit, letters of guarantee, etc., from banks or other financial institutions. Causing major damage to banks or other financial institutions is punishable by up to 3 years in prison. Additional or alternative fines: both imprisonment and a fine, or potentially just a fine. Causing particularly large losses, or other particularly serious circumstances, is punishable by 3 to 7 years plus a fine. The threshold for police to initiate prosecution is direct economic damage from ⟦500000⟧. Having no intention to repay, using fabricated reasons for capital-attracting projects, fake economic contracts, forged supporting documents, or forged asset certificates to fraudulently borrow money constitutes the crime of loan fraud. This crime is prosecuted if ⟦50000⟧ is defrauded, punishable by up to 5 years in prison plus a fine of ⟦20000~200000⟧. Very large amounts or other serious circumstances are punishable by 5 to 10 years; particularly large amounts are 10 years or more up to life imprisonment. Forging, altering, buying, or selling official documents, papers, or seals of state agencies is punishable by up to 3 years in prison; serious circumstances are 3 to 10 years. Official case: a gang of 126 people across 16 provinces and cities turned unemployed people into "good customers," fraudulently borrowing more than ⟦30000000⟧ at over 80 bank transaction points. Those with "clean profiles" who stood for the loans received 30% of the loan amount as a fee. The Procuratorate (China) prosecuted 105 "clean profile" individuals. Among the 80 people sentenced in the first instance in 2026, 76 were convicted of loan fraud, receiving sentences from 1 year and 4 months to 6 years and 6 months in prison plus fines. An additional 4 people, for withdrawing cash on behalf of the gang, were sentenced for the combined crimes of loan fraud and money laundering (combining the two crimes into a single sentence). These 4 individuals received from 2 years and 4 months to 7 years and 6 months (China-wide). The crime of obtaining loans in this section follows the text of the Eleventh Amendment to the Criminal Law, applicable from March 2021.
If you find a bank card, do not withdraw money; if you find a phone or wallet, contact the owner or turn it in to the police, do not pocket it
A

Keeping found items for use, if the amount reaches a "relatively large" level and you refuse to hand it over, is punishable by up to 2 years in prison; very large amounts are 2 to 5 years. Taking a found bank card to an ATM to withdraw money is even more severe, considered as using someone else's credit card: a relatively large amount is punishable by up to 5 years in prison, plus a fine of ⟦20000~200000⟧. For this type of withdrawal, the police initiate a case immediately without the owner needing to sue personally.
Costs no money, takes a few minutes. Make a phone call to find the owner, or take the item to a police station.

If you find items dropped by others, you must return them to the owner, notify them promptly to collect them, or hand them over to the police and relevant agencies. Keeping items left behind by others for use, if the amount reaches a "relatively large" level and you refuse to hand it over, is the crime of embezzlement, punishable by up to 2 years in prison. Very large amounts are 2 to 5 years. Finding someone else's credit card and using it at an ATM falls under "using someone else's credit card." "Credit card" in the Criminal Law (China), according to the 2004 explanation by the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress of China, refers to electronic payment cards issued by banks and financial institutions. Cards that have all or part of the functions of purchasing payments, credit loans, transfers, and cash deposits/withdrawals are included. Therefore, common bank cards that can withdraw cash are also included. If the level of crime is met, it is prosecuted as credit card fraud: relatively large amounts are punishable by up to 5 years in prison, plus a fine of ⟦20000~200000⟧. Very large amounts or other serious circumstances are punishable by 5 to 10 years, plus a fine of ⟦50000~500000⟧ (China-wide)
Receive promotions using your real identity; do not buy virtual numbers to register mass secondary accounts, do not exploit loopholes for repeated reception
A

Using a real identity, where each account receives a discount voucher once, is not within the scope of punishment. Registering mass fake users, self-placing and self-receiving orders to get more, is treated as fraud. Defrauding up to the starting threshold set by each province (⟦3000~10000⟧) is punishable by up to 3 years in prison; reaching ⟦30000~100000⟧ is 3 to 10 years. There was a delivery driver who used virtual numbers costing ⟦0.1⟧ per number to farm discount vouchers, converting them into more than ⟦90000⟧ in cash; 12 people in the same case were sentenced to prison.

Costs no money. Ignore activities in "promotion hunting groups." If you discover a platform has a loophole, do not touch it. The difficulty lies in restraining the thought of promotions as a mass-replicable source of income.

Defrauding to obtain money or property from others or the state, if the amount is relatively large, is punishable by up to 3 years in prison, with an additional or alternative fine (both prison and fine, or potentially just a fine). Very large amounts, or other serious circumstances, are punishable by 3 to 10 years plus a fine. Particularly large amounts, or other particularly serious circumstances, are punishable by 10 years or more or life imprisonment, plus a fine or confiscation of property. The three levels—relatively large, very large, and particularly large—are defined by each province within the following ranges. Relatively large is from ⟦3000~10000⟧ and above. Very large is from ⟦30000~100000⟧ and above, particularly large is from ⟦500000⟧ and above. Teaching the method to others or selling "tutorials" is prosecuted as the crime of teaching criminal methods, punishable by up to 5 years in prison; serious circumstances 5 to 10 years, particularly serious 10 years or more or life imprisonment. People buying and selling phone numbers and verification codes at the upstream and downstream stages are prosecuted for the crime of infringing on citizens' personal information, up to 3 years in prison, particularly serious 3 to 7 years. Mass account systems, automatic IP address changing, and mass verification message platforms themselves are explicitly prohibited by Article 14 of the Anti-Telecom and Network Fraud Law (China). Illegal buying, selling, leasing, or lending of SIM cards and internet accounts, helping others bypass real-name verification, falls under Article 31. Violating Article 14 results in the confiscation of all earnings, followed by a fine of 1 to 10 times the earnings. If no money was made, or earnings were under ⟦50000⟧, the fine is up to ⟦500000⟧, and serious circumstances also carry up to 15 days of detention. Violating Article 31 also results in a 1 to 10 times fine; if no money was made or earnings were under ⟦20000⟧, the fine is up to ⟦200000⟧, and serious circumstances also carry up to 15 days of detention. Participating in telecom and network fraud that does not reach the level of imprisonment results in 10 to 15 days of detention. Earnings are confiscated, followed by a 1 to 10 times fine. If no money was made or earnings were under ⟦10000⟧, the fine is up to ⟦100000⟧. First official case: food delivery driver Liu XX bought virtual phone numbers for ⟦0.1⟧ each to register new users on a platform. He received "buy 29 get 15 off" vouchers for new users to place orders, then resold the goods to small shops for cash. He also used virtual numbers to invite each other to receive rewards from ⟦2~20⟧. He and delivery driver Tan XX defrauded more than 90,000 and more than ⟦70000⟧ respectively. The Yangpu District Procuratorate, Shanghai prosecuted 12 people for fraud; the court sentenced them from 3 years and 6 months in prison to 3 months of criminal detention (short-term detention). Second official case: Wang XX exploited the time lag between refunds at an online store and the recovery of virtual draw coins. He refunded 1,156 times, taking 224 character models worth more than ⟦249000⟧. He also resold them on a second-hand platform for money; the court sentenced him for fraud to 3 years in prison suspended for 4 years, plus a fine of ⟦30000⟧. During the trial, he returned the property and prepaid the fine, totaling ⟦330000⟧. Third official case: new user discount vouchers and driver subsidies from a ride-hailing platform were defrauded by running fake trips "self-calling and self-receiving," involving 19 provinces and over 70 cities, with an amount exceeding ⟦2000000⟧. The Longcheng District Procuratorate, Chaoyang City, Liaoning Province prosecuted 163 people, all of whom were convicted. The two masterminds, Huang XX and Cai XX, were sentenced for the combined crimes of fraud, infringing on citizens' personal information, and teaching criminal methods (combining several crimes into a single sentence), each receiving 3 years and 6 months. An additional 34 helpers with minor circumstances were not prosecuted by the procuratorate but were still transferred to the police for administrative punishment (China-wide)
Do not throw anything from balconies or windows; cigarette butts, trash bags, and wine bottles all count
A

Throwing things down, even if they hit no one, can result in up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to ⟦1000⟧; serious circumstances result in 10 to 15 days of detention. Hitting someone changes the charge: a person on the 21st floor who drunkenly threw empty bottles and glass cups onto a schoolyard, seriously injuring a 13-year-old student, was sentenced to 10 years in prison. Another person threw 8 bricks from the 32nd floor, killing 1 person, and was approved for the death penalty in 2024.
Costs no money and no time. Cigarette butts, trash bags, and wine bottles should all be taken to the indoor trash can, not thrown through windows or balconies.

Throwing items from upstairs or other high places, as long as there is a risk of injuring people, damaging property, or threatening public safety, can lead to up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to ⟦1000⟧. Serious circumstances result in 10 to 15 days of detention, and can also include an additional fine of up to ⟦1000⟧. If it is serious enough to constitute the crime of throwing objects from a height, it is punishable by up to 1 year in prison, with an additional or alternative fine (both prison and fine, or potentially just a fine). Injuring or killing someone is prosecuted under a more severe charge. Official case: Li XX Chen on the 21st floor drunkenly threw empty wine bottles and glass cups onto the sports field below, hitting a 13-year-old student and causing second-degree serious injury. He was sentenced to 10 years in prison for the crime of endangering public safety by dangerous means. Zhou XX threw 8 bricks from the 32nd floor into a crowd, killing 1 person; in 2024, the Supreme People's Court (China) approved the death penalty (China-wide)
Do not buy imitation guns, steel ball guns, or air guns online; do not buy "toy guns" of unknown origin
A

Steel ball guns and air guns bought online, if the specific muzzle kinetic energy reaches 1.8 J/cm², are identified as firearms. Possessing them without a license is punishable by up to 3 years in prison; serious circumstances are 3 to 7 years. A couple sold "toy guns," and out of 43 guns, 18 were appraised as firearms; only because it could not be proven they knew were they not prosecuted.
Costs no money. If you want to shoot guns, go to a legal shooting range.

Possessing or hiding firearms without a license is punishable by up to 3 years in prison; serious circumstances are 3 to 7 years. Non-standard guns that cannot fire standard ammunition, as long as the specific muzzle kinetic energy is 1.8 J/cm² or higher, are all identified as firearms. Specific muzzle kinetic energy is the energy per cm² carried by the bullet as it leaves the barrel. Not a few steel ball guns and air guns bought online exceed this number. Since 2018, the Supreme People's Court and the Supreme People's Procuratorate (China) have required: for air guns with low specific kinetic energy, a comprehensive evaluation must be made before deciding whether to convict. Evaluate the appearance, material, price, use, and whether the person themselves knew... Official case: Zhao XX and spouse sold "toy guns" at a fair; 43 were seized, of which 18 were appraised to meet firearm standards. Because there was insufficient evidence to prove they knew they were firearms, they were not prosecuted due to doubtful evidence (China-wide)
When buying a drone, register with your real name first; do not fly at airports, military zones, or managed airspace in cities; do not crack altitude limits
A

Flying without real-name registration results in a fine of up to ⟦200⟧; serious circumstances result in a fine of ⟦2000~20000⟧. Flying in managed airspace without permission results in a fine of up to ⟦500⟧; serious circumstances result in the confiscation of the drone and an additional fine of ⟦1000~10000⟧. Relatively severe circumstances can also lead to 5 to 10 days of detention. Someone paid to crack the altitude limit, flew to nearly 3,000 m to film clouds and posted it online, and was detained for 5 days.
Real-name registration costs no money and takes a few minutes. Before each takeoff, check through official channels to see if the area you plan to fly in is managed airspace.

Flying without real-name registration results in a forced correction and a potential fine of up to ⟦200⟧; serious circumstances result in a fine of ⟦2000~20000⟧. Flying micro, light, or small drones in managed airspace without permission results in a forced stop of the flight and a potential fine of up to ⟦500⟧. In this case, serious circumstances result in the confiscation of the drone plus a fine of ⟦1000~10000⟧. Flying in violation of airspace management regulations, if the circumstances are relatively severe, results in 5 to 10 days of detention. Official case: Li XX paid to crack the altitude limit, flew a drone to nearly 3,000 m to film clouds and posted it online, and was detained for 5 days. Zhang XX cracked altitude limits and no-fly zone limits for others for more than 20 units, earning more than ⟦15000⟧. He was convicted of providing programs and tools for illegal intrusion into and control of computer information systems. Sentenced to 6 months in prison, suspended for 1 year, plus a fine (China-wide, from January 2024)
Do not secretly film others; do not install cameras in rental rooms, homestays, or hotel rooms
A

Secretly filming, peeping, or spreading the private affairs of others results in up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to ⟦1000⟧; relatively severe circumstances result in 5 to 10 days of detention. Using specialized equipment for secret filming, causing serious consequences, is punishable by up to 2 years in prison. Two people installed equipment in rooms of three hotels for remote secret filming and were sentenced to 1 year and 3 months and 1 year in prison respectively. Do not film rooms occupied by others without consent.
Costs no money and no time. Do not secretly film others, and do not install cameras in rental rooms, homestays, or hotel rooms.

Peeping, secretly filming, eavesdropping, or spreading the private affairs of others results in up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to ⟦1000⟧. Relatively severe circumstances result in 5 to 10 days of detention, and can also include an additional fine of up to ⟦1000⟧. Illegal use of specialized equipment for eavesdropping or secret filming, causing serious consequences, is punishable by up to 2 years in prison. Specialized eavesdropping and secret filming equipment are devices made specifically for spying and secret recording. Official case: Yan XX Ping and Yan XX Jian bought secret filming equipment online and installed it in multiple rooms of three hotels for remote secret filming; they were sentenced to 1 year and 3 months and 1 year in prison respectively. Article 1033 of the Civil Code (China) adds another layer: unless the law provides otherwise or the person explicitly consents, no one may "enter, photograph, or peep into private spaces such as others' residences or hotel rooms," nor may they "photograph, peep into, eavesdrop on, or make public the private activities of others" (China-wide)
Mahjong and card games can be played; do not collect a house cut, do not act as the house, do not organize gambling dens for profit, and do not gamble online
B

Relatives and friends playing cards for small amounts of money is not regulated by law. Providing conditions for gambling for profit, or participating in gambling with relatively large stakes, results in up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to ⟦1000⟧. Gathering people for gambling for profit or making a living from gambling is punishable by up to 3 years in prison; opening a casino is up to 5 years. How much constitutes "relatively large stakes" is determined by each locality; there is no single national figure.

Costs no money. Relatives and friends playing for fun with small amounts is fine. Do not take a percentage from the game, do not act as the house, and do not organize gambling dens for profit. The difficulty lies in restraining yourself from accepting the role when someone stands up to organize it.

Providing favorable conditions for gambling for profit, or participating in gambling with relatively large stakes, results in up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to ⟦1000⟧. Serious circumstances result in 10 to 15 days of detention, plus a fine of ⟦1000~5000⟧. Gathering people for gambling for profit, or making a living from gambling, is punishable by up to 3 years in prison plus a fine. Opening a casino is punishable by up to 5 years in prison plus a fine; serious circumstances are 5 to 10 years (China-wide)
Do not eat bushmeat, do not trade, and do not keep protected animals as pets; also do not dig up or trade wild orchids, Thuja sutchuenensis, or yew trees
A

Eating wild animals under key state protection results in confiscation, followed by a fine of 2 to 20 times the value. Trading or transporting rare or endangered animals is punishable by up to 5 years in prison; severe cases are 5 to 10 years. Pets bred by humans where breeding techniques are mature and large-scale are usually not considered a crime to trade; those caught from the wild are not treated this way. Most wild orchids on mountains are protected; someone who dug up 3 plants intending to sell them was placed under criminal detention (short-term detention).

Costs no money. Only buy pet breeds with legal origins that are human-bred. If you see wild orchids on a mountain, do not dig them up; only buy potted orchids or yew trees grown in flower markets or nurseries.

Eating wild animals under key state protection, or buying them to eat, results in confiscation, followed by a fine of 2 to 20 times their value. Breeding wild animals under key state protection without a license results in confiscation plus a fine of 1 to 10 times. Illegal purchasing, transporting, or selling of rare and endangered wild animals under key state protection and products derived from them is punishable by up to 5 years in prison plus a fine. In this crime, serious circumstances are 5 to 10 years, and particularly serious circumstances are 10 years or more. Hunting, purchasing, transporting, or selling other terrestrial wild animals for food, if the circumstances are serious, is punishable by up to 3 years in prison. Official case: Wang XX, a bird breeder, and 2 others sold more than 40 Fischer's lovebirds (Agapornis fischeri, national level II protection) bred by humans, with a total price of less than ⟦400⟧. In 2021, the procuratorate decided not to prosecute. Since 2022, the Supreme People's Court and the Supreme People's Procuratorate (China) have clarified: for species with mature breeding techniques and large-scale production, trading and transporting them as pets is generally not prosecuted as a crime (China-wide). Wild plants have a separate crime. Illegally harvesting or destroying plants under key state protection, or purchasing, transporting, processing, or selling these plants and their products, all fall under this crime. Punishable by up to 3 years in prison plus a fine; serious circumstances 3 to 7 years. The 2023 explanation by the Supreme People's Court (China) set the thresholds. For level I protected wild plants, 1 plant; level II, 2 plants; or a value from ⟦20000⟧ is enough for conviction. Level I, 5 plants; level II, 10 plants; or a value from ⟦200000⟧ constitutes serious circumstances. The buyer must know it was stolen for it to count. In the 2021 catalog, the Thuja genus and all species of the Taxus (yew) genus are level I. All species of the Cymbidium (orchid) genus are level II, including Chunlan, Huilan, and Lianbianlan. Within the Cymbidium genus, only Cymbidium lancifolium is not in the catalog, while Cymbidium insigne and Cymbidium wenshanense are level I. Digging them up to plant at home is also convicted as illegal harvesting; the replanting will be considered during sentencing. Human-cultivated plants do not count, except for ancient and famous trees. Official case: in 2022, a person in Nanzhao, Henan dug up 3 wild orchids on a hillside and filmed a video intending to sell them. He was sentenced to 6 months of criminal detention, suspended for 10 months, and fined ⟦3000⟧. A group in Suizhou, Hubei dug up more than 30,000 wild Chunlan and Huilan orchids over two years. In 2025, one person in the group was sentenced to 1 year and 7 months in prison, suspended for 2 years (China-wide)
When collecting debt, do not detain people, do not lock people up, and do not follow people to their homes to cause a scene and prevent them from leaving
A

Even if they truly owe you money, you are not allowed to detain or lock them up: the law explicitly states that doing so to collect debt is still prosecuted as illegal detention. If it does not reach the level of imprisonment, it results in administrative detention for 10 to 15 days, plus a fine of ⟦1000~2000⟧. If it constitutes the crime of illegal detention, it is punishable by up to 3 years in prison; causing serious injury is 3 to 10 years; causing death is 10 years or more. For debt collection, sue in court.

Costs no money. If the other party owes money and won't pay, sue in court. For how to write a promissory note, see Chapter 8, Section 18 (Promissory Notes). The difficulty lies in restraining yourself from taking action or following them home when the other party defaults.

Illegally restricting the personal freedom of others, trespassing into others' homes, or illegally searching a person results in 10 to 15 days of detention, plus a fine of ⟦1000~2000⟧. Minor circumstances result in 5 to 10 days of detention, plus a fine of up to ⟦1000⟧. Illegal detention is punishable by up to 3 years of fixed-term imprisonment, criminal detention (short-term), public surveillance (not imprisoned but restricted in movement), or deprivation of political rights. Causing serious injury is punishable by 3 to 10 years; causing death is 10 years or more. Detaining or locking people up to collect debt is prosecuted under these exact regulations, even if the debt is real (China-wide)
Do not lend your ID, use someone else's ID, or take someone else's documents to register, open cards, or buy tickets
A

Lending, renting, or transferring your ID to another person results in a warning and a fine of up to ⟦200⟧. Impersonating someone else using their ID, or using an ID obtained through fraud, results in a fine of ⟦200~1000⟧, or detention for up to 10 days. In places where real-name registration is mandatory, such as buying train tickets or renting rooms, using forged documents or stolen documents from others can lead to criminal detention or public surveillance if the circumstances are serious.
No cost. Simply refuse if someone asks to borrow it. If you must provide a photocopy, clearly write on the copy the specific purpose for which it is intended.

Renting, lending, or transferring your resident identity card to others results in a warning and a fine of up to ⟦200⟧. Impersonating someone else using their ID, or using an ID obtained through fraud, results in a fine of ⟦200~1000⟧, or detention for up to 10 days. Buying, selling, or using forged or altered IDs carries the same penalty. There are places where state regulations require the presentation of personal identification. Using forged, altered, or stolen documents in such places is subject to criminal prosecution if the circumstances are serious. Documents include IDs, passports, social security cards, driver's licenses, etc. Penalties include criminal detention (short-term imprisonment) or public surveillance (no imprisonment but restricted movement), accompanied by or solely consisting of a fine: both detention and a fine, or potentially just a fine (China-wide)
Cooperate if stopped or taken away by the police: do not shove, hit, or grab recording devices; be especially patient if you have been drinking
A

Obstructing the performance of official duties on the spot results in a warning or a fine of up to ⟦500⟧; serious circumstances lead to 5 to 10 days of detention. Striking a police officer is a different level: biting, slapping, kicking, hitting, tackling, throwing objects, or causing at least a 'minimal injury' (the lowest level in China's injury classification, below the 'minor injury' in section 19) constitutes a violent assault on a police officer, punishable by up to 3 years in prison. Using guns, controlled knives, or driving a vehicle to ram them results in 3 to 7 years. Ordinary resistance such as flailing arms or pulling away does not count.

No cost. Do not use force on the spot. If you have objections, raise them later: through complaints, administrative reconsiderations, or lawsuits. The difficulty lies in restraining anger during the few minutes of being stopped, especially after drinking alcohol.

Obstructing staff of state organs from performing their duties according to the law results in a warning or a fine of up to ⟦500⟧. Serious circumstances lead to 5 to 10 days of detention, and may include an additional fine of up to ⟦1000⟧. If the person obstructed is a people's policeman, the punishment is more severe. Violently attacking a people's policeman performing duties according to the law is punishable by up to 3 years in prison. Using guns, controlled knives, or driving a vehicle to ram or seriously threaten the physical safety of the police results in 3 to 7 years. Biting, slapping, kicking, hitting, tackling, or throwing objects causing at least a minimal injury is considered a 'violent attack'. Ordinary resistance like flailing, pulling away, or stomping does not count (China-wide)
Do not have sexual relations if the other person is under 14; 'the girl's consent' is not a defense
A

If the other person is under 14, whether they consent or not, it is prosecuted as rape with a heavier penalty, with a basic sentence of 3 to 10 years in prison. If the other person is under 12, you are always deemed to 'should have known'. For those aged 12 to 14, if their physical development, gestures, or style of dress suggest they could be a child and you still proceed, you are deemed to 'clearly know'. Claims of truly not knowing are scrutinized very strictly by the court.
No cost. If you are unsure of the other person's age, do not have sexual relations.

Having sexual relations with a girl under 14 is prosecuted as rape with a heavier penalty, with a basic sentence of 3 to 10 years in prison. The interpretation of the Supreme People's Court (China) is as follows: if violence, threats, or other coercive means are used, it is rape regardless of whether the person knew the victim was a child. If no coercive means are used, for victims under 12, the perpetrator is always deemed to 'should have known'. For those aged 12 to 14, if physical development, speech, gestures, dress, etc., indicate they could be a child and the act is still committed, it is deemed 'clearly knowing'. The 'truly did not know' exception is applied very strictly (China-wide)
Before striking someone, calculate the costs clearly: detention, compensation, and prison
A

Striking someone once requires payment: 5 to 10 days of administrative detention, plus a fine of ⟦500~1000⟧. Causing a minor injury becomes a criminal case, punishable by up to 3 years in prison; causing a serious injury results in 3 to 10 years. Compensation is calculated separately: one person who broke three of another's ribs paid ⟦113000⟧ in a settlement to avoid prosecution. Another person who broke someone's radius and did not pay compensation was sentenced to 10 months in prison.
No money or time required. The hardest part is the few seconds before taking action.

Beating another person or intentionally causing injury results in 5 to 10 days of detention, plus a fine of ⟦500~1000⟧. Gang fighting, or beating the disabled, pregnant women, the elderly, or children, or beating people multiple times or multiple people at once, results in 10 to 15 days of detention, plus a fine of ⟦1000~2000⟧. Causing minor injury is the crime of intentional injury, punishable by up to 3 years of fixed-term imprisonment, criminal detention (short-term), or public surveillance (restricted movement). Causing serious injury results in 3 to 10 years. Civilly, one must also compensate for medical expenses, lost income (money lost from being unable to work), caregiver costs, travel expenses, hospital meal allowances, and nutritional supplements. If the victim is disabled, additional disability compensation is required. Disability compensation is calculated based on the average per capita disposable income of urban residents in the previous year at the place of the court, multiplied by 20 years. For injured persons aged 60 or older, one year is deducted for each year of age; for those 75 or older, it is calculated as 5 years. In 2022, procuratorates nationwide (China) handled over 70,000 cases of minor injury, most originating from marital, family, or neighbor conflicts or random incidents. A typical case from the Supreme People's Procuratorate (China): Lu broke three of the other person's ribs (second-degree minor injury) and paid ⟦113000⟧ to settle, thereby avoiding prosecution. Shi broke the other person's radius (second-degree minor injury), did not compensate, and was sentenced to ten months of fixed-term imprisonment (China-wide, Public Security Administration Punishment Law applicable from January 1, 2026)

If you cannot raise a child you gave birth to, the only legal way out is to register with civil affairs: receiving money and handing the child to others can be prosecuted as child trafficking; abandoning the child is the crime of abandonment
A

If you cannot raise a child, there is a way out, but there is only one legal way: go to the civil affairs department to register for adoption; the adoption relationship is only formed from the date of registration. Giving a child to others yourself, especially if money is received, can turn 'giving for adoption' into the crime of child trafficking, which carries a starting sentence of 5 years or more. Abandoning a child and refusing to provide support, if the circumstances are flagrant, is the crime of abandonment, punishable by up to 5 years in prison.

No cost. Go to the civil affairs department at the county level or above to register for adoption; you must submit documents and wait for the verification and assessment of the adoption, which takes some time.

Article 240 of the Criminal Law (China): 'Whoever abducts and sells a woman or a child shall be sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of not less than five years but not more than ten years and shall also be fined.' Aggravating circumstances lead to ten years or more or life imprisonment, plus a fine or confiscation of property. 'If the circumstances are especially serious, the death penalty shall be imposed, plus confiscation of property.' Article 17 of the 'Opinions on Handling Crimes of Abducting and Selling Women and Children According to Law' (China) discusses how to distinguish selling one's own child from folk adoption. The distinguishing standard is 'the key lies in whether the person has the purpose of illegal profit.' That is, whether they want to make money from it. Three cases may be identified as selling one's own child, resulting in a conviction for trafficking: First, 'using childbirth as a means of illegal profit, selling the child after birth.' Second, 'clearly knowing the other party has no intention of raising the child, or being completely indifferent to whether they do, yet "giving" the child to receive money.' Third, '"giving" the child to receive a large sum of money that is clearly not "upbringing expenses" or "gratitude money".' Conversely, if not for profit and truly due to life hardships, giving a child for adoption and receiving only a small amount of compensation or gratitude money is considered folk adoption and is not a crime. See also Article 261 of the Criminal Law (China): 'Whoever has the duty to support an aged person, a minor, a sick person, or any other person who lacks the ability to live independently but refuses to do so, if the circumstances are flagrant, shall be sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of not more than five years, criminal detention, or public surveillance.' Article 1094 of the Civil Code (China) stipulates only three types of people can be placers for adoption: guardians of orphans, child welfare institutions, and biological parents who have special difficulties and are unable to raise the child. Article 1105: 'The adoption shall be registered with the civil affairs department of the people's government at or above the county level. The adoption relationship is formed as of the date of registration.'
Do not stage fake accidents or inflate damages to defraud insurance: this is insurance fraud; witnesses, mechanics, and appraisers who help you will also be charged
A

Fabricating accidents or inflating losses to claim compensation is the crime of insurance fraud; if the amount is relatively large, it is punishable by up to 5 years in prison plus a fine of ⟦10000~100000⟧. Witnesses, appraisers, or asset valuers who help you by intentionally providing false certificates will be convicted as accomplices. Mechanics who conspire with you to fabricate claims are also considered accomplices. In a case in Xuancheng, Anhui, 8 people were sentenced to 2 to 4 years in prison, each fined ⟦10000⟧.
No money or time required; simply do not do it.

Article 198 of the Criminal Law (China) lists five cases: (1) The policyholder intentionally fabricates the subject of insurance, i.e., an object that does not exist. (2) The policyholder, the insured, or the beneficiary fabricates a false cause for an insurance event that has occurred, or inflates the level of loss. (3) Fabricating an insurance event that never happened. (4) The policyholder or the insured intentionally causes an insurance event resulting in property damage. (5) The policyholder or the beneficiary intentionally causes the death, disability, or illness of the insured. If the amount is relatively large, the penalty is up to 5 years of fixed-term imprisonment or criminal detention, plus a fine of ⟦10000~100000⟧. If the amount is very large or there are other serious circumstances, 5 to 10 years plus a fine of ⟦20000~200000⟧. If the amount is especially large or there are other especially serious circumstances, 10 years or more plus a fine of ⟦20000~200000⟧ or confiscation of property. The final paragraph of this article covers helpers: appraisers, witnesses, and asset valuers. If they intentionally provide false documents to facilitate insurance fraud, they are prosecuted as accomplices. Mechanics do not fall into these three categories but are accomplices if they conspire with you. Article 25 of the Criminal Law (China): 'A joint crime refers to an intentional crime committed by two or more persons jointly.' In 2021, the Changping District Court in Beijing announced that motor vehicle insurance fraud cases concluded since 2019 'are mainly joint crimes, with repair shops being a key industry for offenses.' Article 27 of the Insurance Law (China): if no insurance event occurs but it is lied about, the insurer has the right to terminate the contract and not refund premiums. Using false or altered documents, or fabricating causes or inflating losses, means the insurer will not compensate for the inflated portion. Already paid compensation must be returned or repaid. Case: In the case of Zhang Song in Xuancheng, Anhui, Wang Xin and 7 others were convicted of insurance fraud, receiving 2 to 4 years in prison and each fined ⟦10000⟧. This case involved a fake lawsuit. The insurer appraised the loss at ⟦20000⟧, but the party used a forged car transfer contract to gain standing to sue, and the court awarded over ⟦70000⟧. This effective civil judgment was vacated through retrial on September 26, 2019. The 'Measures for Anti-Insurance Fraud' (China) require risk information checks at both the underwriting and claims settlement stages. It also seeks to establish an industry anti-fraud information platform for multiple types of insurance and an anti-fraud intelligence center. These platforms screen data for suspected fraud and hand clues to industry associations, anti-fraud organizations, and insurers for verification. Suspected crimes are reported promptly to the police. The National Financial Regulatory Administration (China) and its branches must establish and improve the mechanism linking administrative law enforcement and criminal justice. The connecting parties are the police, people's procuratorates, and people's courts (China-wide, issued July 31, 2024)

Do not sell your organs, and do not help others find donors: the kidney you sell only gets you over 20,000, while the same kidney is resold for 200,000; the money will be confiscated and you will be fined 10 to 20 times the transaction amount
A

Organs from living persons can only be donated to a spouse, lineal blood relatives, or collateral blood relatives within three generations; buying or selling is illegal. In a case in Beijing, the kidney seller received only over ⟦20000⟧, while the same kidney was sold to a patient for ⟦180000~220000⟧. The proceeds are confiscated, followed by a fine of 10 to 20 times the transaction amount. For the price the body pays after losing a kidney, see Chapter 1, Section 35 (the remaining kidney works for two).
No money or time required; simply do not do it.

Article 5 of the 'Regulations on Human Organ Donation and Transplantation' (China): 'No organization or individual may trade in human organs in any form, or engage in activities related to the trade in human organs.' Article 10: 'No organization or individual may harvest organs from living persons under the age of 18 for transplantation.' Article 11: 'Recipients of organs from living persons are limited to the donor's spouse, lineal blood relatives, or collateral blood relatives within three generations.' Article 37 stipulates penalties for organ trading. Trading in human organs or engaging in related activities is handled by the health department of the local people's government at or above the county level. First, illegal income—the entire amount from the transaction—is confiscated. Then, a fine of 10 to 20 times the transaction amount is imposed. Participating medical personnel will have their practice licenses revoked and be banned for life from medical services. If it constitutes a crime, criminal responsibility is pursued according to law (China-wide, applicable from May 1, 2024, replacing the old 'Regulations on Human Organ Transplantation'). Article 234-1 of the Criminal Law (China): 'Whoever organizes others to sell human organs shall be sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of not more than five years and shall also be fined; if the circumstances are serious, the sentence shall be fixed-term imprisonment of not less than five years and shall also be fined or have property confiscated.' Three other cases are prosecuted under Articles 234 and 232 of the Criminal Law (China): harvesting organs without the person's consent; harvesting organs from persons under eighteen; or coercing or deceiving others into donating. These are prosecuted as intentional injury or homicide. Case 1: The case of Zheng Wei and 14 others, heard on appeal by the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court on August 20, 2014, involved 51 kidneys and over ⟦10340000⟧. Kidney sellers (donors) 'only received remuneration of ⟦20000~25000⟧.' Patients waiting for kidneys (recipients) paid 'previously 180,000 or 190,000 per kidney, later 210,000 or 220,000.' The harvesting site was a rented four-story house for ⟦7500⟧ per month; the gang's head nurse testified it was 'filthy and messy, lacking even emergency equipment.' Organizer Zheng Wei was sentenced to 12 years for organizing others to sell human organs; the other 14 were sentenced to between 3.5 and 9 years. Case 2: The 'teenager sells kidney for iPhone' case released by the Supreme People's Procuratorate (China). 17-year-old Wang had his right kidney removed in Chenzhou on the night of April 28, 2011. The surgery took place in a department subcontracted to others in a hospital unqualified for transplants. Upon discharge on May 2, he received ⟦22000⟧, while the recipient paid intermediaries ⟦150000⟧ and 10,000 USD, with the mastermind profiting over ⟦56000⟧. Post-surgery, Wang suffered renal failure, 'the injury constituting a serious injury, grade three disability'
Do not solicit prostitutes: the default penalty is 10 to 15 days of detention, not just paying a small fine
A

Being caught is not solved by just paying a small fine. The default level in the law is 10 to 15 days of detention, and may include a fine of up to ⟦5000⟧. Only when circumstances are minor is the penalty up to 5 days of detention or a fine of up to ⟦1000⟧. Furthermore, soliciting while knowing you have syphilis or gonorrhea is a crime punishable by up to 5 years in prison.
No money or time required; simply do not do it.

Article 78 of the Public Security Administration Punishment Law (China): Prostitution or soliciting prostitution results in detention of ten to fifteen days, and may include a fine of up to ⟦5000⟧. If circumstances are minor, detention is up to five days or a fine of up to ⟦1000⟧. Soliciting in public places results in up to five days of detention or a fine of up to ⟦1000⟧. Article 79: Inducing, sheltering, or brokering prostitution results in ten to fifteen days of detention, and may include a fine of up to ⟦5000⟧. If circumstances are minor, detention is up to five days or a fine of ⟦1000~2000⟧. Article 87: Staff of hotels, catering, entertainment, or taxi units who tip off violators during police inspections or otherwise facilitate such activities face ten to fifteen days of detention.
