The level from the Hunan Provincial Emergency Management Department is to rinse the wound for 20 to 30 minutes, "longer for strong chemicals". Between the two levels, take the longer one. Step three, for eyes, you must "pull the eyelids open to ensure the water flows over the entire eyeball and the inner surface of the eyelids", "absolutely do not rub the eyes", and go to the ophthalmology department immediately after rinsing. Use water at room temperature or slightly warm; using hot water is forbidden. Do not apply ointment, mercurochrome, or anything else to a fresh wound, and do not wrap it with dirty cloth; applying these will make it difficult for the doctor to assess the depth. Legally, "chemical skin burns" and "chemical eye burns" are both included in the statutory list of occupational diseases (China); if they occur during work, they are handled according to the occupational disease and work injury systems. When an acute incident causing an occupational disease occurs, the employer "must promptly organize treatment, health examinations, and medical observation, with costs borne by the employer" (applicable nationwide).
Hot weather with dizziness, nausea, no sweating, or drowsiness: move to a cool place immediately, remove clothing, pour water to cool down; do not give drinks to drowsy people, call 120
B

Hot, red skin, slurred speech, and confusion are signs of heatstroke. Body temperature can rise above 41 °C within 10 to 15 minutes; severe cases have a very high mortality rate. Move to a cool, ventilated place immediately, remove excess clothing, use cool water and wet towels to lower the temperature, and call 120 at the same time. For someone who is drowsy, do not give them even a single sip of water.
Free.

US National Weather Service: heatstroke is a "serious medical emergency". Signs include a body temperature above 103°F (39.4°C), confusion, slurred speech, and hot, red skin. Management is to call emergency services immediately, move to a cool place, use cool water and wet towels to lower the temperature, and "do not give anything to drink". Heat exhaustion is characterized by heavy sweating, exhaustion, cool clammy skin, and a fast, weak pulse; management is to move to a cool place, loosen clothing, and take small sips of water. If vomiting occurs, symptoms worsen, or there is no improvement after 1 hour, seek medical attention. The Yunnan Provincial CDC (China) advises: move to a cool, ventilated place immediately, use cold wet towels to lower the temperature; if the person is conscious, give water with salt; if symptoms are severe, call emergency services immediately. This agency also states that severe heatstroke has a "very high mortality rate". China CDC advises: cool down first, transfer to the hospital later; cool down within the "golden half-hour" after the patient loses consciousness. If conditions allow, young, healthy people without underlying diseases can soak in cold water for rapid cooling; for the elderly and those with underlying diseases, spray water on the skin and cool down through evaporation. The 2024 updated guidelines on heat-related illness from the Wilderness Medical Society state that cold water immersion is the most important way to treat severe heat-related illness and cools the fastest. If ice water is not available, use the coolest water at hand; if immersion is not possible, spray water with a fan, at a speed about half that of immersion. The US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) states that when heatstroke occurs, body temperature can rise to 106°F (about 41 °C) or higher within 10 to 15 minutes. Symptoms listed include "hot, dry skin or profuse sweating". The 2014 version of the China CDC's heatstroke prevention and management guidelines lists heatstroke manifestations as "red, hot, dry skin, no sweat", and requires "do not give the patient water to drink"; if the patient vomits, turn them on their side and keep the airway clear.

People with heat exhaustion or heatstroke who are still conscious should drink cool dilute salt water or sports drinks, in small amounts multiple times; do not gulp, and do not drink alcohol or high-sugar drinks
B

Only people who are still conscious are allowed to drink: cool dilute salt water or sports drinks, taken in small amounts multiple times, 500 to 1000 ml per hour. Do not drink alcohol or high-sugar drinks, as they cause further dehydration. Cool down first before rehydrating; for those who are drowsy or have slurred speech, do not give even a single sip.
Free. A bottle of sports drink costs a few yuan.

The China CDC once issued the "Guidelines for the Prevention and Emergency Management of Heatstroke for the Public (2014 Edition)". It states "drink at least 2 to 4 cups of cool water (500 to 1000 ml) every hour, the water should not be too warm, drink in small amounts multiple times". It also states "do not drink alcoholic or high-sugar beverages. These beverages cause more body fluid loss. At the same time, avoid drinking excessively cold iced drinks". For heatstroke, it clearly states "do not give the patient water to drink". US NIOSH: for heat exhaustion, "encourage drinking cool water in small sips frequently"; for heat cramps, drink a sports drink with sugar and electrolytes every 15 to 20 minutes, "do not use salt tablets".
In a fire, crawl close to the ground, touch the door before opening, do not open if the door is hot, use stairs not elevators, and do not go back once out
B

Stay low to the ground and crawl under the smoke toward the exit. Before opening a door, touch the handle and the door itself; if it is hot or there is smoke in the door gap, do not open it and switch to a second exit; if you do open it, do so slowly, and if thick smoke pours in, close it immediately. Use the stairs, not the elevator, and do not go back to get belongings once you are out. If clothes catch fire, stop, drop, and roll, and cover your face with your hands.
Install 1 to 2 independent smoke detectors in the house, costing a few dozen yuan. Preview the two escape routes in the hallway and stairs.

US FEMA escape guidelines, verbatim: "stay low to the ground and crawl under the smoke toward the exit". Before opening a door, touch the handle and the door, "if it is hot, or there is smoke in the door gap, do not open this door, use a second exit". Open the door slowly; if there is thick smoke, close it immediately. If clothes catch fire, "stop, drop, and roll", and cover your face with your hands. If you cannot get out, close the door, use cloth or tape to seal door gaps and vents, and call to report your location. Fire self-rescue advice from the Ministry of Emergency Management (China) says the same. Do not use elevators for escape; if the fire is not yet large, try to run to a lower floor, use a wet towel or mask to cover your nose and mouth, and crawl or crouch low to escape.
Seeing a person drowning: call for help and call 110/120 first, reach out with a pole, throw a floating object, do not enter the water yourself
C

Call for help, call 110/120 first, stand on the shore and reach out with a pole or throw a floating object, do not enter the water yourself. If the person is pulled up and is unresponsive or not breathing normally, perform CPR immediately. Those who are trained should perform chest compressions with rescue breaths. If you do not know how, are unable, or do not want to give rescue breaths, just perform continuous chest compressions while listening to the emergency dispatcher's instructions.
Free. The difficulty is resisting the urge to jump in.

WHO: about 300,000 people drown worldwide every year, 92% in low- and middle-income countries. Drowning is the fourth leading cause of death in children aged 1 to 4, and the third in children aged 5 to 14. The WHO recommended measure is "safe rescue and resuscitation training", for example, learning rescue methods that do not require entering the water beforehand. First, shout for help, call 110/120, then from the shore reach out with a long pole, rope, or throw lifebuoys, empty barrels, and other floating objects. The 2025 International First Aid Guidelines from the Red Cross state: when rescuing someone, try not to enter the water; from the shore or a boat, extend a rigid object (such as a pole or tree branch), or throw a rope or floatable object. Rescuers should not touch a person struggling in the water, as there is a risk of being pulled under. Those who have entered the water to rescue must understand the current conditions and bring a floating object. If the person is recovered and is unresponsive or breathing abnormally, perform CPR immediately. The 2024 Resuscitation Guidelines for Drowning from the American Heart Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics emphasize: cardiac arrest due to drowning is usually caused by severe hypoxia. Trained rescuers must perform rescue breaths along with chest compressions. If you do not know how, are unable, or do not want to give rescue breaths, perform continuous chest compressions until the rescue team arrives. When calling emergency services, turn on the speakerphone and listen to the dispatcher's instructions.
Someone is choking and cannot speak: for those aged 1 and older, stand behind them, give 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts; if they collapse, perform CPR
B

First ask "Are you choking? Can you speak?"; if they can still cough or make sounds, let them cough on their own. For those aged 1 and older who cannot speak, stand behind them, give 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts; for pregnant women and very obese people, switch to chest thrusts. Repeat until the foreign object comes out or the person collapses; if they collapse, perform CPR and ask someone to call emergency services. Do not put your hand in their mouth to hook out something you cannot see.
Free. Watch the movement once: place one hand in a fist just above the navel, wrap the other hand around the fist, and pull sharply inward and upward.

U.S. National Library of Medicine, verbatim: first ask "are you choking, can you speak". "If the person can cough strongly and speak, do not interfere"; the cough itself usually expels the foreign object. If they cannot speak, "repeat 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the foreign object comes out or the person loses consciousness". "If they lose consciousness, start CPR", and ask someone to call emergency services. For pregnant women and obese people, switch to chest thrusts. The 2025 International First Aid Guidelines from the Red Cross state: do not put your fingers in the mouth to feel around, as this may push the foreign object deeper; only use fingers to remove a solid object if you can see it.
Lost or vehicle breakdown in the wilderness, desert, or uninhabited areas: stay in place or by the vehicle, report your location first, then seek shade and stay warm, save water, do not wander
C

Stay in place or by the vehicle; the vehicle is the largest source of shade. The order is: if there is a signal, send your location first then call → seek shade and stay warm → save water → do not wander → signal using a reflective mirror, smoke, or three fires. Before entering, inform others of your route, destination, return date, vehicle type, and license plate number.

Before entering uninhabited areas, inform others of your route, destination, return date, vehicle type, and license plate number. At least 4 liters of water per person per day. Satellite communication devices or BeiDou short messaging devices cost over a thousand yuan, or a few hundred yuan to rent once. The difficulty is "staying in place and not wandering."

The Mojave National Preserve page of the U.S. National Park Service has three verbatim sentences. One is "at least 1 gallon (about 3.8 liters) of water per person per day, 2 gallons per person per day for hikers and cyclists". Another is "tell someone your route, destination, return date, vehicle type, and license plate number". Another is "cell phone service is intermittent". The Death Valley page, verbatim: "when it is hot, do not walk on the valley floor and low-lying areas"; the wilderness "has almost no cell phone service", recommending satellite phones. The Mojave desert driving page, verbatim: "in an emergency, staying with your vehicle is the most important thing you can do". This page also mentions that while it doesn't happen often, people have indeed died from exposure to heat or cold while walking back to the main road. Priority is divided into five steps. Step one is reporting the news and coordinates; if there is a signal, send the location first then call. Step two is seeking shade and staying warm; the vehicle is the largest shelter. Step three is saving water. Step four is not wandering. Step five is signaling. Advice from the Chongqing Municipal Emergency Management Bureau (China): three fires arranged in a triangle is an internationally recognized distress signal. If nearby, call out "three short, three long, then three short", repeating every 1 minute. If there is sunlight, use a mirror, a tin can lid, or other shiny objects to reflect light. The Ministry of Culture and Tourism (China) reminds self-driving tourists to consider carefully when going to uninhabited areas, try to travel with multiple vehicles, and rent a satellite phone when necessary.
Shivering, slurred speech, and stumbling are signs of hypothermia: change out of wet clothes, wrap up tightly, warm the torso first, drink hot sugary drinks, do not drink alcohol
B

A body temperature below 35°C is hypothermia; the person will shiver, have slurred speech, stumble, and be unable to think clearly. Change out of wet clothes, wrap in a thermal blanket or dry clothes, warm the torso first, do not warm the limbs first. Give hot sugary drinks, do not give alcohol, as alcohol reduces the shivering reflex. If they are unresponsive and not breathing normally, perform CPR according to section 1 of this chapter (push hard on the chest).
A foil thermal blanket costs a few yuan, plus a spare set of dry clothes. Learning to recognize the signs is free.

U.S. National Weather Service, verbatim: a body temperature below 95°F (35°C) is hypothermia, "if you feel cold, sluggish, and can't think clearly, seek medical attention immediately". Treatment is "seek medical attention immediately, move the person into a heated room, warm the center of the body first", and give hot drinks. "Alcohol reduces the shivering reflex", so do not drink it. "If unconscious, perform CPR"; whether chest compressions are needed and how to check is in section 1 of this chapter (not breathing normally). For frostbite, rewarm with warm water or body heat, "do not use hot water or radiant heat like a heater". The 2019 Hypothermia Guidelines from the Wilderness Medical Society are the practice guidelines for this field.
Snakebite: sit down and do not move, remove rings and watches, go to the hospital for antivenom as soon as possible, do not cut, do not suck, do not tie tightly
B

Sit down and do not move, keep the bitten limb still, immediately remove rings and watches so they don't constrict when swelling occurs. Go to a hospital that has antivenom as soon as possible; antivenom is the most effective way to prevent or reverse most of the venom's damage. Do not cut, do not suck with your mouth, do not apply ice, do not rub, do not tie with a cord, and do not walk around. If you can take a photo of the snake, do so, but do not try to catch it.
Free. Know in advance which nearby hospital has antivenom. The difficulty is resisting the urge to handle the bite yourself.

WHO has three verbatim sentences. One is "immediately immobilize the bitten part of the body completely, and quickly transport to the nearest medical facility". Another is "avoid using tourniquets, avoid cutting the wound". Another is "treatment with antivenom appropriate for the local snake species". "High-quality antivenom is the most effective treatment to prevent or reverse most of the damage caused by snake venom". Every year, about 81,000 to 138,000 people worldwide die from snakebites, and the number of people with permanent amputations and disabilities is about 3 times the number of deaths. The 2024 Chinese Snakebite Treatment Guidelines estimate 250,000 to 280,000 venomous snakebite cases in the country annually. Most victims are aged 50 and older. Hospitals in 11 provinces in the Yangtze River basin and southern China treated 40,817 snakebite victims from 2017 to 2021. There were 23 deaths during hospitalization (0.06%). The 2025 International First Aid Guidelines from the Red Cross state: the victim should try to move as little as possible; if bitten on the leg, do not walk. Remove jewelry, watches, and tight clothing to avoid constriction when swelling occurs. Do not use tourniquets, do not suck, do not apply cold, do not rub, do not use a knife to cut; these methods are useless and can cause further harm. If you can safely take a photo of the snake, do so, but do not try to catch or kill it.

In an earthquake, first check what kind of building you are in: if the building meets seismic standards, hide in place; if it is an old building that might collapse and the door is only a few steps away, run outside
B

First, check what kind of building you are in. If the building is built according to seismic standards and going outside requires taking stairs and passing through a lobby, hide in place: cover your head and neck, crawl under a sturdy table, and hold on tight to the table legs. If it is a single-story house, an old brick house, or a self-built house without seismic design, and the door is only a few steps away, run outside. In any case, do not jump from the building, do not use the elevator, and do not go down the stairs while the building is shaking.
Free. Check in advance how many steps it takes to get to the door of your house, which path to take, and which table is sturdy.

The educational video "Earthquake strikes: hide or run?" from the China Earthquake Administration has the catchphrase "when it shakes, hide in the nearest place; when the shaking stops, evacuate quickly", and clearly limits this to "buildings that meet seismic design requirements". The reason is that for this type of building, "the possibility of total collapse is quite small". Verbatim, it says "falling structural components and decorations" "are the greatest threat to life". Whereas "running around without protection during shaking" "makes it easy to be hit by falling ceilings, chandeliers (ceiling fans), and other objects". The way to hide is to "use your hands or other soft objects to protect your head and neck" "and hold on tight to the table legs"; if there is no table, "quickly crouch against a load-bearing wall" "avoiding exterior walls, windows, and balconies". "If you are outdoors" then "immediately evacuate to an open area to avoid the earthquake". Looking back, the 1988 Armenia earthquake involved the mass collapse of Soviet-style prefabricated panel buildings. A case-control study on that event wrote: "leaving the building after the first shock was a protective behavior". People who stayed indoors were 4.40 times more likely to be injured than those who ran out (odds ratio OR = 4.40), 95% confidence interval from 2.24 to 8.71. The likelihood of injury when inside a structure was 12.20 times higher than when outdoors (from 3.62 to 63.79). Being in a building of 5 floors or more was 3.65 times riskier than in lower buildings (from 2.12 to 6.33). Earthquake education materials from the Ministry of Emergency Management (China) state: "people living in old brick-concrete structures should be more proactive in seeking opportunities to evacuate quickly". For those in single-story houses, "if you are near the door or window, and there are no other dangerous structures outside, you can run immediately to an open yard". During an earthquake "never use the elevator"; on the first or second floor "do not choose to jump from the building to escape", and in high-rise buildings "be careful not to go downstairs". Once outdoors, avoid buildings with glass walls, overpasses, utility poles, streetlights, and billboards.
Encountering bears, wild boars, or packs of stray dogs: do not run, turn sideways and slowly back away
B

If you encounter a bear, do not run; they can run as fast as a racehorse both uphill and downhill; also do not climb trees, as both black and brown bears can climb. Stand still, talk to it continuously in a low voice, wait for it to stand still, then turn sideways and slowly back away. If a brown bear charges, lie face down and play dead, with hands clasped behind your neck; if a black bear charges, run into a car or a house; if you cannot run, fight back. If scratched or bitten by a dog, wash the wound and get vaccinated according to section 13.
Free. Bring trekking poles when going into the mountains, go in a group, and make noise as you go so the animal knows you are coming beforehand. The difficulty is standing still and not running.

The U.S. National Park Service has six verbatim sentences about bears. One is "do not run, bears can run as fast as a racehorse both uphill and downhill". One is "stay calm, most bears do not want to attack you; they just want to be left alone". One is "talk to the bear continuously in a low voice". One is "when the bear is standing still, turn sideways and slowly back away, so you can see the bear and avoid tripping". One is "make yourself look as large as possible". Another is "do not climb trees, both grizzly and black bears can climb trees". If attacked by a brown bear, "play dead, lie face down, hands clasped behind your neck, legs spread". If attacked by a black bear, "do not play dead, run into a car or house; if you cannot run, use anything at hand to fight back". If bitten by a dog, handle it according to section 13.
Encountering lightning outdoors: get into a hard-top car or a building, avoid ridges, lone trees, water surfaces, and metal
B

In a thunderstorm area, nowhere outdoors is safe. Get into a hard-top car or a building; convertibles, motorcycles, tents, picnic shelters, under trees, or under rocky overhangs do not count. Avoid open fields, mountain ridges and peaks, large lone trees, water surfaces, and iron railings; if the group cannot move, stand apart. If you hear thunder, retreat; it is only considered safe 30 minutes after the last clap of thunder.
Free. The price is interrupting the trip for half an hour or more. The difficulty is being willing to turn back immediately when the thunder is still far away.

In a thunderstorm area, nowhere outdoors is safe. It is only considered safe 30 minutes after the last clap of thunder. The U.S. National Weather Service states: you must run into a sturdy building or a hard-top car. Tents do not block lightning at all, and picnic shelters open on four sides are also unsafe. Cave entrances and small rocky overhangs are also dangerous; electric arcs can jump across gaps. Sheltering under a tree is the second leading cause of lightning casualties. If you hear thunder, you are likely already within lightning range, "when thunder roars, go indoors".
When going to high altitudes, increase elevation gradually based on sleeping location (the altitude at which you sleep that night); if symptoms worsen, go lower, do not try to endure it
A

What matters is the altitude at which you sleep, not how high you reached during the day. Sleeping at an altitude of 2,450 meters or higher already carries a risk of altitude sickness. Beyond the 3,000-meter mark, the sleeping altitude should increase by a maximum of 500 meters per night, and for every additional 1,000 meters, rest an extra day to acclimatize. If you have a headache or nausea, do not go higher to sleep; if symptoms worsen despite resting, go lower. Stumbling or being short of breath even while sitting still: descending and breathing oxygen are more effective than taking medicine.

It takes an extra one to two days for the body to acclimatize. Preventive medication is prescription-only; you must consult a doctor before going. The difficulty is being willing to set aside these days even when the schedule is tight.

Sleeping at an altitude of 2,450 meters or higher already carries a risk of altitude sickness. High-altitude cerebral edema and high-altitude pulmonary edema (fluid accumulation in the brain and lungs) can be fatal if you do not descend in time. The Yellow Book from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) provides three principles to avoid severe forms: know the early symptoms and be willing to admit you have them; when symptoms occur, no matter how mild, do not go higher to sleep; if symptoms worsen while resting or being treated at the same altitude, descend. Acute mountain sickness usually improves quickly when descending 300 meters or more. In remote areas, if high-altitude cerebral edema is suspected, descend immediately; if dexamethasone and oxygen are available, use them as well. In most cases of high-altitude pulmonary edema, you must descend immediately; descending and breathing oxygen are both significantly more effective than taking medicine.
If bitten by a tick: use fine-tipped tweezers to grasp it close to the skin and pull out steadily; do not apply oil, do not use fire
B

Use fine-tipped tweezers to grasp the tick's head close to the skin and pull straight out with steady pressure. Do not apply oil, do not use fire, and do not twist or jerk: doing so will agitate the tick, causing it to squeeze pathogen-containing fluids into the skin, and it may also leave the mouthparts in the flesh. After removal, record the date. If you develop a fever, rash, or fatigue in the following weeks, tell your doctor you were bitten by a tick when you go for a check-up.
A pair of fine-tipped tweezers.

Applying oil, using fire, or twisting and jerking will agitate the tick, causing it to squeeze pathogen-containing fluids into the skin. Doing so also makes it easy to leave the mouthparts (oral organs) embedded in the flesh. In China, ticks transmit a disease called severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome. In 2024, 6,602 cases and 306 deaths were reported nationwide, both the highest since the disease was discovered. The average mortality rate for the 2010–2024 period was 4.79%, increasing with age, reaching 9.15% for those aged 85 and older.
Outdoor water must be boiled before drinking, one minute of rolling boil is enough; at common travel altitudes, longer boiling is not necessary
B

All waterborne pathogenic microorganisms die within seconds at boiling temperature. Boiling for an additional minute is only to compensate for cases of "mistakenly seeing it as boiling"; at common travel altitudes, longer boiling is not necessary. If boiling is not possible, use a filter or disinfection tablets; both methods have types of pathogens they cannot treat, so boil if you can. Clear-looking stream water can still contain parasites.
Carry an extra stove set and fuel.

All waterborne pathogenic microorganisms are killed (inactivated) within seconds at boiling water temperature. "At high altitudes, boiling water is not hot enough" is a common misunderstanding. The same page clearly states that the other two methods have flaws: most portable filters cannot block viruses; chlorine and iodine at practical doses almost cannot kill Cryptosporidium parasites. In places with many people and animals passing through, clear-looking surface water must still be guarded against all intestinal pathogens, including Cryptosporidium. Water in remote areas with few people mainly requires precautions against Giardia and intestinal bacteria.
When blocked by strangers demanding money in a remote place: give the money, do not fight back, remember characteristics, escape and then report to the police
C

When blocked face-to-face and physical safety is threatened, prioritize your life; do not risk fighting back or chasing for money. After the opponent takes the money and leaves, chasing to reclaim property may still be considered justifiable defense, but it depends on the local situation and the method used. Once escaped, record their appearance, voice, license plate, direction of flight, and call 110.
The amount of cash carried on your person. The difficulty lies in suppressing anger.

Life is more expensive than money, while the opponent is risking a serious crime for a few hundred yuan. Article 263 of the Criminal Law of China stipulates: using violence, threats, or other methods to rob public or private property is punishable by three to ten years in prison and a fine. Cases such as carrying a gun, breaking into a house, or causing serious injury or death to others are punishable by ten years or more, up to the death penalty. Justifiable defense in Article 20 of the Criminal Law of China protects acts of "stopping an ongoing unlawful infringement." The 2020 guiding opinions of the Supreme People's Court, the Supreme People's Procuratorate, and the Ministry of Public Security (China) clearly state: although property has been taken, if it can be reclaimed by chasing or blocking, the infringement can be considered ongoing. Whether it counts as justifiable defense depends on the situation at the time and the purpose of stopping the infringement. To conclude that the limits of justifiable defense were exceeded, two conditions must be met simultaneously: clearly exceeding what is necessary, and causing serious damage. One cannot conclude that the defense has ended simply because the opponent turned away with the money. For your own safety, do not risk fighting back or chasing for money. Once escaped, immediately record the appearance, voice, license plate, direction of flight, and call 110.

If you encounter a group of people fighting, step back and leave, do not rush in to intervene, do not stand and watch, do not pick up items from the ground; if you want to report to the police, retreat to a safe distance and call 110
B

If you strike a blow, you turn from intervening to participating in a fight; the right thing to do is to step back and leave. Actively participating in a brawling assembly is punishable by up to 3 years in prison. Large-scale brawls involving many people that seriously disrupt public order on the street or involve weapons are punishable by 3 to 10 years in prison. If you want to report to the police, retreat to a safe distance and call 110, clearly stating the location, number of people, whether they have knives or sticks, and if anyone is lying motionless.

No cost. The difficulty is suppressing two impulses: wanting to rush in to pull people out, and wanting to stay and watch. After reporting to the police, you may be called back to give a statement once, taking at most half a day.

Article 292 of the Criminal Law of China: "In cases of brawling, the ringleaders and active participants shall be sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of not more than three years, criminal detention, or public surveillance." For brawling multiple times, involving many people, on a large scale, with bad social impact, seriously disrupting social order in public places or on major traffic routes, or involving weapons, the punishment is "imprisonment from three to ten years." "Brawling that causes serious injury or death to others" is handled as intentional injury or murder. The Public Security Administration Punishment Law (China) also has sanctions. Striking another person results in administrative detention for 5 to 10 days and a fine of ⟦500~1000⟧. Gathering a gang to fight is handled as picking quarrels and provoking trouble, with a maximum of 15 days detention and a fine of ⟦2000⟧. Article 5 of the "Guiding Opinions on the Application of the System of Justifiable Defense According to Law" (China): unlawful infringement "includes not only infringement directed at oneself, but also infringement endangering the state, public interests, or directed at others." Article 9 of that document states: if one party strikes first and the method is clearly excessive, the counter-attacker is generally considered to be acting in defense. If one party strikes first while the other party has tried to avoid conflict but the infringement continues, the same applies.
Possible HIV exposure: go get preventive medication within 72 hours, the sooner the better
B

If you suspect you may have been exposed to the HIV virus, 72 hours is a hard deadline; it is best to take the medication within 2 hours. The medication must be taken for 28 consecutive days. After 72 hours, this path is closed, so do not wait until the next day to decide.

A 28-day course of medication costs over ⟦1000⟧, which must be self-paid in most regions of China. You must rush to the hospital even in the middle of the night. The difficulty is admitting at that moment that you might have been infected and leaving the house immediately.

The HIV prevention knowledge section of the Beijing Municipal Government (China) states: preventive medication used after exposure is called post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), and one should "take preventive medication within 2 hours if possible, preferably within 24 hours, and no later than 72 hours." It also requires "continuous intake for 28 days." Starting after 72 hours is not recommended; this is a hard time limit. The Beijing article also clearly states "taking medication regularly every day results in better preventive efficacy than forgetting doses." Technical guidelines from the National Center for AIDS/STD Control and Prevention of the China CDC clearly state: forgetting doses or stopping medication arbitrarily reduces preventive efficacy. The guidelines require monitoring for side effects in the 2nd week after starting, and HIV and Hepatitis C antibody testing on the 30th and 90th days after exposure. The Chongqing Municipal CDC (China) announced in 2024: there are 29 clinics in 26 districts and counties across the city that can prescribe pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis, with 14 locations providing 24-hour service.
If injured or losing money while rescuing someone: claim from the perpetrator and health insurance first, then apply for recognition as a courageous act for a righteous cause
B

If you suffer a loss while rescuing someone, you don't have to just accept the bad luck. People injured while performing righteous deeds are treated first and billed later; medical expenses are paid by the perpetrator; if they flee or cannot afford it, basic medical insurance covers it. If there is no perpetrator, you make a request, and the person you rescued is legally required to provide appropriate compensation. Simultaneously apply for recognition as a courageous act for a righteous cause; if injured and eligible, you receive benefits similar to work-related injuries.
No cost. Applying for recognition requires submitting a dossier, waiting for review, and traveling back and forth several times, taking several weeks to several months.

Article 183 of the Civil Code of China: "Where a person suffers damage for protecting the civil rights and interests of others, the infringer shall bear civil liability, and the beneficiary may provide appropriate compensation. If there is no infringer, the infringer has fled, or is unable to bear civil liability, and the victim requests compensation, the beneficiary shall provide appropriate compensation." Document No. 39 of 2012 from the State Council General Office (China) addresses the treatment of people injured while performing righteous deeds. Medical institutions must establish a green channel, "upholding the principle of 'treatment first, payment later'." Regarding medical fees, the text states "medical expenses incurred due to emergency rescue shall be borne by the perpetrator or responsible party; if there is no perpetrator or responsible party, or if they flee or are unable to pay, it shall be resolved through the basic medical security system according to regulations." In case of death, "those meeting the criteria for martyr recognition shall be recognized as martyrs according to law"; "those falling under cases deemed as work-related injuries shall receive a one-time funeral subsidy and a special allowance for dependents equal to 40 months of their own salary." In case of disability, "those eligible for work-related injury insurance benefits shall follow the corresponding system under the Work-Related Injury Insurance Regulations; those ineligible shall have their disability level assessed by civil affairs departments and follow the corresponding system." Regarding employment, "priority shall be given for inclusion in employment assistance and key support," and public welfare job positions "shall be prioritized for eligible individuals performing righteous deeds." Regarding housing, "priority shall be given for inclusion in the housing security system, with priority for renting or purchasing social housing or receiving rental subsidies."
Knives, iron bars, or glass shards piercing the body: press around the foreign object to stop bleeding, do not pull it out
B

Pulling it out can cause massive bleeding and makes it difficult for doctors to know how deep the wound is. Method: call 120, use hands or gauze to press around the foreign object to stop bleeding, wedge the object to keep it still, and do not let it shake. If an abdominal wound results in protruding intestines or organs, do not push them back in; cover them with a clean, moist gauze. If a chest wound is bubbling, do not seal it tightly with plastic; sealing it can cause lung collapse.
No cost. The difficulty is suppressing the instinct to "pull it out first" and sitting to hold the injured person while waiting for the ambulance.

The 2025 International First Aid Guidelines from the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC): "The first aider should press around the foreign object piercing the body (e.g., a knife), keep the object fixed, and not pull it out." "Do not pull out any foreign object embedded in an abdominal or chest wound; pulling it out can cause massive bleeding and also makes it difficult for doctors to assess the severity of the wound." "Foreign objects embedded in the body must be kept fixed; if the object pulsates with the pulse, let it pulsate, just hold it loosely to keep it fixed." "The first aider should not push protruding internal organs back into the body." An open wound in the chest wall without gushing blood "can be left open, without applying gauze, because sealing the wound can cause air to accumulate in the chest cavity, causing the lung to partially or totally collapse (pneumothorax)." All penetrating wounds to the chest or abdomen require an immediate emergency call.
Suspected fracture: do not move that part anymore: support it to keep it still, apply cold for no more than 20 minutes, do not try to reset it yourself
B

If a limb is injured, treat it as a fracture first; being able to stand or move does not rule it out. Keep the injured area still, support it with your hands or use a rigid board to splint it in its current position; apply cold for no more than 20 minutes at a time. Do not try to straighten it yourself; if bone protrudes through the skin, stop the bleeding first and do not push the bone back in. X-rays can miss fractures; if the film is normal but the doctor still suspects a fracture or ligament damage, follow up or get an MRI as advised by the doctor.
No cost. Find a rigid board, a rolled-up magazine, or clothing to use as a support splint. For cold items, wrap them in a layer of cloth before applying.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) has issued the 2025 International First Aid Guidelines. It states "all limb injuries should be treated initially as possible fractures." It also says "the only way to accurately diagnose a fracture is through X-ray. If unsure, treat it as a fracture." The purpose of immobilization is to "minimize movement and pain to the maximum extent." Cold application "should be for a maximum of 20 continuous minutes at a time, which can reduce pain; longer cold exposure can damage the skin." "When a long bone like the femur is broken, bleeding from the bone itself can be fatal." Severe pain or swelling, signs of shock, a femur fracture, or a clearly misaligned limb require an emergency call. If a fracture is angled, two conditions must be met simultaneously to consider resetting it on-site (reduction). First, "in a remote location (or limited conditions), and the part of the limb below the bend is cold, pale, or the first aider cannot immobilize it for transport." Second, the first aider must be trained. Open fractures (broken bone piercing the skin) require stopping bleeding and preventing infection first. However, a first X-ray not showing a fracture does not mean there isn't one. The UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has a guideline on hip fractures. It states: if X-rays are normal but a hip fracture is still suspected, "perform magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)." If MRI is unavailable within 24 hours, consider a CT scan. NICE guidelines on fractures state: if a scaphoid fracture in the wrist is suspected, "after a thorough clinical examination, consider MRI first." The scaphoid is a small bone in the wrist. A Cochrane review states: "initial X-rays do not rule out fractures." In pooled studies, among people with normal X-rays where doctors still suspected a scaphoid fracture, the median rate of actual fracture was 20%. The American College of Radiology has a set of Appropriateness Criteria for knee trauma imaging. It states: if X-rays show no fracture but an occult fracture or internal joint injury is still suspected, the next step is "usually appropriate" for an MRI. The criteria also state MRI is very accurate in detecting occult fractures, meniscal, and ligament injuries.
After sexual assault: get to safety first then call 110; before the forensic exam do not bathe, do not wash clothes, do not clean the room, get to a hospital within 72 hours
B

Traces left on the body, on clothes, and in the room are the most important evidence to identify the perpetrator. Therefore, before the injury examination, try not to bathe, wash clothes, or clean the room; call 110 as soon as possible. Emergency contraceptive pills are available at any pharmacy; the sooner they are taken, the more effective they are. Go to a hospital within 72 hours so a doctor can determine if HIV preventive medication is needed.

Reporting to the police is free. Emergency contraceptive pills are over-the-counter drugs (China), available at any pharmacy. A course of HIV preventive medication costs over ⟦1000⟧; whether it is necessary is decided by a doctor, see section 38 of this chapter (getting preventive medication within 72 hours). The difficulty is that it is very hard to speak up at that time, and there is a strong urge to bathe immediately.

A prosecutor from the Beijing Municipal People's Procuratorate (China) said: "Whether a minor or an adult, if you encounter assault, you should call 110 to report to the police immediately." Timely reporting and examination "help investigative organs promptly examine the scene, collect traces and physical evidence, and fix evidence." A sexual assault prevention manual from the People's Daily (China), reposted by the Guizhou Provincial Department of Civil Affairs, states: "If unfortunately sexually assaulted, the most important thing is to preserve evidence." One must keep "body fluids, hair, skin scales, communication history, and other evidence," "after being assaulted, do not arbitrarily bathe, wash clothes, clean the room, or throw things away." If committed by an acquaintance, keep call logs and messages. If the perpetrator subsequently threatens or bribes you, evidence of that must also be kept. The Xicheng District People's Procuratorate in Beijing wrote: "try not to bathe before the physical examination." The World Health Organization (WHO) says emergency contraception can be used when "a woman has been sexually assaulted without effective contraceptive protection." It is recommended for use within 5 days, the sooner the better. Emergency contraceptive pills containing levonorgestrel (a type of progestin) have a pregnancy rate of 1.2% to 2.1% among women who used them. Levonorgestrel tablets sold in Chinese pharmacies are over-the-counter. The Wuhan Municipal Health Commission (China) stated: after unprotected intercourse, "within 72 hours, the sooner the pill is taken, the better the contraceptive effect." HIV preventive medication must be taken within 2 hours if possible, and no later than 72 hours (national).
Infant under 1 year choking, not crying: place face down and give 5 back blows, flip over and give 5 chest thrusts, alternate these, do not perform abdominal thrusts
B

If the child can still cough or cry, let them cough on their own and monitor them. If they cannot cry and their face turns blue, have someone call 120. Place the child face down on your forearm, use the heel of your hand to give 5 blows between the shoulder blades; if it doesn't come out, flip them over and give 5 quick thrusts to the center of the chest. Alternate these two actions; do not perform abdominal thrusts; if the child becomes unresponsive, switch to CPR.
No cost. Watch the movements once or take a short first aid class for infants, taking a few minutes to half a day. The difficulty is remembering to flip the child face down first while panicking.

The American Heart Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics have issued the 2025 Pediatric Basic Life Support guidelines. The guidelines state: choking (e.g., foreign body airway obstruction) "is one of the leading causes of death in infants and children." The thing infants most commonly choke on is liquid. Still coughing or making sound is mild; let the child cough on their own while monitoring for worsening. Very weak coughing, inability to cough or cry, and cyanosis (blue skin) are severe. For severe cases, call emergency services first, then "repeat 5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts until the object comes out or the child becomes unresponsive." The guidelines do not recommend abdominal thrusts for infants because they can damage internal organs. Chest thrusts are now recommended using the heel of one hand, as it presses deeper than the previous two-finger method. If the child becomes unresponsive, start CPR, beginning with chest compressions, without checking for a pulse. Before rescue breaths, if a foreign body is visible, remove it. The guidelines clearly state "do not perform blind finger sweeps." The 2025 International First Aid Guidelines from the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) also follow this sequence. First, give up to 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades; if unsuccessful, flip the child and give up to 5 chest thrusts; if still unsuccessful, call emergency services immediately. The IFRC chest thrust method involves wrapping both hands around the chest and pressing with both thumbs. The Fujian Provincial Red Cross Emergency Rescue Training Center (China) says for children under 1 year, perform "5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts." When giving back blows, place the infant face down on the forearm with the head lower than the torso.
Infant under 1 year unresponsive, not breathing normally: use speakerphone to call 120, perform infant CPR: 30 compressions, 2 breaths
B

If the child does not respond to flicking the sole of the foot and is not breathing normally, use speakerphone to call 120 without stopping your hands. Wrap both hands around the chest and press with both thumbs; if you cannot wrap around, use the heel of one hand, pressing about 4 cm deep, about 2 times per second. Every 30 compressions, cover the child's mouth and nose with your mouth and give 2 breaths. Most infant cardiac arrests are due to respiratory failure; more infants survive when CPR includes rescue breaths.
No cost. Infant CPR requires attending a class and practicing once, taking half a day to a day. The difficulty is having to breathe into the child's mouth and nose, and not daring to press hard.

The American Heart Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics have issued the 2025 Pediatric Basic Life Support guidelines. The guidelines state: for infants and children in cardiac arrest, the primary cause remains respiratory issues. For out-of-hospital infant cardiac arrest, only 6.6% survive to discharge. Laypeople encountering an infant or child who is unresponsive, not breathing normally, and showing no signs of life "must start CPR immediately" without checking for a pulse. Compression depth should be at least one-third of the anterior-posterior diameter of the chest, which in infants is "about 1.5 inches (4 cm)." Frequency is 100 to 120 times per minute. A single rescuer performs 30 compressions and 2 breaths. Two rescuers perform 15 compressions and 2 breaths. For infants, use the heel of one hand, or wrap both hands around the chest and press with both thumbs. If you cannot wrap around, use the heel of the hand. The two-finger compression method has been discarded as it does not press deep enough. The guidelines also state that for out-of-hospital infant and child cardiac arrest, chest compressions combined with rescue breaths increase survival rates. A US registry tracked 3,900 children under 18 with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, 59.4% of whom were infants. When CPR was performed by a bystander, the adjusted survival rate to discharge was 13.2%, compared to 9.5% without. Adjusted OR 1.57 (about 57% higher chance of survival), 95% confidence interval 1.25 to 1.96. In infants, CPR with rescue breaths is associated with higher survival rates, and survivors also have better neurological recovery. Chest compressions alone without rescue breaths yielded results similar to no CPR. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) also issued 2025 International First Aid Guidelines. The guidelines state: to check if an infant is responsive, pick them up or flick the sole of the foot. If you are alone, use speakerphone to call emergency services. If no phone is available to call while compressing, perform 1 minute of CPR before going to call. The Capital Institute of Pediatrics (China) has a knowledge dissemination article, reposted by the Beijing Municipal Health Commission. The article states: "If there is only 1 person on site, perform 2 minutes of CPR before calling the 120 ambulance." Compression depth for "infants is 4 cm." For children under 1 year, perform "mouth-to-mouth-and-nose" breathing.
Child swallows a button battery, or swallows two or more magnets: go immediately to an emergency room with gastric endoscopy, do not wait for it to pass in the stool, do not induce vomiting
B

A button battery stuck in the esophagus can cause severe burns in as little as 2 hours, even if the child initially appears normal. Two or more magnets will attract each other through the intestinal walls, potentially squeezing and perforating the gut. If you suspect a child has swallowed them, go to the hospital for an X-ray immediately; do not induce vomiting, do not wait for it to pass in the stool, and do not wait for symptoms to appear.

Free; emergency X-ray and foreign body removal costs are separate. Daily, tighten the battery compartment covers of remote controls, digital scales, and car keys. Keep spare batteries and magnets out of children's reach. The difficulty is that in most cases, no one sees the child swallow them, and the child may initially have no symptoms.

Data from the US National Poison Data System from 1985 to 2009 showed a 6.7-fold increase in the rate of severe injury or death from swallowing button batteries. The most dangerous are 20 mm diameter lithium batteries. For children under 4, lithium batteries 20 mm or larger lead to significantly worse outcomes. A battery stuck in the esophagus can cause severe burns leaving permanent sequelae in just 2 to 2.5 hours. In 92% of fatal cases and 56% of severe injury cases, no one saw the child swallow the battery. At least 54% of fatal cases and 27% of severe injury cases were initially misdiagnosed because symptoms were atypical. Even after the battery is removed, the damage can continue to deepen. In some cases, esophageal perforation, tracheoesophageal fistula, or aortoenteric fistula with massive bleeding occurred several days later. In another analysis of 8,648 cases, 61.8% of batteries swallowed by children under 6 were taken directly from electronic devices. Handling guidelines from the US National Capital Poison Center state: if swallowing is suspected, "do not induce vomiting." A battery stuck in the esophagus "can cause severe burns in as little as 2 hours," "do not wait for symptoms." Children under 12 must have an immediate X-ray to locate the battery. Injury surveillance by the CDC of Guangdong Province (China) shows nearly one hundred injury cases related to accidental battery ingestion in the last five years, mostly button batteries. 92.9% of those injured were children aged 0 to 6. Moderate or severe injuries accounted for 39.3%, and hospitalizations accounted for 25.0%. Their recommendation is to "seek medical attention immediately; absolutely do not induce vomiting or give the child food or drink." The same surveillance report states that swallowing magnets (Buckyballs) into the abdomen causes magnets in adjacent intestinal segments to "attract each other and press on the intestinal wall, causing intestinal obstruction or perforation"; if accidental ingestion is suspected, "must be taken to the hospital for immediate treatment." A 2025 review including 130 children found all had fistulas between intestinal segments (enteroenteric fistulas) after swallowing 2 or more magnets. The median age was 3.3 years; 95.5% required surgery, 19% had postoperative complications, including 1 death.

If someone is drunk, place them on their side, always have someone watch them, do not let them sleep alone; if they are unresponsive, breathing slowly or irregularly, having seizures, or cold to the touch, call 120
B

A person drunk enough to fall asleep can choke to death on their own vomit, or their breathing may slow down and stop. Place them on their side, always have someone watch them, and do not leave them to sleep alone in a room. If they are unresponsive, breathing slowly or irregularly, having seizures, or have cold, bluish skin, call 120. Do not give them coffee, do not give them a cold bath, and do not stick a finger down their throat to induce vomiting.
Free. Someone must watch them for several hours, usually all night. The difficulty is that you may have been drinking too and want to go to sleep, and everyone thinks "they'll be fine after a nap."

The UK National Health Service (NHS) lists signs of alcohol poisoning: confusion, slurred speech, loss of coordination, vomiting, incontinence, pale or bluish skin, slow or irregular breathing, seizures, and unresponsiveness. If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, or if they have seizures, lose consciousness, or stop breathing, call emergency services. What must be done is to stay with them, "as they could choke on their own vomit or stop breathing." If the person is conscious, help them sit up. If they have passed out, place them on their side in the recovery position and check if they are breathing normally. If conscious, able to swallow, and not vomiting, they can take small sips of water. Cover them with a jacket or blanket to keep them warm. There are five things not to do. Do not give more alcohol. Do not give food, as they may choke. Do not give coffee or caffeinated drinks, as they worsen dehydration. Do not give a cold shower or soak in cold water, as they may get cold, fall, or faint in the water. Do not try to make them vomit. An article by an emergency physician on the Shaanxi Provincial Health Commission (China) website states: drunk people have weakened gag reflexes; when vomiting, they easily inhale into the trachea, which in severe cases leads to "immediate death from suffocation." Emergency departments frequently receive deceased drunk patients with large amounts of vomit suctioned from the trachea. In the coma stage, with a pale face, blue lips, cold clammy skin, decreased body temperature, and shallow breathing, call 120. At this point, place them on their side, "do not induce vomiting, do not give food," cover with a blanket for warmth, and turn them periodically. If the heart or breathing stops, perform CPR immediately. A public education article from a hospital reposted by the Beijing Municipal Health Commission (China) states: "Absolutely do not let a drunk person sleep alone, lest no one saves them if they suffocate." An article by a pharmacist reposted by the Fujian Provincial Drug Administration (China) says a drunk person "must lie on their side," as excessively low body temperature can cause cardiac arrest. The US CDC statistics show that from 2010 to 2012, an average of 2,221 people aged 15 and older died from alcohol poisoning each year in the US, equivalent to about 6 people per day.

Severed fingers or toes: apply firm pressure to the wound to stop bleeding first, wrap the severed part in moist gauze and place in a sealed bag, put the bag in ice water, go to a hospital with a hand surgery department
B

First, use your hand to apply firm pressure to the wound to stop bleeding, and call 120. Wrap the severed part in clean, moistened gauze, place it in a sealed bag, and put the bag in ice water; do not let it touch the ice directly, and do not soak it directly in water. Without cooling, a severed finger can only wait for about 4 to 6 hours. More than eight out of ten replanted fingers survive.

Free. Keep a pack of clean gauze and several zip-lock plastic bags at home. The difficulty is that during the panic, one still worries about the person first before the severed finger, and must resist the urge to bury the finger directly in ice or soak it in water.

The MedlinePlus first aid page of the US National Library of Medicine states: apply direct pressure to the wound to stop bleeding and elevate the injured area. If bleeding is life-threatening, a tourniquet may be used. The severed part must be kept and brought with the injured person. If the cut surface is dirty, rinse it gently first. Wrap in clean moist cloth, place in a sealed plastic bag, and put the bag in ice water. If not in a bag, do not drop it into water or ice, and do not place it directly on ice. Dry ice must not be used, as it will cause frostbite to the severed finger. If cold water is unavailable, try to keep it from getting hot. Cooling helps the severed finger last longer; without cooling, it is "only about 4 to 6 hours" that it remains replantable. Do not think the severed part is too small to keep. Do not push the severed part or bone back in. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons page on fingertip injuries states similar advice and adds that it is best to go to a hospital with a hand surgeon on call. Aggregating 31 studies, replanted fingers had an 86.8% survival rate (1,976 successful fingers, 300 failures). Among 1,087 people who had replantations, 82.9% were able to return to work. Another meta-analysis of 12 studies found a survival rate of 85.3% for replanted fingers. Yet another meta-analysis of 12 studies involving 3,645 people found that if a severed finger suffered ischemia for 8 hours or more before surgery, it was more likely to become necrotic after replantation. This probability is about 2.25 times higher than under 8 hours: OR = 2.25, 95% CI from 1.43 to 3.54.

Permanent tooth (tooth grown after baby teeth fall out) knocked out completely: hold the crown and rinse it, replant it if possible, if not, soak it in milk and see a dentist immediately; do not replant baby teeth
B

Hold the crown, do not touch the root; if dirty, rinse gently with milk or saline, replant it into the original socket if possible, and bite down on a clean cloth. If it cannot be replanted, soak it in milk and see a dentist immediately; do not wrap it dry in a tissue. For teeth replanted immediately on-site, the root fuses with the bone in about two out of ten cases later; for teeth left dry for over an hour, it is more than eight out of ten. Do not replant baby teeth.

Free. Milk and saline are available at home or in convenience stores; dental exam fees are separate. The difficulty is having the courage to replant the fallen tooth back into the gum yourself, and distinguishing on the spot whether the fallen tooth is a baby tooth or a permanent tooth.

The UK National Health Service (NHS) dental injury page states: hold the crown, which is the white part visible above the gum, and do not touch the root. If the tooth is dirty, rinse it gently with milk, saline, or saliva. Try to place it back into the original socket in the gum. If successful, bite gently on a clean cloth to hold it and see a dentist as soon as possible. If it cannot be replaced, soak it in milk or saliva. Do not replant baby teeth, as it will damage the permanent tooth growing underneath. If a knocked-out tooth cannot be found, an emergency dental appointment is still necessary. The "Save Your Tooth" poster by the International Association of Dental Traumatology has similar steps: find the tooth, hold the crown, plug the sink and rinse under cold water. Then choose one of three: put it back in place, soak it in a cup of milk or saline, or hold it between the cheek and gum. Finally, see a dentist immediately. The dental trauma database of Copenhagen University Hospital, Denmark, selected 145 permanent teeth from 116 people that were knocked out and then replanted, following them for 7 months to 23 years. They looked at the risk of the tooth root fusing with the alveolar bone (ankylosis); once fused, the root will gradually resorb. For teeth replanted immediately on-site, the risk was 17.2%; for those soaked in saliva or saline before replanting, 55.3%; and for those left dry for over 1 hour, 85.7%. This hospital previously followed a group of 400 teeth and re-analyzed them in 2020. For children's teeth with incomplete root development, the risk of ankylosis was 33.9% if left dry for under 20 minutes, and 60.0% if over 60 minutes. For teeth with complete root development, it increased from 59.4% to 86.4%. Both groups were estimates at 900 days after replantation. A 1995 study on this group of 400 teeth also found that soaking in tap water for more than 20 minutes would cause most to suffer root resorption. During the follow-up period, 30% of these 400 teeth eventually had to be extracted.
Turn on two-step verification for email, payment accounts, and social networks; prioritize clicking confirm on phone push notifications, followed by SMS codes
A

Two-step verification means that when logging in, besides the password, you must confirm one more time that it is really you. Having the phone display a notification for you to click confirm blocks more than nine out of ten account hijacking attempts; SMS codes are easier to steal than push notifications. The old method of answering questions like "where did you last log in" or "what is your recovery email" sometimes only blocks one-tenth of hijacking attempts.
Free. Set it up once for each account; it takes two or three minutes.

Google statistics on 350,000 actual account takeover attempts (also known as account hijacking). One type is device-based verification, such as a phone displaying a notification for you to click confirm, or plugging in a security key. This type blocked "over 94% of account takeovers originating from phishing and 100% of automated account takeovers." Phishing is tricking you into entering your password on a fake website; automated is using leaked passwords to try accounts in bulk. The other type is verification by answering questions, such as asking where you last logged in or what your recovery email is. This type "only blocked as low as 10% of takeovers by phishing and 73% of automated takeovers." Among device-based verifications, SMS codes are weaker than push notifications. Scammers correctly answered 4% of SMS codes, while push notifications were only tricked 1%. In targeted attacks aimed at a specific person, SMS only blocked 76%, while push notifications blocked 90%.
Use a unique password for your email, not shared with any other website
C

A password stolen from another website will be used to log directly into your email. If someone gains access to your email, all accounts that use email for password recovery will also be lost. Therefore, the email password must be unique and not used anywhere else.
Free. Saving it in a password manager means you don't have to remember it yourself. The difficulty is breaking the old habit of using one password everywhere.

Taking usernames and passwords leaked elsewhere to try logging in sequentially is called credential stuffing; your email will also be tested this way. If someone gains access to your email, every account that recovers passwords through it is lost. The recommendation from the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is: use a different strong password for each account, at least 16 characters long, and let a password manager store them.
Set a screen lock password for your phone and a PIN for your SIM card
C

A SIM is the small card in your phone that allows you to receive SMS verification codes. If you lose your phone, the person who finds it can remove this card and insert it into another device to receive verification codes, then sequentially reset your account passwords. Setting a SIM PIN means that when the card is moved to another device, this code must be entered as soon as the device is turned on, cutting off that path.
Free. Setting a screen lock password and a PIN each takes only one time.

If a phone is lost, the fastest way for the finder is to insert the SIM into another device to receive your SMS verification codes. With the verification code, they can reset each of your accounts. If the SIM has a PIN, when moved to another device, the password must be entered upon power-up, so the finder cannot use it to receive codes. In October 2020, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (China) reported a real case. A user had their phone stolen but did not report the SIM lost in time, giving the criminal time to exploit it. The criminal used the "phone number plus verification code" to log into a public service app, obtaining the user's ID number and other information. They then changed the subscriber's service password. Although the user later reported the SIM lost, the criminal used deception against the carrier's customer service to reactivate the card. Finally, they exploited the "forgot password" vulnerability of an online lending platform, reset the payment password, and stole loan money. The Ministry used this case to remind users to set a SIM password and report a lost phone immediately. Regarding screen lock passwords, the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) recommendation is: set a strong password for the phone to restrict others from using it. When a phone is lost or stolen, it prevents others from incurring charges and prevents your personal data from being used unauthorizedly.
If you lose your phone, follow this order: report the SIM lost, lock the device remotely, change passwords, report to the police, and freeze bank cards
C

Following the correct order is more important than speed. The first step is to report the SIM lost to cut off the path for receiving verification codes. Next, lock the phone remotely, then use a computer to change email and payment account passwords, then report to the police to get a receipt, and finally, depending on the situation, freeze bank cards. If you don't have your phone with you, borrow someone else's to call the carrier's hotline to report it lost.
Free. Completing the full set takes about ten-plus minutes.

Order is more important than speed. Step one: report the SIM lost so others cannot receive your verification codes. Step two: remotely lock the phone and wipe its contents. Step three: change email and payment account passwords from a computer. Step four: report to the police and get a receipt. Finally, if necessary, freeze bank cards. The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) reminder is the same: even if you think it's just dropped, lock it remotely. If stolen, report to the police immediately, providing the model and IMEI number (the phone's unique identifier), and notify the carrier immediately.

If your card is used fraudulently, report it lost and freeze it first, then report to the police, then demand compensation from the bank: proving "you were the one who swiped it" is the bank's responsibility
A

If your card is used fraudulently, you must provide evidence first, such as a police report and a loss report. If the bank claims the transaction was made by you, the bank must provide evidence; if they cannot, they must compensate you. The condition is that you must report the loss and freeze it immediately upon discovery. If you hesitate to report the loss, you will bear any additional damages incurred thereafter.

Free. If you notice unusual activity on the card, report it lost or freeze it immediately. Keep the police report, loss report, and transaction notifications sent by the bank. If the card is still in your possession, immediately make a small transaction nearby, such as checking the balance or depositing/withdrawing money, to leave evidence that the real card was in your hands when the incident occurred. The difficulty is resisting the urge to argue with the hotline operator first; report it lost first.

Regulations from the Supreme People's Court (China) clearly separate "who must provide evidence." If you claim this is a fraudulent swipe using a counterfeit card or a fraudulent online transaction, you provide evidence first. A counterfeit card swipe is when someone copies your card to another one to swipe. The following can all be used as proof: effective legal documents, where the real card was during the transaction, where the transaction occurred, as well as account transaction statements, transaction notifications, police reports, loss reports, etc. Conversely, if the issuing bank or a non-bank payment institution (third-party payment wallet) claims the transaction was made by the cardholder themselves or authorized by the cardholder, they must provide the evidence. If after you have notified the bank, the bank fails to verify promptly, or fails to promptly provide or preserve transaction records and camera footage, resulting in the inability to obtain evidence, the bank bears the consequences of failing to provide evidence. Once a fraudulent swipe is confirmed: debit card (savings card) holders have the right to request the issuing bank to return the principal and interest of the fraudulently swiped deposit and compensate for damages. Credit card holders have the right to request a refund of the principal, interest, and penalties of the fraudulently swiped overdraft and compensate for damages; if the bank turns around and demands you pay that overdraft, the court will not accept it. You also have the right to request the issuing bank to promptly clear the corresponding bad credit record (all-China, effective from May 25, 2021).
Occasionally review the list of logged-in devices and authorized apps for your accounts; remove any that are not in use
C

"Logged-in devices" are the phones and computers that can currently access your account. If the list shows a device you don't recognize, or software you deleted long ago is still connected to the account, change your password first, then log out from everywhere. For email, also check if there are any automatic forwarding rules that you did not set.
Free. Each review takes a few minutes. The difficulty is that no one reminds you; you must remember to check yourself.

The list of logged-in devices in an account records the phones and computers that can currently use this account. The list of authorized apps records third-party software that you have allowed to log in using this account. Unrecognized devices in the list and third-party software deleted long ago are the easiest traces to detect. The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) lists "logging in, or attempting to log in, from an unusual location or at an unusual time" as signs to check when an account is compromised. The agency also states that criminals often set a forwarding rule in email so that every message sent to you is automatically sent to them, allowing them to reset your passwords. The processing order provided by this agency is: find and delete unrecognized forwarding rules first, then change the password, then log out all devices and apps from the account. Once logged out, others wanting to use your account must enter the new password. The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) also advises that once you regain access to an account, log out of all devices and delete forwarding rules not set by you.
Do not click "Agree to All" just to use an app: if the information is unnecessary, you do not have to agree, and they cannot refuse to serve you
A

If an app requests your information and it is not mandatory for providing the service, you can refuse to provide it, and they cannot deny you access because of that. The data they are allowed to collect is limited to what is necessary. A map app requesting your location is necessary; a flashlight app requesting your contacts is not.
Free. The difficulty lies in exercising restraint and not clicking "Agree to All".

The Personal Information Protection Law (China) explicitly states two points. First, a provider may not refuse to provide products or services on the grounds that an individual does not consent to, or withdraws consent for, the processing of personal information, unless processing such information is necessary for providing the service. Second, collection must be limited to the minimum scope necessary to achieve the processing purpose, and only what is needed may be collected.
You have the right to view, copy, correct, and delete your personal information; if refused, you can file a lawsuit
A

You have the right to request that a business allows you to view, copy, correct, and delete your information. If the service stops, the retention period expires, or you withdraw consent, the business is inherently required to delete it. If they refuse, they must state the reason; if they fail to act, you can sue them directly in court. Deleting an account and deleting information are two different things; after deleting an account, you must separately request the deletion of information.

Free. You only need to file a complaint or lawsuit if the other party stalls. Going to court takes at least several months and you bear your own legal fees, so filing a complaint first is more worthwhile. The difficulty is that you must repeatedly follow up when the other party stalls.

According to the Personal Information Protection Law (China), there are several cases where a business must proactively delete data: the service stops, the agreed retention period expires, you withdraw consent, the original collection purpose has been achieved, etc. If they do not delete it, you can request deletion. If they refuse to let you exercise these rights, they must state the reason. You can sue directly in a Chinese court.
Facial scanning is not mandatory: if there are other methods, they cannot force facial scanning, and if you disagree, they must provide an alternative
A

As long as there is another way to perform the same task, the other party cannot only offer facial scanning. If you do not agree to a facial scan, they must provide an alternative such as swiping a card, a password, or an ID card, and they cannot use the excuse "then the procedure cannot be completed" to coerce you. No one is allowed to install facial recognition devices in hotel rooms, public baths, changing rooms, or restrooms.
Free. When asked to scan your face, ask "is there another verification method?". If they say no, demand they provide one. The difficulty is having to ask directly.

The Measures for the Management of Facial Recognition Technology Application Security (China) explicitly state: "To achieve the same purpose or business requirement, if there are other methods that do not use facial recognition technology, facial recognition technology shall not be used as the sole verification method. If an individual does not agree to identity verification using facial information, a reasonable and convenient alternative must be provided." These measures also state: "No organization or individual may use the excuse of completing procedures or improving service quality... to mislead, deceive, or coerce individuals into accepting identity verification via facial recognition technology." If facial information is processed based on your consent, they must obtain "separate consent, given voluntarily and explicitly on the basis of full knowledge": they must ask you specifically about this, and it only counts if you personally agree. You have the right to withdraw consent, and the processor must provide a convenient way to do so. Processing facial information of children under 14 requires consent from parents or other guardians. Installing facial recognition devices in public places "must be necessary to maintain public safety" and must have conspicuous signs. Inside private spaces in public areas such as hotel rooms, public baths, public changing rooms, and public restrooms, no organization or individual may install them. Facial information must be stored in the recognition device and not transmitted via the internet. There are two exceptions: where laws or administrative regulations provide otherwise, or where separate consent has been obtained (Nationwide China, effective from June 1, 2025).
Do not hand over source code, secret keys, or private documents to "AI relay stations" of unknown origin, especially when letting AI run commands autonomously
B

A relay station stands between you and the AI model provider; it can see and modify both the content you send and the answers you receive. A study measured over 400 relay stations: 9 stations injected malware into answers, and 17 stations accessed cloud service keys intentionally placed by the research team. For those who let AI run commands autonomously, a single modified command could lead to malware being installed on the computer.

Connecting directly to official providers is usually more expensive than relay stations, and topping up funds is not as convenient. The difficulty is that relay stations are cheap and provide a single portal to call models from many providers.

In June 2026, the Ministry of State Security (China) issued a risk warning. Some relay stations retain user data on their servers; some secretly keep it and sell it to other large model companies for training. Some stations install backdoors, implant malware into user devices, steal account keys and cloud credentials, or even install remote control programs. The warning advises using official direct connections and properly licensed platforms; do not use platforms of unknown origin, without operating licenses, or without security guarantees. When using them, mask or delete sensitive information in private data and project documents first, manage secret keys strictly, and change them periodically. If you encounter abnormal charges, groundless account locks, or abnormal data, stop using the service immediately, change keys, run virus scans, and preserve evidence.
