The authors' conclusion is that the window for testicular salvage may be longer than the often-cited 6 to 8 hour mark. Therefore, even if the pain has lasted quite a while, one must still seek treatment; do not think "it's too late anyway" and fail to go. In U.S. pediatric hospitalization data for the years 2000, 2003, and 2006, there were 2,443 boys aged 1 month to under 18 years who underwent surgery for testicular torsion. The age of onset has two peaks: one in the first year of life, and one at the beginning of puberty.
Do not postpone necessary medical treatment to "wait until after exams": some windows follow bone age, not exam schedules
A

Scoliosis is a sideways curvature of the spine. A brace is a hard-shell vest worn on the body to support and straighten the spine. When worn while bones are still growing, 75% of children do not reach a 50-degree curve by the time bone growth stops; in the observation-only group without braces, this was only 42%. The time during which a brace can be worn follows the cessation of bone growth, not the schedule for high school or university entrance exams; waiting until after exams might be too late.

Costs no money, only requires a decision to act early or late. Taking time off for follow-up visits takes time; treatment costs are separate. The difficulty lies in the fact that the brace must be worn for at least 18 hours a day, which the child must endure throughout.

A multi-center trial selected 242 adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis who met the criteria for bracing. Among them, 116 were randomized into groups, and 126 chose whether to wear a brace. The success criteria were predefined: a curve increasing to over 50 degrees was a treatment failure, while not reaching that level by the time bone growth stopped was a success. Children in the bracing group were asked to wear it for at least 18 hours a day. Results were calculated based on the original assigned groups, regardless of whether they actually wore it enough. The randomized bracing group had a 75% success rate, while the randomized observation-only group had 42% (OR = 4.11, 95% CI from 1.85 to 9.16), with the chance of success being about 4 times higher than observation alone. Combining both the randomized and preference groups, it was 72% compared to 48% (after balancing existing differences between the two groups, OR = 1.93, from 1.08 to 3.46, still about 1.9 times). The more hours worn per day, the higher the success rate (P < 0.001, this association is unlikely to be random). The trial was stopped early because the brace was clearly effective.
If a child is bullied: report it to the school on the same day and request a written resolution; if there is physical assault, theft, or rumor-mongering, report it to the police immediately
A

Children bullied by peers are about 2.2 times more likely to have suicidal thoughts than those not bullied, and about 2.6 times more likely to have attempted suicide. Upon receiving a report, the school must investigate immediately; if bullying is confirmed, they must discipline or handle it, and serious cases must not be hidden but reported to the police. Therefore, report it on the same day, request the proper determination procedure, and keep written records.

Costs no money. Meet with the homeroom teacher and the school's student bullying handling organization. If a police report is needed, call 110. The difficulty lies in standing firm against advice like "don't make a big deal out of it."

A pool of 34 studies involving 284,375 children and adolescents showed that being bullied by peers is associated with suicidal ideation, OR = 2.23 (95% CI from 2.10 to 2.37), with the chance of having these thoughts being about 2.2 times higher than for non-bullied children. An additional 9 studies involving 70,102 people showed being bullied is associated with suicide attempts, OR = 2.55 (from 1.95 to 3.34), about 2.6 times. Results were consistent across genders, ages, and study quality. Cyberbullying is more strongly associated with suicidal ideation than in-person bullying. Article 21 of the "Regulations on the Protection of Minors in Schools" (China) lists five groups of behaviors: hitting, kicking, slapping, scratching/biting, pushing, pulling; verbal abuse, ridicule, insulting nicknames; grabbing, extorting, or intentionally destroying property; intentional isolation or exclusion; and fabricating facts online to slander or spread rumors. It also stipulates that if a party with an advantage in age, physical strength, or numbers intentionally or maliciously commits the above acts, causing physical harm, property damage, or mental distress, it can be determined as bullying. Article 22 requires teachers and staff who notice students with abnormal emotions or physical injuries to promptly investigate and report. Article 23 requires schools receiving a report to investigate immediately, refer it to the bullying handling organization for determination and action, and notify parents to participate. If determined as bullying, educational disciplinary measures or disciplinary actions must be applied. Serious bullying behavior that violates public security management or shows signs of a crime must not be hidden and must be promptly reported to public security organs and education administrative departments (national China, effective from September 1, 2021).
Give children 2 hours of outdoor time daily: among no-cost, drug-free methods, this is the only myopia prevention method currently supported by randomized trials
A

First-grade students who had an extra 40 minutes of outdoor time daily saw the rate of new myopia cases drop from about four in ten to about three in ten after three years. The level set by the Health Commission (China) is at least 2 hours outdoors during the day daily, or a total of 14 hours per week. Overcast days also count.

Costs no money. However, time must be set aside every day, mostly by reducing time spent on homework and online learning. The difficulty is that it must be done every day; doing it a few times is not enough.

First-grade students at 12 primary schools in Guangzhou were randomized by school unit (952 in the intervention group, 951 in the control group, average age 6.6). The intervention consisted of one extra 40-minute outdoor activity period per school day, and parents were encouraged to take their children outside more after school. The 3-year cumulative incidence of myopia: 30.4% in the intervention group (259 cases among 853 eligible students); 39.5% in the control group (287 cases among 726 students). The difference between the two groups was −9.1 percentage points (95% CI from −14.1 to −4.1, P < 0.001); the true difference lies between 4 and 14 percentage points lower. The 3-year change in spherical equivalent refraction was −1.42 D vs −1.59 D, a difference of 0.17 D (P = 0.04). The intervention group had a slightly smaller increase in myopia. D is the unit for refractive power. No difference was found in axial length growth (the front-to-back length of the eye) between the two groups (P = 0.07). "Ten Core Knowledge Points for Myopia Prevention and Control in Children and Adolescents" (China) requires children and adolescents to have at least 2 hours of outdoor activity during the day daily, or a cumulative 14 hours per week. The document explicitly states that outdoor activities on overcast days still have a protective effect and advises avoiding peak early afternoon hours with intense sun and high heat. Pharmacological prevention of myopia also has randomized trials. In Hong Kong, 474 non-myopic children aged 4 to 9 were divided into three groups, receiving one eye drop every night for two years. The 0.05% atropine group had a 2-year myopia incidence of 28.4%, while the placebo group was 53.0%. The 0.01% atropine group was 45.9%, showing no significant difference compared to the placebo.
No screen time for ages 0 to 3, minimize it for ages 3 to 6, and no more than 1 hour daily for students for non-educational use
B

The National Health Commission (China) requires no screen time for ages 0 to 3 and to try to avoid it for ages 3 to 6. For primary and secondary students using screens for non-educational purposes, each session should not exceed 15 minutes, and the daily total should not exceed 1 hour. The reason is that prolonged near-vision work causes myopia to appear early. Evidence regarding screens and myopia is not as certain; what has been proven by trials is 2 hours of outdoor time daily.
Costs no money. The difficulty is taking the screen out of the child's hands, and the fact that parents themselves must reduce their phone use in front of the child.

The original text of the fourth point of "Ten Core Knowledge Points for Myopia Prevention and Control in Children and Adolescents" (China) is: "children aged 0–3 should not use phones, tablets, computers, and other electronic devices with screens; children aged 3–6 should try to avoid contact with and use of phones, tablets, computers, and other electronic devices with screens; for primary and secondary students using electronic screens for non-learning purposes, each session should not exceed 15 minutes, and the daily total should not exceed 1 hour." The same point clearly states that "prolonged use of electronic screen devices at a close distance easily depletes a child's hyperopic reserve, which is an important reason for the early and widespread appearance of myopia in children and adolescents." The 2018 implementation plan by the Ministry of Education and seven other departments (China) sets similar requirements for parents, adding the sentence "the younger the age, the shorter the continuous use time of electronic devices should be." Research evidence is much weaker: a systematic review collected 33 studies, with 11 included in a meta-analysis, involving subjects from 3 months to 33 years old. Considering only phones and tablets, the odds ratio for myopia was 1.26 (95% CI from 1.00 to 1.60, I² = 77%). Including computers, it was 1.77 (from 1.28 to 2.45, I² = 87%). The authors' conclusion only went as far as "there may be an association" and noted that none of the 33 studies measured screen time in a reliable manner.
View myopia as a long-term permanent injury: the higher the degree, the more retinal detachment, macular disease, and glaucoma later in life
A

Myopia does not go away on its own, and the degree cannot be reduced. It is also not just a matter of "wearing a pair of glasses." Compared to non-myopic people, the likelihood of myopic macular degeneration in those with mild myopia is over ten times higher, and in those with 6 diopters or more, it is several hundred times higher. For retinal detachment: mild myopia is about 3 times higher, and 6 diopters or more is about 13 times higher. Therefore, the deeper your child's myopia progresses, the greater the risk they must bear later.
Costs no money. This item itself requires no action; the necessary actions are in items 4 and 5 (2 hours outdoors, age-appropriate screen management).

A systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized studies prior to June 2019, dividing myopia into three levels: mild (−0.5 to −3.00 D), moderate (−3.00 to −6.00 D), and severe (≤ −6.00 D, i.e., 6 diopters or more). Compared to non-myopic individuals, the odds ratios for myopic macular degeneration were 13.57 (95% CI from 6.18 to 29.79), 72.74 (from 33.18 to 159.48), and 845.08 (from 230.05 to 3,104.34), respectively. For retinal detachment, they were 3.15 (from 1.92 to 5.17), 8.74 (from 7.28 to 10.50), and 12.62 (from 6.65 to 23.94). For posterior subcapsular cataracts, they were 1.56 (from 1.32 to 1.84), 2.55 (from 1.98 to 3.28), and 4.55 (from 2.66 to 7.75). For open-angle glaucoma: mild myopia was 1.59 (from 1.33 to 1.91), and moderate/severe myopia combined was 2.92 (from 1.89 to 4.52). The odds ratio for visual impairment after age 60 for the three levels were 1.71 (from 1.07 to 2.74), 5.54 (from 3.12 to 9.85), and 87.63 (from 34.50 to 222.58). "Ten Core Knowledge Points for Myopia Prevention and Control in Children and Adolescents" (China) states similarly: 6 diopters or more is high myopia; in this group, the incidence of blinding eye diseases such as cataracts, open-angle glaucoma, myopic macular disease, retinal detachment, and myopic optic neuropathy is significantly higher than in others, and "myopia is preventable and controllable, but not reversible."
Read the annual student health examination result sheet yourself; if any item is abnormal, take the child to the hospital for a check-up that same year
B

Primary and secondary schools organize a student health examination once a year. On the result sheet, the items to check carefully are overweight, obesity, malnutrition, abnormal spinal curvature, poor vision, and dental caries. Do not just glance at height and weight and put it away. If there are abnormalities in these items, take the child to a specialist for a clear check-up within that same year.
Costs no money. During the compulsory education stage (China), health examination fees are covered by the school's public funds; parents do not have to pay extra.

The "Management Measures for Health Examinations of Primary and Secondary School Students (2021 Edition)" (China) stipulates that primary and secondary schools organize one health examination per year for enrolled students. Surgical examinations include the head, neck, chest, spine, limbs, skin, and lymph nodes. Eye examinations include external appearance, distance vision, and refraction (myopia, hyperopia). The result sheet issued to each student must include examination results, a general assessment, and health guidance advice. Among these, overweight, obesity, malnutrition, abnormal spinal curvature, poor vision, and dental caries must be the focus of guidance. Education administrative departments must establish files for students with health problems and provide follow-up (recording and then monitoring closely). Health examination fees for students in the compulsory education stage are covered by the school's public funds; parents do not have to pay extra (national China, issued September 2021).
Have children aged 12 to 18 undergo a one-time depression screening; do not consider school psychological tests as a diagnosis
B

U.S. preventive guidelines recommend screening for major depressive disorder in children aged 12 to 18; there is insufficient evidence for those aged 11 and under. In the U.S., suicide is the second leading cause of death among children aged 10 to 19. Annual school psychological tests are only broad surveys and cannot be used for diagnosis. If a child says they feel distressed, take them directly to a psychiatric department or clinical psychology department.
From 0 to several dozen yuan, filling out a screening questionnaire at a community clinic or hospital. The two hotlines 12355 and 12356 (China) are free to call.

In 2022, the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) issued a recommendation statement. The statement recommends screening for major depressive disorder in adolescents aged 12 to 18 (Grade B recommendation). Grade B means there is moderate certainty that the net benefit is moderate, making it worth doing. There is insufficient evidence for screening major depressive disorder in children aged 11 and under (I statement, meaning evidence is insufficient to make a recommendation). For screening specifically for suicide risk in children and adolescents, evidence of benefits and harms is insufficient (I statement). The document points out that suicide is the second leading cause of death in the 10 to 19 age group. The document also indicates that major depression in children and adolescents is closely linked to many later problems. These problems include recurrent depression in adulthood, other psychiatric disorders, and an increased risk of suicidal ideation, suicide attempts, and death by suicide. "Ten Measures to Further Strengthen Mental Health Work for Primary and Secondary School Students" (China) requires the establishment of a three-tier service system: head teachers, full-time or part-time mental health teachers, and psychiatrists. Each student undergoes a psychological test each school year, usually no more than once. The document also requires promoting mechanisms for psychiatric referral and returning to school after recovery. The document requires leveraging the role of the 12355 youth support hotline and the 12356 psychological support hotline (national China, issued October 2025).
Do not purchase products or services claiming to "cure myopia" or "reduce diopters"
B

The State Administration for Market Regulation (China) states bluntly that "under current medical technical conditions, myopia cannot be cured." Advertisements using terms like "recovery," "degree reduction," "curing myopia," or "correcting diopters" must be strictly handled. If you see these words, exclude them immediately without comparing prices. Eye protection machines are medical devices; e-commerce platforms are responsible for checking whether sellers are qualified to sell them.
Costs no money; on the contrary, it saves this expense.

A notice regarding a special rectification period from November 2021 to March 2022 by the Office of the State Administration for Market Regulation (China) clearly states: "under current medical technical conditions, myopia cannot be cured." The notice requires strict legal handling of misleading terms such as "functional recovery," "rehabilitation," "degree reduction," "curing myopia," "myopia nemesis," and "correcting diopters" used to market myopia prevention and control products for children and adolescents. The notice requires strengthening the handling of acts that impersonate Traditional Chinese Medicine or use TCM theories and techniques to deceive consumers in advertisements. The notice also requires strict handling of two types of false and illegal advertisements: using the name or image of patients to compare effects before and after treatment, and providing guarantees regarding the safety and efficacy of treatment. The notice requires e-commerce platforms to strictly fulfill their responsibility to verify the business qualifications for eye protection machines and related medical devices and special goods (checking clearly whether the seller is qualified to sell) (national China).
Sleep, homework, exercise, and rankings are all regulated by written rules; if the school fails to comply, suggestions can be made
B

Official documents (China) clearly state: primary school students should sleep 10 hours a day, junior high students 9 hours, and senior high students 8 hours. Primary schools usually do not start classes before 8:20 AM, and secondary schools not before 8:00 AM. In 2025, it was further regulated that there must be at least 2 hours of physical activity daily, and ranking by test scores is prohibited. If a child suffers from chronic sleep deprivation, first compare their schedule against these rules; do not be quick to blame the child for being slow.
Costs no money. Knowing these rules is enough; when necessary, report to the school or local educational administration. The difficulty lies in speaking up.

"Notice on Further Strengthening the Management of Sleep for Primary and Secondary School Students" (China) stipulates: primary school students must sleep 10 hours a day, junior high students 9 hours, and senior high students 8 hours. Primary schools usually do not start classes before 8:20 AM, and secondary schools usually not before 8:00 AM. Schools must not require students to arrive early for collective educational activities. Primary school students should usually go to bed no later than 21:20, junior high students no later than 22:00, and senior high students no later than 23:00. Off-campus tutoring institutions must not end later than 20:30, and online livestreaming classes must not end later than 21:00. From 22:00 to 8:00 the next day, game services must not be provided to minors (national China, issued March 2021). "Ten Measures to Further Strengthen Mental Health Work for Primary and Secondary School Students" (China) adds several regulations: fully implement a total daily physical activity time for students of no less than 2 hours, and encourage the adoption of "15-minute breaks." The document also stipulates that students must not be ranked by test scores, strictly prohibits assigning mechanical repetitive homework or punitive homework, and encourages one "no-homework day" per week (national China, issued October 2025).
If a child can no longer cope, they can take a leave of absence; the school is required to maintain their enrollment status for up to 1 year
B

There is an official system for leave of absence (China). Parents or other guardians submit an application, the school confirms it, and then submits it to higher authorities for approval. Each leave is for a maximum of 1 year; if further leave is needed upon expiration, a new application must be submitted. During the leave, the school must maintain the child's enrollment status; when returning, they continue their studies. Specific procedures are regulated by each province; ask the school's academic affairs office or the local education department.
Costs no money. Parents or other legal guardians submit the application to the school. The difficulty lies in first accepting that the child needs to stop for a while.

Article 16 of the "Measures for the Management of Student Enrollment in Primary and Secondary Schools" (China) stipulates the procedures for taking a leave of absence. Student leave is applied for by parents or other legal guardians. The school confirms and submits it to the higher enrollment management authority for approval. Upon returning to school, the school must promptly complete the relevant procedures. Each leave application shall not exceed 1 year; if further leave is truly necessary upon expiration, a new application must be submitted. During the student's leave of absence, the school must maintain their enrollment status (preserving their student status and place). Specific procedures for leave and return are stipulated by provincial-level educational administrative departments (national China, issued January 2025). "Ten Measures to Further Strengthen Mental Health Work for Primary and Secondary School Students" (China) requires promoting the construction of mechanisms for psychiatric referral and returning to school after recovery, and guiding schools to establish plans for handling sudden psychological crises on campus.
If poor vision is detected, go to a hospital for cycloplegic refraction, then follow up at intervals scheduled by the doctor
B

Cycloplegic refraction involves applying a type of eye drop first to relax the ciliary muscles in the eye before measuring the degree. This is done at a hospital and is the most accurate way to diagnose myopia. The Health Commission (China) clearly states that these drops do not harm healthy eyes; once the medication is stopped, things return to normal. Do not take a single machine measurement at a glasses shop as a diagnosis, and do not avoid getting glasses for your child out of "fear of increasing the degree."

Several dozen to several hundred yuan for the examination and glasses. After cycloplegic drops, the child will be sensitive to light and have blurred near vision, which takes half a day to one or two days to resolve.

"Ten Core Knowledge Points for Myopia Prevention and Control in Children and Adolescents" (China) clearly explains what cycloplegic refraction is. First, ciliary paralytic drugs are used, then refraction is measured. Ciliary paralytic drugs are eye drops that relax the muscles responsible for accommodation in the eye. Cycloplegic refraction is a medical refraction performed in hospitals and is the "gold standard" (most accurate method) for diagnosing myopia. Cycloplegic drops do not harm healthy eyes; after use, there may be temporary light sensitivity and blurred near vision, which recovers normally after stopping the medication. Once myopia is diagnosed, intervention must be timely and appropriate, corrected by wearing glasses and other methods. Properly fitted glasses can effectively correct blurred vision and slow the progression of myopia. For glasses wearers with normal vision: preschool children and primary school students should have a follow-up every 3 to 6 months; junior and senior high school students every 6 to 12 months, deciding whether to change glasses based on the situation. Children aged 1 to 3, 4 to 6, and from 7 onwards should undergo regular refractive screening (degree measurement) to monitor hyperopia reserve (national China, issued July 2023).
Once permanent molars have erupted, perform pit and fissure sealing
A

Pit and fissure sealing involves using a resin sealant to plug the grooves on the chewing surfaces of molars so that food debris cannot get stuck. Two years after completion, the chance of developing cavities is only about one-eighth compared to no sealing. If 16% of tooth surfaces would have decayed without sealing, only about 5% do after sealing. The effect still persists four years later.
Each tooth costs several dozen to one or two hundred yuan. No anesthesia, no drilling, each session takes a few minutes. Many places have free programs for children of the appropriate age.

38 trials involving 7,924 children aged 5 to 16 were collected by Cochrane according to standard procedures and pooled for analysis. Resin-based sealants were compared with no sealing. For the first permanent molars of children aged 5 to 10, at 24 months after sealing, the OR for developing cavities = 0.12 (95% CI 0.08 to 0.19), meaning the chance of decay was only about one-eighth compared to no sealing. This result came from 7 trials with 1,548 children randomized and 1,322 children followed to the end; the quality of evidence was moderate. If the control group had 16% of tooth surfaces decayed within 24 months, it was 5.2% (from 3.13% to 7.37%) after sealing. If the control group was 40%, it was 6.25% (from 3.84% to 9.63%). If the control group was 70%, it was 19% (from 12.3% to 27.2%). At 48 to 54 months after sealing, OR = 0.21 (from 0.16 to 0.28), still about one-fifth compared to no sealing. The authors concluded that resin sealants at 24 months reduced the number of cavities by 11% to 51% compared to no sealing. In 4 trials that recorded adverse effects, none were found. There is insufficient evidence to determine which material is better among other types like glass ionomer.
If a child is obsessed with gaming: first check if sleep, homework, and outdoor exercise time are being displaced; do not just focus on counting how long they play
B

The number of people who truly reach the level of "gaming disorder" is only about two or three in a hundred. Questionnaires set low thresholds; if only adolescents are surveyed, the rate will be inflated. Actual data from gaming companies shows almost no correlation between playing time and well-being. According to regulations (China), minors are only allowed to play from 8 PM to 9 PM on Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays.
Costs no money. Check once a week: what time the child goes to bed, whether homework is submitted, and whether they go out for exercise.

A meta-analysis synthesized 53 studies across 17 countries involving 226,247 people. The prevalence of gaming disorder was 3.05% (95% CI 2.38 to 3.91). When only considering studies with more rigorous sampling, it was 1.96%. Results varied widely between studies, with 77% of the variance attributed to the type of questionnaire used. Adolescent samples, low threshold scores, and small samples all inflated the rates. Another study obtained data from 7 gaming companies, linking actual playtime over six weeks for 38,935 players with their self-reported well-being. Almost no evidence was found that playtime affects well-being. The National Press and Publication Administration (China) stipulates that gaming companies may only provide 1 hour of service to minors, from 20:00 to 21:00 daily on Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays, and statutory holidays (national China / international, since 2021).

If a child says they like someone of the same sex: do not scold, do not kick them out of the house, and do not send them for "correction"; family attitude is linked to whether the child attempts suicide
B

Among secondary school students in China, those who like the same sex or both sexes have a rate of suicide attempts within a year that is about 3 to 5.5 times higher than others. Foreign research shows that children who face strong family rejection during puberty have significantly more suicide attempts later in life. Children sent by parents for "correction" also have significantly more suicide attempts.
Costs no money. The difficulty lies in parents having to process their own emotions first and not saying harsh words in the moment.

A survey in China covered 506 secondary schools in 7 provinces, totaling 150,822 students from grades 7 to 12. The rate of suicide attempts in the past year: among male students, the group only attracted to the opposite sex was 2.2%, the group only attracted to the same sex was 6.9%, and the group attracted to both was 12.2%. For female students, the rates were 3.1%, 8.9%, and 10.9% respectively. This calculates to approximately 3 to 5.5 times higher than peers only attracted to the opposite sex. The research team adjusted for the effects of age, academic pressure, family economy, and bullying. After adjustment, the OR for these two groups in male students was 3.13 (95% CI 2.28 to 4.28) and 3.83 (2.85 to 5.14), about two to three times higher. A meta-analysis synthesizing 35 studies calculated that sexual minority adolescents have an OR for suicide attempts of 3.50 (2.98 to 4.12). A U.S. study interviewed 224 gay and bisexual young adults aged 21 to 25, asking them to recall family reactions during puberty. Compared to peers who faced almost no family rejection, those with high levels of family rejection had an OR for suicide attempts of 8.4. In another study, where parents tried to change their child's sexual orientation themselves, the OR for the child having attempted suicide was 3.08 (1.39 to 6.83). If parents also took the child to a therapist or religious leader, it was 5.07 (2.38 to 10.79) (China / multiple countries / USA).
Teach children without hitting, shouting, or calling them stupid: children who are frequently hit or scolded have more behavioral and emotional problems
A

Children who are frequently hit exhibit more aggression and psychological problems, are more distant from parents, and are more likely to be severely beaten. Evidence is unclear on whether hitting makes children obey in the moment. 13-year-olds who are frequently shouted at or called stupid have more trouble-making behavior and depression later; no amount of parental affection on ordinary days can compensate for this.

Costs no money. The difficulty lies in being able to stop one's hands and mouth when angry, and switching to a teaching method without hitting or scolding. For alternative methods, see section 17 of this chapter (parenting classes for specific techniques).

First, regarding hitting. A meta-analysis focused on one type: "spanking or hitting the hands or legs." It synthesized 75 studies, 111 effect sizes, totaling 160,927 children. Out of 17 outcomes, 13 were significantly associated with being hit, and all were in a negative direction. d is the effect size; 0.2 is small, 0.5 is medium. Aggression in childhood d = 0.37 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.61). Externalizing problems 0.41, such as hitting others or breaking rules. Internalizing problems 0.24, such as anxiety and depression. Mental health problems 0.53, poor relationship with parents 0.51, low self-esteem 0.15, poor cognitive ability 0.17. Physical abuse by parents 0.64. Antisocial behavior in adulthood 0.36, mental health problems in adulthood 0.24. Pooling all 111 effect sizes gave d = 0.33 (0.29 to 0.38). Whether the child obeyed immediately was not clearly related to being hit (d = 0.14, from −0.19 to 0.47), with only 5 effect sizes for this item. Another review looked only at longitudinal studies, totaling 69 studies. Consistent physical punishment predicted an increase in children's behavioral problems later; it was not associated with any long-term positive outcomes. Among these, 7 studies looked at the frequency of hitting; 5 found that the more hitting, the more severe the problems. Next, regarding shouting. A U.S. study followed 976 two-parent families. When children were 13, if parents frequently shouted, cursed, or called them stupid or lazy, both misconduct and depressive symptoms increased between ages 13 and 14. Whether parents were affectionate on ordinary days did not erase this link. The reverse was also true: 13-year-olds with high misconduct were scolded more later. Regarding the law (China), parents must not use domestic violence against children. Article 2 of the "Anti-Domestic Violence Law" (China) lists forms of domestic violence: beating, binding, injuring, restricting physical freedom, and frequent scolding or threats. Article 12 of this law requires guardians to conduct family education in a civilized manner. If parents violate a child's rights, neighborhood or village committees (China) must advise and stop them; serious cases must be reported to the police. If police, procuratorates, or courts discover this, they must reprimand the parents and may compel them to receive family education guidance (national China).
If a child is difficult to teach and you cannot help but hit or scold: attend a parenting course for specific techniques
A

For children who are inherently difficult to teach, after parents attend classes on specific teaching methods, the child's aggression and rule-breaking decrease, and the parents' mood improves. Hitting and scolding also decrease, most noticeably immediately after the course; the effect remains after one or two years but is much smaller. Shanghai has also trialed this type of class with effective results.

Parent schools opened by schools or kindergartens and online parent schools opened by provincial-level governments or above (China) are legally designated as non-profit. The type of class with evidence involves one session every week or two, each lasting one to two hours, for four to twenty-four weeks. Practice at home is required. The difficulty lies in completing the course and practicing daily.

Cochrane synthesized 13 trials, including 10 randomized controlled trials, totaling 1,078 parents. Children were aged 3 to 12, all with behavioral problems. The classes included were held every week or two, one to two hours per session, for at least three sessions. Short courses lasted 4 consecutive weeks, long ones 24 consecutive weeks. For parents who attended, children's behavioral problems decreased. Parents' self-assessment was SMD = −0.53 (95% CI −0.72 to −0.34), and independent external assessment was −0.44 (from −0.77 to −0.11). SMD and d are the same measure; 0.5 is medium. Parents' mental health improved, −0.36 (from −0.52 to −0.20). Negative or harsh parenting decreased; parents' self-assessment −0.77 (from −0.96 to −0.59), external assessment −0.42 (from −0.67 to −0.16). The authors stated these are short-term effects. Another meta-analysis filtered 346 randomized controlled trials, of which 60 measured behaviors like hitting or scolding, spread across 22 countries. Hitting and scolding decreased immediately after the course, d = −0.46 (from −0.59 to −0.33). After 1 to 6 months, it was −0.24 (from −0.37 to −0.11). After 7 to 24 months, it was −0.18 (from −0.34 to −0.02), becoming smaller over time. Most of this data was self-reported by parents. There have also been trials in China. 81 parents in Shanghai were randomized, with some attending Triple P group classes. After the course, children's adjustment problems, parenting methods, and parents' moods were all better than the waiting-list group, with effects remaining after 6 months. In a rural kindergarten involving 191 adult caregivers, some self-studied an online course plus two group discussions. Two weeks after the course, their self-reported child maltreatment was about 33% lower than the group only given books to read (IRR = 0.67). Three months later, children's behavioral problems also decreased (d = −0.40). The "Family Education Promotion Law" (China) requires parents to consciously learn family education knowledge. Primary schools, secondary schools, and kindergartens may open parent schools to regularly organize non-profit family education guidance. Neighborhood and village committees may open community parent schools. Provincial-level governments and above must open online parent schools and non-profit service hotlines. Family education guidance institutions must not organize for-profit training (national China, effective from 01/01/2022).

Do not send children to "internet addiction schools" or closed-management "special training camps": the law prohibits methods that cause physical or mental harm to treat internet addiction; children have been locked up until death
C

The law (China) explicitly prohibits using methods that harm a child's physical or mental health to intervene in internet addiction. A special training school in Hefei handcuffed a boy who had just arrived in a solitary confinement room; he died approximately 44 hours later. Yuzhang Academy in Nanchang locked students in solitary confinement; four people were sentenced to prison; the court rejected the parents' request for a refund of tuition fees.

Costs no money and saves a sum of tuition. The difficulty lies in the fact that when a child is at their most rebellious, parents must restrain themselves from handing the child over to outsiders for "closed-management discipline."

Article 68 of the "Law on the Protection of Minors" (China) stipulates that no organization or individual may use methods that infringe upon the physical or mental health of minors to intervene in a minor's internet addiction. The following two cases both involve court judgments. The first case occurred in Hefei, Anhui. In August 2017, the parents of an 18-year-old young man signed an agreement with a special training school to send him for internet addiction treatment. School personnel forcibly took him away, locked him in solitary confinement, and handcuffed both his hands to window bars. They restricted his food, water, and rest, and beat him. Approximately 44 hours later, the young man died. The forensic conclusion was that high temperature, restricted posture, lack of food and water, and trauma caused water and electrolyte imbalances leading to death. On October 31, 2018, the Hefei Intermediate People's Court (China) held a first-instance trial. The person in charge of the school committed the crimes of intentional injury and illegal detention and was sentenced to 16 years in prison. Four instructors were sentenced to terms ranging from 1 year to 8 years and 6 months. On December 28, 2018, the Anhui Provincial Higher People's Court upheld the original judgment in the second instance. The appeal decision clearly stated that this school was not approved by the competent authorities, and none of the defendants held teacher qualifications. The second case occurred in Nanchang, Jiangxi. Yuzhang Academy opened in 2013 and was dissolved and ceased operations in November 2017. During its operation, the school placed some students in "melancholy relief rooms" for solitary confinement under guard, locking them up for three to ten days at a time. On April 28, 2023, the Anyuan District People's Court of Pingxiang City pronounced a first-instance retrial verdict, finding five defendants guilty of illegal detention. Four were sentenced; the original text from Xinhua News Agency states "fixed-term imprisonment ranging from two years and ten months to eleven months respectively" (i.e., between 11 months and 2 years 10 months for each). These four were also banned from education-related professions for a certain period; one person was exempted from punishment. The parents demanded compensation for tuition and travel expenses, which the court did not accept (National China / Anhui / Jiangxi)

Teach children about private body parts; tell them to come home and report if they are touched by others or kept secret; believe them first when they tell you, do not scold them, take them to the police and for a medical exam
B

Children who attended sexual abuse prevention classes showed significantly more self-protective actions during drills with strangers. What they learned was still retained six months later, and the children did not become more fearful. Whether it actually reduces abuse has not yet been measured. Among child sexual abusers, acquaintances account for a high proportion, so children must be taught which areas others must not touch; if touched or kept secret, they must come home and tell.

Costs no money. Conveniently teach a few sentences while bathing or changing clothes, and occasionally ask again. The difficulty is that parents themselves are often shy about naming body parts, and when a child actually tells, parents must suppress anger to avoid scolding the child.

In 2015, Cochrane synthesized 24 trials of school-based sexual abuse prevention classes involving a total of 5,802 students aged 5 to 18. These classes mostly taught: safety rules, that the body belongs to oneself, and where private parts are. They also taught children to distinguish which types of touching are not allowed, which secrets should not be kept, and whom to tell. Many classes emphasized that if something happens, it is not the child's fault. First, looking at whether children know how to protect themselves: researchers used actors posing as strangers to lure children in 2 trials with 102 participants. Children who had learned showed protective actions with OR = 5.71 (95% CI 1.98 to 16.51), about 5.7 times the chance of children who had not learned. Converted to original text: for every 1,000 uneducated children, about 390 could do it; for educated children, about 795. Next is knowledge: 18 trials, 4,657 people, questionnaire score SMD = 0.61 (0.45 to 0.78), where 0.5 is medium. Six months later, it was still 0.69 (0.51 to 0.87). 3 studies with 795 people looked at harm: children's anxiety and fear neither increased nor decreased (SMD = −0.08, −0.22 to 0.07). 3 studies with 1,788 people looked at whether children disclosed. Disclosing past sexual abuse had an OR = 3.56 (1.13 to 11.24), increasing from about 4 per 1,000 children to about 14. However, since children in the same class or school are similar, once this was adjusted for, the difference was no longer clear (OR = 3.04, 0.75 to 12.33). The quality of evidence for all results was moderate. The authors noted that long-term monitoring is needed to know if these classes actually reduce sexual abuse. In 2018, UNESCO and five other UN agencies issued sex education guidelines. The guidelines recommend teaching children the names of body parts, including genitals, from ages 5 to 8. They also teach children which body parts are private. If someone touches them and makes them uncomfortable, they should say "no," leave, and tell a trusted adult. The guidelines state that sexual abuse is never the fault of the victimized child, even if committed by an acquaintance, a trusted person, or a family member. A sexual abuse prevention handbook by People's Daily (China) provides a memorable rule: areas covered by a tank top and shorts are not for others to look at or touch. Article 16 of the "Law on the Protection of Minors" (China) requires parents to provide safety education and enhance children's awareness and self-protection abilities. Article 40 requires schools and kindergartens to provide age-appropriate sex education. Schools and kindergartens that discover sexual abuse or harassment must not hide it and must promptly report to the police and education authorities. In 2020, the Supreme People's Procuratorate (China) and eight other agencies established a mandatory reporting system. Those required to report include staff at schools, kindergartens, hospitals, childcare facilities, neighborhood committees, village committees, hotels, etc. If they discover a child has been or is suspected of being abused during their work, they must report to the police immediately. Cases that must be reported include: genitals or private parts suspected of having abnormal injuries, girls under 14 suspected of being sexually abused, pregnancy, or miscarriage. The reporter's information must be kept secret. If a dispute arises due to reporting, the reporter bears no legal liability. In 2025, procuratorates (China) prosecuted 42,873 people for sexual abuse crimes against minors such as rape and molestation, a 5.5% decrease from the previous year. This figure accounted for 58.9% of all people prosecuted for crimes against minors. Among the cases of minor abuse prosecuted that year, 3,852 cases originated from mandatory reporting clues, accounting for 7.1%. A 2025 opinion from the Supreme People's Court (China) and 15 other agencies stated that acquaintances account for a high proportion of such cases. Some young children lack defensive awareness, and guardians are negligent, leading to children being sexually abused without even knowing it themselves (National China / Multiple countries)

Do not let children under 12 ride bicycles on the road, or those under 16 ride electric bicycles on the road: if they hit someone, parents pay; if they are hit, they may have to bear part of the responsibility themselves
B

One must be at least 12 years old to ride a bicycle on the road and 16 years old to ride an electric bicycle (China). A 14-year-old child scanned their mother's code to use a shared electric bike and hit someone, causing a grade 10 disability; the court ordered the parents to pay approximately ⟦187000⟧. If an underage child is hit while riding, even if the other party is entirely at fault, some courts rule that the child's side must bear a portion of the responsibility.
Costs no money, but requires changing the commute: parents drop off/pick up, take the bus, or walk. The difficulty is that when classmates all ride bikes, the child will make a fuss.

Article 72 of the "Regulations for the Implementation of the Road Traffic Safety Law" (China) stipulates that on roads, "drivers of bicycles and tricycles must be at least 12 years old." The same article also stipulates that "drivers of electric bicycles and motorized wheelchairs for the disabled must be at least 16 years old." Violations are subject to a warning or a fine of ⟦5~50⟧ according to Article 89 of the "Road Traffic Safety Law" (China); refusal to pay the fine may result in the vehicle being impounded. The fine is small; the important thing is the debt after an incident. Article 1188 of the 民法典 (Civil Code of China) stipulates that if a minor causes damage to others, the guardian bears the responsibility for compensation. If the child has personal assets, those are used first; if insufficient, the guardian pays. The Lianjiang County People's Court in Fujian (China) once handled a case. In May 2022, a child who had just turned 14 used their mother's account to scan a code for a shared electric bike. He hit an electric bike rider who suffered a grade 10 disability; traffic police determined he was entirely at fault. The rental company and insurance company argued that the user agreement required age 16 or older, so the child was not a legal rider and they would not pay. The court ordered the parents to pay approximately ⟦187000⟧ (specifically ⟦187017.83⟧). Children are also at a disadvantage if they are hit. A Beijing judge once wrote about a case: a 10-year-old child riding a bike after school was hit by an electric bike, resulting in a grade 10 disability; traffic police determined the other side was entirely at fault. Article 1173 of the Civil Code stipulates that if the infringed party is at fault for the occurrence of the damage, the infringer's liability may be reduced. Based on this, the court determined that since the child was under 12 and on the road without the guardian preventing it, the child's side should bear part of the damages. Injuries are also more severe. A trauma center in Israel from 2014 to 2016 hospitalized 337 children injured in traffic. Among children injured while riding electric bikes, traumatic brain injuries accounted for 13%, compared to 3% for regular bicycles. After accounting for other factors, the chance of severe injury was about 2.6 times higher than for regular bicycle riders (OR = 2.56, 95% CI 1.1 to 5.88) (National China / Fujian / Beijing / Israel)

If a child hits their head while playing sports and then has a headache, dizziness, or seems dazed: do not let them back on the field that day; if they vomit repeatedly, become increasingly sleepy, or the headache worsens, go to the emergency room immediately
B

Children with concussions who continue to play take an average of 44 days to recover; those who leave the field immediately take about 22 days. If something feels wrong after hitting the head, do not return to the field that day; wait for a doctor's permission before playing again. Persistent vomiting, increasing sleepiness (unable to wake), worsening headache, slurred speech, and seizures are all signs to seek emergency care immediately.

Costs no money. Remove the child from the field and do not allow training or competition for the rest of the day. The difficulty is when the game is intense, the child says "I'm fine," and both the coach and parents want the child to keep playing.

A concussion is a temporary disturbance in brain function after a head impact; imaging often shows nothing. A US study followed 69 athletes with sports-related concussions, average age about 15. 35 left the field immediately, recovering in an average of 22.0 days. 34 continued to play with symptoms, taking an average of 44.4 days (P=0.003, unlikely to be random). The group that continued playing had an 8.80 times higher chance of recovery lasting over 21 days than the group that left. In 2022, the International Conference on Concussion in Sport in Amsterdam issued a consensus statement. It stated that individuals showing loss of consciousness, seizures, unsteadiness, confusion, behavioral changes, or memory loss must leave the field immediately. These individuals should not return to competition or training that day. An exception is if an experienced medical professional performs an on-site exam and confirms it is not a concussion. US CDC guidelines for parents and coaches are even more direct: if there are suspicious symptoms, leave the field immediately, do not return that day, and wait for a doctor's clearance to play again. The guidelines also say not to assess the severity yourself; only medical personnel can do that. The guidelines list signs requiring immediate emergency care: seizures, not recognizing people or places, nausea, repeated vomiting, unusual behavior, increasing confusion or restlessness. Also fainting followed by increasing sleepiness, inability to wake, slurred speech, weakness or numbness in limbs. Furthermore, worsening headache that does not subside, pupils of different sizes, or double vision (USA / Multiple countries)
Check thresholds first: the age and education requirements for the twelve paths are mostly written strictly in documents
A

The thresholds for these twelve paths are mostly clearly stated in documents. To be employed, one must be at least 16 years old. Military service is for males at least 18 years old; university and college graduates can be extended to 24. Civil service exams usually require being between 18 and 35 years old with an associate degree or higher. Self-study exams have no age or education limits, but full-time students currently enrolled cannot register. Opening an individual industrial and commercial household only requires "having business capacity."
Costs no money. Spend ten minutes checking them all to see if you qualify.

For military service, see the 兵役法 (Military Service Law of China): "Male citizens who reach the age of eighteen shall be called up for active service; those not called up that year may still be called up before the age of twenty-two. The age for call-up of graduates from regular universities and colleges may be extended to twenty-four, and for postgraduates to twenty-six." For civil service exams, see Article 18 of the "Regulations on Civil Service Recruitment" (China). Conditions include "being between eighteen and thirty-five years of age" (including those exactly 35) and "having an education level of associate degree or higher." These two conditions can be adjusted if approved by civil service management authorities at the provincial level or above. Article 19 lists five groups ineligible to apply, such as those previously criminally punished for crimes, those dismissed from public office, or those on the joint punishment list for dishonesty. For firefighters, see the "Measures for the Recruitment of Firefighters of the National Comprehensive Fire and Rescue Team" (China). Article 5: "between 18 and 22 years of age" (including exactly 22; see specific recruitment notices for age limits), "having a high school education or higher." Article 6: "those with an associate degree or higher, discharged soldiers from the PLA and Armed Police... age can be extended to 24." For military civilian personnel, see Article 9 of the "Regulations on Civilian Personnel of the People's Liberation Army," basic conditions include "being 18 years old." Article 19 clearly states: the maximum age for first-time recruitment into entry-level positions is 35. Entry-level positions are those at the starting grade. For public institutions, see Article 8 of the "Regulations on the Personnel Management of Public Institutions" (China): "Public institutions recruiting new staff shall conduct open recruitment to the public." For individual industrial and commercial households, see the "Regulations on Promoting the Development of Individual Industrial and Commercial Households" (China): "Citizens with business capacity... who register as individual industrial and commercial households according to law shall apply these regulations." For self-study exams, see the "Interim Regulations on Higher Education Self-Study Examinations" (China). Article 3: "Citizens of the People's Republic of China, regardless of gender, age, ethnicity, race, and existing education level, may participate in higher education self-study examinations according to these regulations." Article 20: "Students currently studying in regular schools of all levels and types may not register for the exams." For government-funded normal students, see Article 2 of the "Implementation Measures for Government-funded Education for Integrated Undergraduate-Master's Normal Students at Normal Universities Directly Under the Ministry of Education" (China). Only six normal universities under the Ministry can recruit: Beijing Normal University, East China Normal University, Northeast Normal University, Central China Normal University, Shaanxi Normal University, and Southwest University. Undergraduate and postgraduate levels are designed as a single block with stage-based assessments; after finishing undergraduate, students continue to a master's. Tuition and dormitory fees during study are borne by the central budget, plus a living allowance. Article 5: "Recruit government-funded normal students in the early admission batch," meaning they are selected before the regular batch. For rural-oriented tuition-free medical students, see the "Notice on Doing a Good Job in Job Placement and Contract Management for Rural-Oriented Order-Based Tuition-Free Medical Students" (China). The notice states: "After being admitted and before receiving the admission notice, students must sign an agreement with the training school and the county-level health management department... and the human resources and social security department of the oriented work location." For working abroad, see the "Regulations on the Management of Foreign Labor Cooperation" (China). Article 5: foreign labor cooperation must be approved by the commerce management department and have business qualifications. Article 7, Clause 4: "Those without a legal foreign labor cooperation business qualification certificate and who have not completed registration procedures shall not engage in foreign labor cooperation." Companies without this certificate that organize people to work abroad are breaking the law. Article 8, Clause 2: "No unit or individual may use the names of commerce, tourism, study abroad... to organize laborers to work abroad." Taking orders via platforms and flexible work have no legal education threshold; for self-paid insurance and occupational injury protection, see sections 11 and 12 of this chapter. For employment, see the 义务教育法 (Compulsory Education Law of China): "Employers are prohibited from recruiting children and adolescents of compulsory education age." Article 2 of the "Provisions on the Prohibition of Using Child Labor" (China) clearly states that no person under 16 may be recruited; for sanctions, see chapter 23, section 1 (under 16 years old).
In the year you turn 18, you must register for military service before October 31; conscripts serve exactly two years
A

Military service registration is a legal obligation, not an application to join the army; registering does not mean you must go. Males turning 18 during the year must complete online registration before October 31. Failure to register results in the county ordering a correction within a time limit; if still not corrected, military service is enforced and a fine is imposed. If one actually joins, conscripts serve exactly two years.
Costs no money. Online registration takes a few minutes. If one actually joins, the cost is two years of full-time service, during which other work cannot be done simultaneously.

For registration, see the "Regulations on Military Service Registration Work" (China). The document states: "The military organs of the people's governments of counties, autonomous counties, non-districted cities, and municipal districts shall organize the initial military service registration for male citizens in their jurisdiction who reach the age of 18 before December 31 of that year, before October 31 each year." The same document states: "Initial military service registration is mainly conducted through online registration, completed by the citizens themselves on the online military service registration platform." What if one doesn't register? See Clause 1, Article 57 of the 兵役法 (Military Service Law of China). This applies to those who "refuse or evade military service registration." Sanctions are: "the county-level people's government shall order correction within a time limit; if not corrected, the county-level people's government shall enforce military service and impose a fine." Article 15 of the Military Service Law defines the target for initial registration as "male citizens who reach the age of eighteen before December thirty-first each year." Clause 2, Article 20 states "based on the needs of the military, female citizens may be called up for active service according to the above provisions." Article 15 of the "Regulations on Military Service Registration Work" states "based on the needs of the military... eligible female citizens may be organized for reserve registration." The Military Service Law also states "the term of active service for conscripts is two years." "Based on the needs of the military and personal willingness, citizens who have reached seventeen but not eighteen years of age may be called up for active service." Non-commissioned officers who "have served for twelve years or meet other conditions prescribed by the State shall be assigned jobs by the county-level or higher local people's government of the placement location." Non-commissioned officers who "have served for thirty years or reached fifty-five years of age or meet other conditions prescribed by the State shall be placed under retirement status." Job assignment means the government provides a job; retirement placement means retiring under the pension system. The "Regulations on Conscription Work" (China) state "priority shall be given to ensuring the recruitment of graduates from regular universities and colleges and those with special requirements for political, physical, or professional skill conditions." These regulations also state "citizens applying for recruitment who are currently enrolled full-time students or new graduates of the year from regular universities and colleges may apply at the location of their household registration before enrollment or the location of the school" (National)
Applying and then refusing to enlist: two years of no exit from the country, no further education or re-enrollment, and inability to enter civil service or state-owned enterprises
A

If you have registered for recruitment and then refuse to go, and fail to correct this after being ordered, the consequences are a chain reaction. You cannot be recruited as a civil servant, and state-owned enterprises and public institutions are also barred from hiring you. For two years, you cannot leave the country, pursue further education, or re-enroll, and you will be placed on the list of serious dishonest subjects in performing national defense obligations. Thus, the thought "just register first and withdraw if it doesn't work out" is a very expensive one.
Costs no money. The price is having to decide clearly whether to go or not before even registering for recruitment.

Clause 1, Point 2 of Article 57 of the 兵役法 (Military Service Law of China) covers cases where "citizens applying for recruitment refuse or evade the call-up for active service." Sanctions are also "the county-level people's government shall order correction within a time limit; if not corrected, the county-level people's government shall enforce military service and impose a fine." Clause 2 of the same article: "Those who commit the acts in Point 2 of the preceding clause and refuse to correct shall not be recruited as civil servants or personnel managed with reference to the 'Civil Servant Law of the People's Republic of China', shall not be recruited or selected as personnel for state-owned enterprises and public institutions, shall not leave the country or pursue further education or re-enrollment for two years, and shall be included in the list of serious dishonest subjects in performing national defense obligations for joint punishment." Joint punishment means multiple agencies use the same list to apply the above restrictions. Article 58 applies the same set of sanctions to those already enlisted. Military personnel who refuse to perform duties or desert their units to evade service face consequences depending on the outcome. Those removed from the military, expelled from military status, or held criminally liable according to law are punished according to Clause 2 of Article 57. Among them, those removed are also fined (National, applicable from October 1, 2021)

Students joining the military, two most certain benefits: tuition reimbursement up to ⟦20000⟧ per year, retention of student status for up to two years after discharge, and separate quotas for master's exams
A

Currently enrolled students, new graduates of the year, and newly admitted students who join the military will have their tuition for school years paid by the State. University and college students get up to ⟦20000⟧ per year, postgraduates up to ⟦25000⟧; if tuition was already lower, only the actual amount paid is reimbursed. Student status is retained during service, and re-enrollment is allowed within two years after discharge. There is also a separate plan for master's exams specifically for discharged student soldiers.
Costs no money. After discharge, submit application documents as required by the school, which may take one or two visits.

A 2024 notice from the Ministry of Finance (China) and four other agencies states that students performing military service have three systems: tuition reimbursement, repayment of national student loans used for tuition, and tuition waivers. Repayment means the State pays off this student loan for you. The limits for these three items "are adjusted accordingly to a maximum of no more than ⟦20000⟧ per person per year for university and college students, and a maximum of no more than ⟦25000⟧ per person per year for postgraduates." The new rates apply from the fall semester of 2024. Regarding how much is actually reimbursed, see this sentence: "Implemented according to the higher amount between the tuition actually paid by the student and the national student loan received (including principal and all interest accrued before full repayment)." This is followed by: "The excess portion shall not be reimbursed, repaid, or waived." Thus, the amount received each year is: take the higher of actual tuition and the student loan, then compare it to the cap and take the smaller number. If annual tuition is ⟦5000⟧, the reimbursement is ⟦5000⟧. The number of years reimbursed is based on years of study, not years of service. The "Management Measures for Student Financial Aid Funds" of 2019 (China) states: "The number of academic years completed according to regulations before enlistment is the number of years for tuition reimbursement or national student loan repayment; the remaining academic years completed after discharge and re-enrollment are the years for tuition waivers." New graduates of the year who join the military receive tuition reimbursement for the entire duration of their program. For student status, see the "Law on the Protection of Discharged Military Personnel" (China). The law states: "Active military personnel who were admitted to or studying at regular universities and colleges before enlistment shall have their admission or student status retained during active service, and may enroll or re-enroll within two years after discharge, and may transfer to other majors in the school according to State regulations." This law also states: "Universities and colleges may recruit discharged military personnel through forms such as separate plans and independent recruitment based on the State's overall arrangements." For master's exams, see the 2026 notice from the Office of the Ministry of Education (China). This plan is called the "discharged student soldier plan." The notice states: "Assigned separately within the total national master's enrollment quota, used exclusively, and shall not be converted into regular quotas or other special plans. Enrollment units determine... initial exam score requirements (usually not higher than the requirement for regular plan candidates in the same major at the unit)... under equal conditions, priority is given to candidates with longer service time." Assigned separately and used exclusively means this quota is completely set aside only for recruiting discharged student soldiers. In 2026, this plan was undertaken by 532 regular universities and colleges (National)
After discharge, only six cases are assigned jobs by the government; those seeking jobs independently must report within 30 days
A

"Being assigned a job after returning from the military" has long ceased to be common. Now only six cases are assigned jobs by the government; conscripts who serve two years and then discharge mostly do not fall into these six cases. Those not assigned jobs by the government are called independent job seekers, and this category has a hard deadline: one must report within 30 days after leaving the military. Without a justifiable reason, exceeding 30 days is considered a waiver of placement benefits.
Costs no money. Take your discharge certificate to the veterans' affairs office at the placement location once.

Article 25 of the "Regulations on the Placement of Discharged Soldiers" (China) lists six cases where the government at the placement location assigns jobs. Original text: "(1) Non-commissioned officers who have served for 12 years; (2) individuals awarded medals or honorary titles during active service; (3) individuals awarded third-class merit, second-class merit or higher during active service; (4) individuals awarded first-class commendation during active service; (5) those disabled due to combat, ranked from grade 5 to grade 8 disability; (6) children of martyrs." The regulations also state: "The government at the placement location must complete the job assignment for discharged non-commissioned officers and conscripts within 6 months of acceptance." Employers "must sign recruitment contracts or medium-to-long-term labor contracts of no less than 3 years according to regulations. Among them, enterprises accepting discharged non-commissioned officers with over 10 years of military service must sign open-ended labor contracts." Open-ended means the contract has no expiration date. During the waiting period for job assignment, they "shall be issued a monthly living allowance according to the local minimum monthly wage." If it is not your fault that you haven't been placed, you "shall be issued a monthly living allowance at a rate no lower than 80% of the average salary of personnel with similar conditions at that unit until starting work." Cases ineligible for job placement include those expelled from the Communist Party of China or those previously criminally punished. The deadline for independent job seekers is in Article 51: "Discharged non-commissioned officers and conscripts under the independent job-seeking category must report to the veterans' affairs management department of the government at the placement location within 30 days from the date of approved discharge. Without a justifiable reason, reporting more than 30 days past the deadline is considered a waiver of placement benefits." (National, applicable from September 1, 2024)
Three benefits after discharge: one-time discharge pay, military years counted as seniority, and a ⟦20000⟧ annual tax deduction for self-employment
A

There are three benefits after discharge. First is the one-time discharge payment for independent job seekers, issued based on years of service, with extra for those who performed merits. Second is that military years count as seniority; years of insurance contributions are accumulated with those from before enlistment and after discharge. Third is tax: if you open your own shop or business, for 3 years, you can reduce your taxes by a limit of ⟦20000⟧ per year; this limit can be increased by up to 20%.

Costs no money. Upon discharge, the military transfers your social insurance relationship and funds. You go to the social insurance agency (social insurance counter) at the placement location to complete the continuation procedures.

For the first benefit, see the "Regulations on the Placement of Discharged Soldiers" (China). The regulations state: "For discharged non-commissioned officers and conscripts under the independent job-seeking category, a one-time discharge payment is issued based on the number of years of active service." Who pays: "Arranged separately by the central budget, with specific rates determined and adjusted timely by the State Council's veterans' affairs management department, the Central Military Commission's political work department, and the State Council's finance department..." The extra payment ratio is divided into five levels. Medals or honorary titles add 25%; first-class merit or first-class commendation adds 20%. Second-class merit, first-class merit, or second-class commendation adds 15%. Third-class merit or second-class merit adds 10%; fourth-class merit or third-class merit adds 5%. The regulations also state: "Discharged military personnel who are not yet employed may apply for unemployment insurance benefits at the human resources and social security agency of their household registration location according to law; years of active service are treated as years of insurance contribution, except for those placed under retirement or nursing status." Treated as contribution years means you don't pay during those years but they count as if you did. For the second benefit, see the "Law on the Protection of Discharged Military Personnel" (China): "The years of active service of discharged military personnel shall be counted as seniority, accumulated with the years of work at the unit after discharge." Seniority is the number of years worked; service years and post-discharge years are added together. This law also states that years of active service and years of contribution to pension, medical, and unemployment insurance before and after enlistment "shall be calculated together according to law," and "the active service period of discharged non-commissioned officers and conscripts shall be regarded as grassroots work experience." "Military Insurance Law" (China): "The years of active service of military personnel shall be regarded as years of contribution to basic medical insurance for employees, calculated together with years of contribution to basic medical insurance for employees before enlistment and after leaving the military." For the third benefit, see Announcement No. 14 of 2023 by the Ministry of Finance, the State Taxation Administration, and the Ministry of Veterans Affairs (China). The announcement describes independent job-seeking discharged soldiers starting their own businesses: "Within 3 years (36 months, same below), each household per year may sequentially deduct from the actual value-added tax, city maintenance and construction tax, education surcharge, local education surcharge, and personal income tax payable for that year according to a limit of ⟦20000⟧. The limit can be increased by up to 20%." Deduction means taking the tax payable for the year and subtracting from it until the limit is reached; it is not a cash payment to you. For employers hiring them, "the quota rate is ⟦6000⟧ per person per year, which can be increased by up to 50%." The application period is from January 1, 2023, to December 31, 2027. If the 3-year period has not expired by the deadline, benefits continue until completion (National)
Entering the state sector is not limited to the civil service exam: completing two years in a grassroots service project allows registration for a dedicated recruitment quota of 10% annually
A

There is more than one way to enter the state sector besides the civil service exam. Completing two years in grassroots service projects such as "Three Supports and One Poverty Alleviation" (China) with a satisfactory evaluation allows you to register for a dedicated recruitment quota reserved solely for this group. Each year, provinces must allocate approximately 10% of their civil service recruitment quotas to hire from this group. Within three years of service, 10 points are also added to the total score of the first round of master's degree entrance exams. The trade-off is that during these two years, you receive a subsidy from the budget.

No monetary cost. The price is two years of service at the grassroots level in townships or towns. During these two years, you receive a budget subsidy rather than a market-based salary; the hardest part is persevering for the full two years.

The notice for the fourth round of the "Three Supports and One Poverty Alleviation" plan states "the service period is two years." The notice also states: "Provinces (autonomous regions, municipalities directly under the Central Government) must allocate approximately 10% of their civil service recruitment quotas each year to specifically recruit participants from grassroots service projects such as the 'Three Supports and One Poverty Alleviation' plan. When county and township public institutions in provinces (autonomous regions, municipalities directly under the Central Government) recruit publicly, they must, based on local conditions, reserve a certain number or proportion of positions specifically for 'Three Supports and One Poverty Alleviation' personnel who have completed their service and received a satisfactory evaluation... after recruitment, the probation period may be waived." Dedicated or specialized recruitment means this quota is only open to those who have worked in grassroots service projects; others cannot register. The same notice states: "'Three Supports and One Poverty Alleviation' personnel who have completed their service with a satisfactory evaluation and take the national master's entrance exam within three years will have 10 points added to their first-round total score, and under equal conditions, will be given priority for admission... vocational college (junior college) graduates who have completed their service with a satisfactory evaluation may be exempted from the entrance exam for top-up undergraduate programs in adult higher education." Exemption from the entrance exam means they can enter the top-up program directly. The notice further states: "Personnel without prior work experience before participating in the 'Three Supports and One Poverty Alleviation' plan, upon completing their service with a satisfactory evaluation, shall for two years enjoy the same policies as fresh graduates in terms of exams (recruitment) for agencies, enterprises, and public institutions, self-employment, household registration, and further education. The years of service at the grassroots level for 'Three Supports and One Poverty Alleviation' personnel shall be counted toward their professional seniority, with the start date of work calculated from the day they report for duty at the grassroots level." The central budget subsidy level is ⟦30000⟧ per person per year in the west, ⟦24000⟧ in the central region, and ⟦12000⟧ in the east. The Opinions of the General Office of the CPC Central Committee and the General Office of the State Council (China) state: "Personnel without prior work experience before participating in grassroots service projects, after completing their service with a satisfactory evaluation, shall for 2 years enjoy the same policies as fresh university and college graduates in terms of exams (recruitment) for agencies and public institutions, employment by various enterprises, self-employment, household registration, and further education." These Opinions also state: "Agencies at the provincial level and above recruiting civil servants, except for special positions, shall as a rule recruit from among those with 2 or more years of grassroots work experience." Another path is the Western Program. This plan is "jointly organized and implemented by the Central Committee of the Communist Youth League, the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Finance, and the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security." The plan recruits fresh university and college graduates or current graduate students to "go to the grassroots in the West to work" as volunteers "for a term of 1 to 3 years" (National).
Special post teachers who complete three years of service with a satisfactory evaluation and wish to stay must be promptly granted permanent establishment (bien che)
A

The Special Post Teacher plan (specifically designated teacher positions, China) is one of the few paths that explicitly states "granted permanent establishment upon expiration." Conditions include a bachelor's degree or higher, primarily in education, being no older than 30, and holding the corresponding teacher certificate.
